lessons.title: V3·RA1 — What actually triggers a re-render
lessons.summary: A render is not a repaint, and a state change is not automatically a render. This sector pins down the four things that actually schedule one, the bailouts that quietly stop one, and the structural moves — pass-through, colocation, keys, external stores — that decide how much of your tree runs.

# V3·RA1 — What actually triggers a re-render

By now you can make things happen on screen. `03_state_events` gave you the
setter, `06_effects` gave you the escape hatch to the outside world, and
`11_performance_patterns` gave you `memo`. What none of those told you is what
a render *is*, and that gap is where almost every "React is slow" complaint and
almost every "why didn't my UI update" bug lives.

Say the words precisely, because the imprecision is the problem:

- **Render** — React calls your component function and gets an element tree
  back. Nothing is on screen yet. It is a phone call, not a paint job.
- **Reconcile** — React compares the returned tree with the previous one and
  works out the minimum set of DOM operations.
- **Commit** — React applies those operations, then runs layout effects, then
  the browser paints, then passive effects run.

Rendering a component is cheap and pure. Committing is not. The whole cost
model of a React application follows from that split: a component that renders
and produces the same output costs you a function call and a diff, which is
usually microseconds — and a component that renders and produces different
output costs you DOM work, layout, and paint, which is not.

## Concept — the four things that schedule a render

There are exactly four, and it is worth being able to recite them:

1. A **state setter** was called on this component and the new value is not
   `Object.is`-equal to the current one.
2. A **parent rendered**, and this component's element was recreated as part of
   the parent's output.
3. A **context this component consumes** got a new value.
4. An **external store** this component subscribed to via
   `useSyncExternalStore` reported a changed snapshot.

Notice what is *not* on the list. Props changing is not on the list — props
change *because* a parent rendered, which is item 2, and a parent that renders
re-renders its children whether or not any prop actually changed. Mutating an
object that happens to be stored in state is not on the list either: nothing
called a setter, so nothing was scheduled.

## Concept — the bailouts

React has two separate ways of doing less than a full subtree render, and
conflating them causes a lot of confusion.

**The state bailout.** When you call a setter, React compares the next value
with the current one using `Object.is`. If they are equal it may skip the render
entirely:

```tsx
const [level, setLevel] = useState(5);
// Nothing is scheduled. No render, no commit, no effects.
setLevel(5);
```

The honest caveat is "may". If the update queue is empty React can compute the
next value eagerly and bail before scheduling anything. If a render is already
in flight, or if the component has other pending updates, React will render your
component once — reach the same state — and then bail out *before* re-rendering
children. You can observe this: a `console.log` in the body sometimes fires once
extra. That is not a bug and you should not build on the exact count; build on
the guarantee, which is that no *commit* happens.

**The element bailout.** During reconciliation, if React encounters an element
object that is `===` the one at the same position in the previous tree, it skips
that subtree entirely without calling the component. This is the mechanism
`memo` piggybacks on, and — crucially — it works without `memo` whenever an
element is created somewhere that did not re-render. That is the entire reason
the `children` pass-through trick in exercise 3 works.

## Concept — position, type and key

Reconciliation matches old tree to new tree **by position and element type**,
not by what the component is called in your source. Same type in the same slot
means the fiber is reused and its hook state survives. A different type, or a
different `key`, means the old fiber is unmounted (effects cleaned up, state
discarded) and a new one is mounted.

```tsx
{isEditing ? <Field label="Name" /> : <Field label="Nickname" />}
```

Both branches are a `Field` in the same position, so switching keeps the typed
text. Sometimes that is what you want and sometimes it is a bug that looks like
haunted state. `key` is the override: it is not "the thing that silences the
list warning", it is **identity**, and giving a component a key derived from
what it is editing is the cleanest state reset React offers.

## Exercise 1 — the equality bailout

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `LevelMeter({ onRender })` renders `Level: <n>` in a
`role="status"` paragraph and a `Raise` button. The level starts at `1` and is
capped at `5`. Call `onRender()` at the top of the component body — the gate
counts it. Once the level is at `5`, pressing `Raise` must schedule nothing.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — mutation schedules nothing

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `TagEditor()` renders an input labelled `New tag`, an
`Add tag` button, `Tags: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, and the tags as
list items. Adding a tag must show it. The stub pushes into the array it already
has; find out why the screen never changes.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — children survive a parent render

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Export `ReportShell({ children })` — it owns a tick
count, renders `Ticks: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, a `Tick` button, and
`{children}` — and `ReportPage({ onReportRender })`, which renders a
`HeavyReport` inside the shell. Ticking must not re-render the report:
`onReportRender` is called exactly once no matter how many ticks happen.
**`memo` is not allowed in this exercise.**

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — automatic batching

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `SavePanel({ save, onRender })` renders a `Save`
button, `Status: idle | saving | saved` in a `role="status"` paragraph and
`Saves: <n>`. Clicking `Save` sets the status to `saving`, awaits `save()`, then
sets the status to `saved` and increments the count. The gate requires exactly
three renders for one complete save: the first paint, one for `saving`, one for
`saved` **and** the incremented count together. Do not use `flushSync`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — move the state down

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `InboxScreen({ messages, onListRender })` renders a
`MessageList` (one `<li>` per message) and a composer with an input labelled
`Draft` and a `role="status"` paragraph reading `Draft length: <n>`. Typing must
not re-render the list: after five keystrokes `onListRender` has been called
once.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — key is identity

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `TabbedNotes()` renders two buttons, `Personal` and
`Work`, and a `NoteEditor` for the active tab with an input labelled `Note` and
a heading naming the tab. Each tab must get its own empty editor: type in
`Personal`, switch to `Work`, and the field is empty; switch back and it is
empty again. `NoteEditor` may not take the draft as a prop and the parent may
not store it.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — derive, do not store

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `PriceForm({ rate, onRender })` renders an input
labelled `Amount`, and `Total: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, where the
total is the amount times the rate rounded to two decimals. The gate types five
characters and requires exactly six renders — the first paint and one per
keystroke. The stub keeps the total in state and syncs it in an effect, which
costs a second render every time.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — an external store as a trigger

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Export `createBoardStore()` — a plain object with
`subscribe(listener)` returning an unsubscribe, `getSnapshot()`, `addCard()` and
`rename(title)` — and `useBoardSlice(store, selector)` built on
`useSyncExternalStore`. `CardCount({ store, onRender })` renders
`Cards: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph. Renaming the board must not
re-render it.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex8
```

## Challenge — a render budget

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `AnalyticsBoard({ rows, onShellRender,
onFilterRender, onChartRender })` renders a refresh area (`Refreshes: <n>` in a
`role="status"` paragraph and a `Refresh` button), a filter bar (an input
labelled `Filter` and `Matches: <n>`), and a chart listing the matching rows'
labels. The gate holds you to a budget:

- typing in the filter re-renders the filter bar and the chart, never the shell;
- pressing `Refresh` re-renders the shell only;
- pressing `Refresh` when the count is already at its cap of `3` renders
  nothing at all.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers challenge
```

## Review — the audit

Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. `SettingsPanel({ onHeaderRender, onFormRender,
onPreviewRender })` is written and works, and every one of the three spies fires
on every interaction. Restructure it — without changing what is on screen or
adding `memo` — so that toggling the `Compact mode` checkbox re-renders the form
and the preview only, and typing in the `Display name` input re-renders the form
only.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers review1
```

# Reading — react/v3ra01_render_triggers

## Notes

**A render is a function call.** React does not "watch" your variables. It has
no proxies, no getters, no dependency graph over your data. The only way a
component runs again is because something told React to schedule it, and the
list of somethings is short: a setter with a changed value, a parent that
rendered, a context value that changed, an external store snapshot that changed.
Every "why isn't this updating" question resolves to *none of those four
happened*, and every "why is this rendering so much" question resolves to
*number two happened more often than you thought*.

**`Object.is`, not `===`, and not deep equality.** React compares with
`Object.is`, which differs from `===` in exactly two places: `Object.is(NaN,
NaN)` is `true` and `Object.is(0, -0)` is `false`. Neither matters often. What
matters constantly is that it is a *reference* comparison for objects, so a
freshly built array with identical contents is a changed value, and a mutated
array with different contents is an unchanged one. Those two facts are ex2 and
half of `d21_memoization`.

**Render is not commit.** A component can render output identical to last time;
React diffs it, finds nothing to do, and touches no DOM. That is why "reduce
re-renders" is bad advice stated baldly: the number that matters is *work done
during renders*, and a hundred renders returning three spans is nothing next to
one render rebuilding a thousand list items.

**Elements are values, and identity survives.** `<HeavyReport />` evaluates to a
plain object: `{ type: HeavyReport, props: {...}, key: null, ... }`. It is
created wherever the JSX is written. If a parent re-renders but a particular
element object came from *somewhere else* and was merely passed through as a
prop, React sees the same object in the same position and skips the subtree
without calling the component. That is the pass-through trick, and it is memoization
you get without a hook because the memoized thing was never rebuilt.

**Automatic batching is universal since React 18.** Before 18, multiple setters
were batched inside React event handlers and *not* inside promises, timeouts or
native event listeners — so a `.then` with three setters rendered three times.
That inconsistency is gone. All updates in the same tick are batched, wherever
they originate. `flushSync` opts out for the rare case where you must read
layout between two updates, and it costs you a synchronous commit and paint.

**Position beats naming.** Reconciliation walks two trees in parallel comparing
`type` and `key` at each position. The same component at the same position means
reuse, even if you wrote the two branches of a ternary as if they were
unrelated; anything else is unmount plus mount. Moving a component to a
different depth — wrapping it in a conditional `<div>` — is a remount, and that
is the classic "my input lost focus when I toggled the wrapper" bug.

## ex1 — a bailout you can see

`setLevel(5)` when the level is already `5` schedules nothing. Written as
`setLevel(Math.min(level + 1, 5))` the cap falls out naturally, but the honest
version is the updater: `setLevel((current) => Math.min(current + 1, 5))`, which
does not read `level` from the closure and therefore behaves correctly even if
two clicks land in the same batch.

The subtlety worth knowing for interviews: React's guarantee is about the
commit, not the render. If React cannot compute the next state eagerly — because
there is already a queued update on this fiber — it renders your component,
discovers the state did not change, and bails out before touching children. Your
render spy may therefore see one extra call in some sequences. Never assert on
"zero renders"; assert on "the DOM did not change" or on children not rendering.

## ex2 — the update that was never scheduled

`tags.push(next)` mutates the array React is already holding. No setter ran, so
nothing is scheduled; and even if you follow it with `setTags(tags)`, the
argument is `Object.is`-equal to the current state, so React bails out. The
array now contains the new tag and the screen does not. This is the failure mode
that convinces beginners React is unreliable.

`setTags((current) => [...current, next])` fixes both halves at once: it is a new
array, so the comparison fails and a render is scheduled, and it reads the
current value from React rather than from a closure, so two rapid adds in one
batch both land.

## ex3 — memoization without a hook

The stub renders `<HeavyReport />` inside the same component that owns the tick
state, so every tick rebuilds that element and React calls `HeavyReport` again.
Splitting the state into `ReportShell` and passing the report as `children`
moves the element's creation into `ReportPage`, which never re-renders — so the
`children` prop is literally the same object, and reconciliation stops at it.

The point is not the trick, it is the principle: **wrap, do not nest**. A
component that owns frequently changing state should render `{children}` rather
than know what is inside it. Unlike `memo`, that cannot be defeated by someone
adding an inline object prop next month.

## ex4 — one commit, two updates

The interesting half is after the `await`. In React 17 that continuation was
outside React's batching window, so `setStatus("saved")` and `setSaves(n + 1)`
committed separately and a careful observer could see the count update after the
label. React 18's automatic batching made all of it one commit, everywhere.

The second thing this exercise pins down is that `saves` must be incremented
with the updater form. After an `await`, the `saves` variable in scope is the one
captured when the handler started — a stale closure. It happens to be right
here, and it stops being right the moment a second save overlaps the first.

## ex5 — colocation is the cheapest optimisation

The draft text belongs to the composer and nothing else reads it, so keeping it
in `InboxScreen` means every keystroke re-renders the message list for no
reason. Moving `useState` into `Composer` ends the problem structurally: the
list is not in the composer's subtree, so it is not part of the render.

The rule to carry: **state should live at the lowest common ancestor of the
components that read it, and no higher.** Reach for that before reaching for
`memo`, always. Memoizing a list to protect it from state that should never have
been above it is treating the symptom.

## ex6 — the same editor, twice

`{tab === "personal" ? <NoteEditor title="Personal" /> : <NoteEditor
title="Work" />}` puts a `NoteEditor` in the same position in both branches, so
React reuses the fiber and the typed draft leaks across tabs. `key={tab}` makes
the two elements different identities, so switching unmounts one and mounts the
other with fresh state.

This is the sanctioned way to reset state on a prop change, and it is much
better than the `useEffect` that sets state back to its initial value: it has no
extra render, no intermediate frame showing the stale value, and it resets
*everything* in the subtree rather than the one field you remembered.

## ex7 — the extra render pass

Storing `total` in state and syncing it with an effect means every keystroke
does: render with the old total, commit, run the effect, set state, render
again, commit again. Two commits per keystroke, and between them the screen
briefly shows a total that does not match the amount. Computing
`amount * rate` during render is one pass, always consistent, and deletes a
hook and an effect.

The counter-argument is "but it is expensive". It is not at these sizes, and
when it genuinely is, the answer is `useMemo` — still derived, still one pass.

## ex8 — subscribing to a slice

`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot)` is React's official bridge to
anything that lives outside React: a Redux-shaped store, `window.matchMedia`,
the URL, a WebSocket. React calls `getSnapshot` after every notification and
re-renders only when the returned value differs by `Object.is`.

That last clause is the exercise. A `getSnapshot` returning `store.getState()`
re-renders on every write, rename included; one returning
`store.getState().cards.length` returns a number, and renaming leaves it alone.
The hazard is a selector that builds a fresh object or array: never
`Object.is`-equal, so React re-renders forever. Select primitives, or cache the
derived object in the store.

## challenge — three moves, one budget

Each clause of the budget maps to one idea: the chart is filtered data so it
must follow the filter; the shell's tick must not reach the filter or the chart,
which is the pass-through; the filter's query must not reach the shell, which is
colocation; and the capped refresh renders nothing, which is the bailout. The
value of stating it as a budget is that it forces you to reason about the tree
shape before writing a line, which is the actual professional skill.

## review1 — reading a profile

The audit is the same three moves applied in reverse: you are handed the counts
and have to infer the structure. The compact-mode flag is read by the form and
the preview, so it belongs to their common ancestor and no higher — the header
must not be in its subtree. The display name is read by the form only, so it
belongs in the form. Nothing here needs a memoization hook, which is exactly the
lesson.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Render and Commit](https://react.dev/learn/render-and-commit)
- [react.dev — State as a Snapshot](https://react.dev/learn/state-as-a-snapshot)
- [react.dev — Preserving and Resetting State](https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state)
- [react.dev — `useSyncExternalStore`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore)
- [react.dev — `flushSync`](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/flushSync)
- [React 18 — Automatic batching](https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/21)
- [MDN — `Object.is()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/is)

# V3·RA1 — What actually triggers a re-render (archive) ## The model in one page React is a pull system pretending to be a push system. Nothing in your data is observed. When something schedules work on a fiber, React re-runs that component and everything beneath it that it cannot prove is unchanged, then diffs the result against the previous tree and applies the difference. Three phases, three costs: | Phase | What happens | Typical cost | | --- | --- | --- | | Render | Your function runs; JSX becomes element objects | microseconds | | Reconcile | Old tree vs new tree, by position/type/key | microseconds | | Commit | DOM mutations, layout effects, then paint | milliseconds | The reason this table matters is that most performance advice about React is about phase one, while most of the cost is in phase three. A component that re-renders and returns structurally identical output commits nothing. ## The four schedulers ```tsx setCount(1); // 1. state, if the value changed // 2. the parent rendered const theme = useContext(ThemeContext); // 3. the context value changed useSyncExternalStore(sub, snap); // 4. the snapshot changed ``` Everything else is one of these wearing a costume. A prop changed? A parent rendered. A ref changed? Nothing was scheduled — that is what refs are for. A module-level variable changed? Nothing was scheduled, and your UI is now lying. ## Worked example — the pass-through ```tsx // Before: every tick calls HeavyReport again. function ReportPage({ onReportRender }: { onReportRender: () => void }) { const [ticks, setTicks] = useState(0); return ( <>

Ticks: {ticks}

); } ``` `` is created inside the component that re-renders, so a new element object is produced every tick and React calls the function again. Move the state up into a wrapper and hand the report in as `children`: ```tsx function ReportShell({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { const [ticks, setTicks] = useState(0); return ( <>

Ticks: {ticks}

{children} ); } function ReportPage({ onReportRender }: { onReportRender: () => void }) { return ( ); } ``` `ReportPage` never re-renders, so the element it created is the same object on every tick, so reconciliation stops there. No `memo`, no dependency array, nothing to keep in step later. ## Worked example — the batching boundary ```tsx async function handleSave() { setStatus("saving"); // ─┐ one render setError(null); // ─┘ await save(); setStatus("saved"); // ─┐ one render (React 18+) setSaves((n) => n + 1); // ─┘ } ``` Two commits, four setters. In React 17 the second pair was two commits because the continuation ran outside React's batching window. If you truly need a commit between two updates — you want to measure the DOM after the first — `flushSync` forces one, and you pay for a synchronous render, commit and layout. ## Worked example — a store snapshot that loops ```tsx // Wrong: a new array every call, so the snapshot is never equal. const visible = useSyncExternalStore( store.subscribe, () => store.getState().cards.filter((c) => !c.archived), ); ``` React calls `getSnapshot` during render and again after each notification, and compares with `Object.is`. A fresh array fails that comparison forever; in a concurrent render React detects the instability and throws "The result of getSnapshot should be cached". Return a primitive, or cache the derived value inside the store and return the cached reference. ## Worked example — the reset that is not an effect ```tsx // Two commits, and one frame showing the previous user's draft. useEffect(() => setDraft(""), [userId]); // One pass, and it resets everything below, not only what you named. ``` The `key` version discards the fiber, so the hook list goes with it. That is the difference between "I remembered to clear the four fields I could think of" and "the component is new". ## Common mistakes - **Mutating state and then setting it.** `list.push(x); setList(list)` — the push worked, the render did not, and the bug survives a refactor because the data really did change. - **Believing props trigger renders.** They do not. Parents do. A child whose props are byte-identical still renders when its parent does, unless the element was not rebuilt or `memo` proves the props are equal. - **Storing derived state.** Any `useState` whose only writer is a `useEffect` that reads other state is a second render pass and an inconsistent frame. - **Using `key={index}`.** Indexes are positions, not identities. Reordering or deleting shifts every subsequent item's identity, so state, focus and animations attach to the wrong rows. - **Resetting with an effect instead of a key.** `useEffect(() => setDraft(""), [id])` shows the previous draft for one frame and resets only what you remembered to reset. - **Asserting on exact render counts of the component you are bailing out of.** React's guarantee is about the commit and about children. Assert there. - **`flushSync` in an event handler "to be safe".** It disables batching and forces a paint. Use it when you must read layout between updates, and nowhere else. ## Interview answer > **"What causes a React component to re-render?"** > > Four things: its own state changed to a value that is not `Object.is`-equal to > the previous one; its parent re-rendered and rebuilt its element; a context it > consumes got a new value; or an external store it reads through > `useSyncExternalStore` reported a new snapshot. Props are not on that list — > props change because a parent rendered, and a parent rendering re-renders > children regardless of whether their props changed. > > The important follow-on is that rendering is not the expensive part. React > renders, diffs, and only commits what actually differs. So the goal is not > "fewer renders", it is "less work in the render and less to commit". The > structural tools are cheaper than the memoization ones: put state at the > lowest component that reads it, and pass expensive subtrees through > `children` so their elements are not rebuilt when the stateful wrapper > re-renders. Both of those work without a hook and cannot be silently defeated > by an inline object prop later. ## Check yourself 1. Name the four things that schedule a render, without looking. 2. Why is `Object.is` the comparison and where does it differ from `===`? 3. A component renders 200 times a second and commits nothing. Is that a problem? What would make it one? 4. `setUser(user)` after `user.name = "Ada"`. What appears on screen, and why? 5. Explain why passing a subtree as `children` behaves like `memo` without a hook. What defeats it? 6. When does changing a `key` unmount a component, and what exactly is lost? 7. Two `` elements in the two branches of a ternary. Does the typed text survive the switch? Why? 8. Four setters, two before an `await` and two after. How many commits in React 17? In React 19? 9. When is `flushSync` the right answer, and what does it cost? 10. Why must `getSnapshot` return a cached or primitive value? 11. Your list re-renders on every keystroke in an unrelated input. Give two fixes and say which you would do first. 12. What is the difference between "a render was scheduled" and "a render happened"? 13. Why is `key={index}` wrong for a reorderable list but harmless for a static one? 14. You add `memo` to a component and nothing changes. Name three causes.

# Long reading — react/v3ra01_render_triggers

## What a fiber is, and why it explains everything

React's internal representation of your UI is a tree of **fibers**. One fiber
per element instance: a mutable object holding the component type, the current
props, a pointer to the DOM node if there is one, the list of hooks, a queue of
pending state updates, and links to its parent, first child and next sibling.
The fiber is the thing that persists across renders. Your component function is
just a recipe that React runs to find out what the fiber's children should be.

That single fact answers most of the questions in this sector.

*Why does state survive a re-render?* Because it lives on the fiber, in a linked
list of hook objects, and the fiber was reused.

*Why do the rules of hooks exist?* Because React walks that linked list
positionally — the first `useState` call in this render gets the first hook
object from the last render. A conditional hook call shifts the whole list.

*Why does changing a `key` reset state?* Because React could not match the new
element to the existing fiber, so it created a new fiber. New fiber, new hook
list, no state.

*Why does moving a component to a different tree position reset it too?* Same
reason. Position is part of identity.

React keeps two trees: `current`, the one on screen, and `workInProgress`, the
one being built. Rendering builds the work-in-progress tree by walking down from
the scheduled fiber, calling components, and creating or reusing child fibers.
Committing swaps the pointers and applies the collected list of DOM effects.
This is why a render can be thrown away — nothing the user can see has happened
yet — and that discardability is the foundation the concurrent features in
`v3ra08_concurrent_features` are built on.

## From `setState` to pixels

Call a setter and React does not render. It **schedules**. Concretely:

1. The update is pushed onto that hook's queue on the fiber, tagged with a lane
   — a bitmask encoding priority. A click is a discrete, high-priority lane; an
   update inside `startTransition` is a low-priority one.
2. React marks the fiber and every ancestor as having pending work, then asks
   the scheduler for a callback at the appropriate priority. Nothing has run
   yet, which is why reading state immediately after setting it gives you the
   old value: the variable in your closure belongs to a render that already
   happened.
3. If the queue for that hook was empty, React tries the **eager state**
   optimisation: it computes the next value right there and, if `Object.is`
   says it equals the current one, it does not mark anything and there is no
   work at all. This is the fast path of the bailout.
4. At the scheduled time React renders from the root, but skips subtrees with no
   pending work. Your component runs, hooks are read positionally from the fiber,
   JSX becomes element objects.
5. Reconciliation compares children by position and by `type`/`key`. Identical
   element references short-circuit the whole subtree. Matching type and key
   reuses the fiber and re-runs the child. Anything else deletes and creates.
6. Commit runs in three sub-phases: *before mutation* (snapshots), *mutation*
   (the actual DOM operations, plus running the previous layout effects'
   cleanups), and *layout* (`useLayoutEffect` bodies and ref attachment). The
   browser paints after that. Passive effects — `useEffect` — are flushed
   asynchronously afterwards, which is why an effect never blocks the first
   paint.

## A short history, because the API shape is a fossil record

The class era had `shouldComponentUpdate` and `PureComponent`, and the mental
model was explicit: React asks the component whether it wants to render. Hooks
inverted that. `memo` is the surviving descendant of `PureComponent`, and it is
deliberately opt-in and shallow, because the framework decided that "render by
default, prove otherwise" is safer than the other way round.

React 16 introduced fibers and made rendering interruptible in principle.
React 17 shipped almost nothing user-facing and existed to make the upgrade to
18 possible. React 18 turned interruptibility on: concurrent rendering,
automatic batching everywhere, `useSyncExternalStore` (added specifically
because external stores could **tear** — show two different values from the same
store in one paint — once rendering could be interrupted), and transitions.
React 19 added `use`, actions, `useOptimistic`, ref as a prop, and ref cleanup
functions, and it is the version where the React Compiler became usable.

The compiler matters to this sector because it changes the advice, not the
mechanism. It analyses your components and inserts memoization automatically, so
the hand-written `useMemo`/`useCallback` that exists purely to keep an element
or callback identity stable becomes unnecessary. What it cannot do is restructure
your tree: it will not colocate your state, it will not convert nesting into a
`children` pass-through, and it will not tell you that you stored derived state.
Those are design decisions, and they are the ones this sector is about.

## Performance notes

**Render cost is roughly linear in the number of components rendered, and the
constant is small.** Ten thousand trivial components will show up in a profile;
a hundred will not. Before restructuring anything, open the React DevTools
Profiler, turn on "Record why each component rendered", and look at the flame
graph. The component with the widest bar is the one to fix; the one that renders
most often frequently is not.

**Commit cost is where the milliseconds are.** A render that produces the same
tree commits nothing. A render that rebuilds a large list commits a lot, and if
that commit changes layout, the browser recalculates styles and reflows.
Long lists want windowing, not memoization.

**Colocation is free and permanent.** Moving state down removes components from
the render path entirely rather than making them cheaper to skip. It costs no
runtime work, has no dependency array to get wrong, and survives the next person
who adds a prop.

**The pass-through has one real limitation.** The subtree passed as `children`
cannot read the wrapper's state, by construction. If it needs to, you are back to
context or props, and back to paying for renders. That limitation is a feature:
it makes the data flow visible in the tree shape.

**Bailouts stop at the first component that has its own pending work.** If a
parent bails out but a grandchild has queued state, that grandchild still
renders. Bailing out is not a subtree-wide veto, it is per-fiber.

## When not to use this

**Do not optimise a render path you have not measured.** Every technique here
has a cost: pass-through changes your component boundaries, colocation can push
you into prop-drilling when a second consumer appears, and `useSyncExternalStore`
brings a whole external state container into a codebase that may have been fine
with `useState`.

**Do not use `useSyncExternalStore` for state React can own.** It exists for
state that already lives outside React: a third-party store, a browser API, a
mutable cache shared with non-React code. Reaching for it because you want
selector-based subscriptions in a component tree that could simply have been
restructured is a large increase in machinery for a small win.

**Do not use `key` as a general reset button.** It is right for "this is now a
different thing" — a different record, a different tab, a different user. It is
wrong for "I want to clear one field", where a plain setter in the handler is
clearer and cheaper than throwing away a subtree.

**Do not chase render counts as a metric.** They are an input to a diagnosis,
not a target. The right target is the profiler's committed duration and the
user's perception of responsiveness, and a component that renders twice as often
but commits nothing is not a regression.

**Do not reach for `flushSync` to fix ordering problems.** If two updates must
be observed together, they should be one piece of state — a reducer, or an
object — not two setters forced into two commits.

## Exercise 1 — the equality bailout

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. Export `LevelMeter({ onRender }: { onRender: () =>
void })`.

It renders `Level: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph and a button reading
`Raise`. The level starts at `1`. Pressing `Raise` adds one, up to a maximum of
`5`. Call `onRender()` as the first statement of the component body — the gate
counts the calls.

The point of the exercise is the cap. Once the level is `5`, pressing `Raise`
must schedule no update at all: the gate presses it three more times and
requires that the number of commits does not grow and that no child work
happens.

Concretely, for the sequence *mount, Raise ×5, Raise ×3*:

- the paragraph reads `Level: 5`;
- the last three presses change nothing on screen.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are not being asked to add an `if`. You are being asked to write the update
so that, at the cap, the value you hand React is the value React already has.
React compares the next state with the current one using `Object.is` before it
schedules anything.

## Hint 2

`Math.min` is the whole trick. Here it is in a different shape — a volume
control that will not go below zero:

```tsx
const quieter = () => setVolume((current) => Math.max(current - 10, 0));
```

At zero, `Math.max(-10, 0)` is `0`, which is what the state already is, so
pressing the button again does nothing at all.

## Hint 3

Write `raise` with the updater form of the setter — `setLevel((current) =>
…)` — and clamp inside it. The decision left to you is what the maximum should
be: a magic `5` inline, or a named module-level constant that the paragraph and
the clamp can both refer to. Prefer the one that will still be right when
someone changes the cap to `10`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the failure. Write the naive version, `setLevel(level + 1)` with an
`if (level < 5)` guard, and describe what happens on the sixth press: the guard
is false, so no setter runs, so nothing is scheduled. That also passes. So why
does the exercise exist?

## Hint 2

Because the guard version is a different mechanism, and it stops working the
moment two presses land in the same batch. `level` in the guard is a snapshot
from the render that created the handler. React's own bailout does not read a
snapshot — it compares against the value in the update queue at the moment it
processes it.

## Hint 3

So express the cap as part of the *value*, not as a condition around the call.
An updater receives the current state and returns the next one; if what it
returns is already the current state, React discards the update. That is one
rule doing two jobs: it clamps and it bails out.

## Exercise 2 — mutation schedules nothing

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. Export `TagEditor()`.

It renders:

- an input labelled `New tag` (a `<label>` with `htmlFor`, not a placeholder);
- a button reading `Add tag`;
- `Tags: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph;
- a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per tag, showing the tag text.

Typing `alpha` and pressing `Add tag` must leave the input empty and the list
reading `alpha`, with the status paragraph reading `Tags: 1`. A blank or
whitespace-only tag is ignored — the count does not move and the input is left
as it is.

The stub does `tags.push(draft)` followed by `setTags(tags)` and renders
nothing new. Understand why both halves of that line are broken before you
replace it.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate things went wrong in `tags.push(draft); setTags(tags)`, and fixing
only one of them still leaves you with a component that does not update. Name
both before you write anything: what did `push` do to the array React is
holding, and what does `setTags` compare its argument against?

## Hint 2

Here is the same shape for an object rather than an array — a settings record
gaining a key:

```tsx
setSettings((current) => ({ ...current, [key]: value }));
```

Nothing is mutated. A new object goes in, so the `Object.is` comparison against
the old one fails, so a render is scheduled.

## Hint 3

Build the next array from the current one with a spread and pass it to the
setter. Use the updater form so you read the current tags from React rather
than from the closure. The decision left to you is where the "ignore blank
tags" rule lives — in the click handler before you call the setter, or inside
the updater. One of those makes the rule visible at the call site; pick
deliberately and be consistent.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Add `console.log(tags)` inside the component body of the broken stub and click
`Add tag` twice. The log does not fire at all — which tells you the component
never re-rendered, which tells you no update was ever scheduled. That is the
whole diagnosis.

## Hint 2

`Object.is(tags, tags)` is `true`. It does not matter that the contents changed;
React compares the reference it was handed with the reference it is storing, and
they are the same object because you mutated it in place. This is the single most
common React bug, and it survives code review because the data really did
change.

## Hint 3

The fix is a rule you can apply without thinking: **never write to something
that is in state.** Every update produces a new value. For arrays that means
`[...current, x]`, `current.filter(...)`, `current.map(...)` and
`current.toSorted(...)` — never `push`, `splice`, `sort` or index assignment.

## Exercise 3 — children survive a parent render

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Export two components.

`ReportShell({ children }: { children: ReactNode })` owns a tick count starting
at `0` and renders `Ticks: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, a button reading
`Tick`, and `{children}`.

`ReportPage({ onReportRender }: { onReportRender: () => void })` renders a
`HeavyReport` inside the shell. `HeavyReport` calls `onReportRender()` at the
top of its body and renders a `Quarterly report` heading.

The gate presses `Tick` four times, requires the paragraph to read `Ticks: 4`,
and requires `onReportRender` to have been called **exactly once** — the mount.

`memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` are not allowed in this file. The whole
exercise is that you do not need them.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

React calls a child component again because the parent produced a *new element
object* for it. Ask a narrower question than "how do I stop the report
rendering": which component's render creates the `<HeavyReport />` element, and
does that component re-render when you press `Tick`?

## Hint 2

An element is an ordinary value and can be created anywhere. This is legal and
does exactly what it looks like:

```tsx
const banner = <Announcement text="Maintenance at 22:00" />;
return <Layout slot={banner} />;
```

If the component that wrote that `const` does not re-render, `banner` is the
same object next time, and React skips it during reconciliation.

## Hint 3

Split the file: the tick state goes in `ReportShell`, which renders
`{children}` and knows nothing about reports; `ReportPage` renders
`<ReportShell><HeavyReport … /></ReportShell>` and holds no state at all. The
decision left to you is whether `HeavyReport` lives in this file as a local
component or is exported too — the gate only requires the two named exports, so
choose on readability.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about *where the JSX is written*, not about what is nested inside what.
Nesting in the rendered output and nesting in the source are different things,
and this exercise is the clearest demonstration of the difference you will get.

## Hint 2

Reconciliation compares the new children with the old ones. Before it compares
props, it checks whether the element is literally the same object as last time.
If it is, that subtree cannot have changed — nothing rebuilt it — so React does
not descend into it at all. `memo` is a way of *simulating* this when the
element genuinely was rebuilt.

## Hint 3

So the goal is to arrange for the report's element to be created by a component
that does not re-render. The component that owns the tick state always
re-renders. Therefore the report's element must be created *above* it and
handed down. `children` is the prop for that, and it needs no special
treatment: it is an ordinary prop that JSX fills in for you.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — automatic batching

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. Export `SavePanel({ save, onRender }: { save: () =>
Promise<void>; onRender: () => void })`.

It renders a button reading `Save`, `Status: <status>` in a `role="status"`
paragraph where the status is `idle`, `saving` or `saved`, and a paragraph
reading `Saves: <n>` starting at `0`. Call `onRender()` at the top of the body.

Clicking `Save` sets the status to `saving` and clears any error, awaits
`save()`, then sets the status to `saved` and increments the count. If `save()`
rejects, the status becomes `failed` and the count does not move.

The gate performs one successful save and requires **exactly three** calls to
`onRender`: the initial render, one commit for going to `saving`, and one commit
that carries `saved` and the new count together. `flushSync` is not allowed.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three renders for four setter calls means the setters are being grouped. You do
not have to do anything to make that happen — but you do have to not accidentally
break it, and there is one line in the naive version that is a stale read rather
than a batching problem.

## Hint 2

React groups every update in the same tick into one commit, including after an
`await`. What it cannot do is give you a fresh value for a variable your handler
captured before the await:

```tsx
async function submit() {
  setBusy(true);
  await send();
  // `attempts` here is the value from the render that created this handler.
  setAttempts(attempts + 1);   // wrong under overlapping submits
  setAttempts((n) => n + 1);   // right
}
```

## Hint 3

Write the handler as a plain `async` function: set status and clear the error,
`await save()` in a `try`, then set status and bump the count with the updater
form; set the failure status in the `catch`. The decision left to you is whether
the error text is a second piece of state or is implied by the status — the gate
only reads the status, so pick the shape you would defend in review.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Count the commits by hand before you write anything. Mount is one. The two
setters before the `await` run in the same tick, so that is two. The two after
the `await` also run in the same tick as each other, so that is three. If you
measure four, something split a pair.

## Hint 2

The way people split a pair is by putting an `await` between two setters, or by
calling one of them inside a `.then` and the other outside it. Keep the pairs
adjacent, with nothing asynchronous between them.

## Hint 3

The other way is `flushSync`, which is banned here precisely because it is the
tempting wrong answer. It forces React to render and commit synchronously before
returning, so a `flushSync` around the first setter gives you a fourth commit and
a forced layout. It exists for the case where you must read the DOM between two
updates, and this is not that case.

Ask who reads the draft. Write down every component that uses the value. If the

## Hint 2

A component that renders is one whose parent rendered. Here is the shape you are

```tsx
function Page({ rows }: { rows: Row[] }) {

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the render path. A keystroke sets state on whichever component owns
it. React then re-renders that component and everything it produces elements
for. Draw that subtree for the stub and the list is inside it.

## Hint 2

There are only two ways to get the list out of that subtree: stop the parent
from rebuilding the list's element (the `children` pass-through from exercise 3),
or stop the parent from re-rendering at all (move the state into a sibling).
Both work here. One of them is a smaller change and leaves the file easier to
read.

## Hint 3

Prefer the move. Colocation removes the list from the render path completely
rather than making it cheaper to skip, and it makes the ownership of the draft
obvious to the next reader. The general rule: **state belongs at the lowest
common ancestor of the components that read it, and no higher.**

## Exercise 6 — key is identity

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export `TabbedNotes()`.

It renders two buttons, `Personal` and `Work`, and below them a `NoteEditor` for
the active tab. `NoteEditor({ title }: { title: string })` renders an `<h2>`
with the title and an input labelled `Note`, and owns its draft text in its own
`useState`.

Each tab must have its own editor:

- type `hello` on `Personal`, switch to `Work` — the field is empty;
- type `report` on `Work`, switch back to `Personal` — the field is empty.

`NoteEditor` may not take the draft or a setter as a prop, and `TabbedNotes` may
not store any draft text. `Personal` starts active.

The stub renders `active === "personal" ? <NoteEditor title="Personal" /> :
<NoteEditor title="Work" />` and the text follows you between tabs. Work out why
before you fix it.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

React matched the new `NoteEditor` to the old one and reused its fiber, which is
where the draft lives. Reconciliation matches by *position and element type*, and
in both branches of that ternary the editor is the same type in the same
position. The title prop changed; nothing about identity did.

## Hint 2

`key` is not only for lists. It is the manual override for identity anywhere:

```tsx
<ProfileForm key={selectedUserId} user={selectedUser} />
```

Selecting a different user unmounts the old form and mounts a new one, so every
piece of internal state in it — drafts, validation, scroll position — starts
clean, with no effect and no reset code.

## Hint 3

Give the editor a `key` derived from the active tab. The decision left to you is
whether to keep the ternary or to render a single `<NoteEditor>` whose `title`
and `key` both come from the active tab — the second is shorter and makes the
identity relationship impossible to miss.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as a question about what React throws away. Unmounting a component
discards its fiber, and the fiber is where the hook list lives. So the question
"how do I reset this state" is the same question as "how do I make React decide
this is a different component instance".

## Hint 2

There are exactly three ways to get a new fiber in a given slot: render a
different element `type` there, render it at a different position in the tree, or
give it a different `key`. The first two are side effects of unrelated
decisions. The third is the one you write on purpose.

## Hint 3

Contrast it with the alternative you have probably written before:
`useEffect(() => setDraft(""), [tab])`. That renders once with the previous
tab's text still on screen, commits, runs the effect, sets state, renders again.
Two commits and a visibly wrong frame — and it resets only the state you
remembered to name. The key resets everything below it, in one pass, with no
hook.

## Exercise 7 — derive, do not store

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. Export `PriceForm({ rate, onRender }: { rate: number;
onRender: () => void })`.

It renders an input labelled `Amount` (a text input, not `type="number"`) and
`Total: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph. The total is the amount multiplied
by `rate`, rounded to two decimal places and rendered with exactly two decimals.
A non-numeric or empty amount shows `Total: 0.00`. Call `onRender()` at the top
of the body.

The gate types five characters and requires **exactly six** calls to
`onRender` — the first render plus one per keystroke. It then changes the `rate`
prop and requires the total to follow with a single further render.

The stub holds `total` in `useState` and writes it from a `useEffect`. That is
two commits per keystroke and one frame in which the amount and the total
disagree.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Count the pieces of state the component actually needs. The amount is typed by
the user, so React must own it. The total is a function of the amount and the
rate — given both, it can be computed on the spot. State is for things that
cannot be derived.

## Hint 2

Everything React needs to render is available during render. This is legal and
is the shape you want:

```tsx
const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
const matches = rows.filter((row) => row.name.includes(query));
```

No hook, no dependency array, no way for `matches` and `query` to disagree.

## Hint 3

Delete the `total` state and the effect and compute the number in the body, then
format it for display. The decision left to you is how to handle input that is
not a number: `Number("")` is `0` and `Number("abc")` is `NaN`, and only one of
those needs guarding. Pick a single expression that handles both and say why it
is correct.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Trace one keystroke through the stub and write the sequence down. Render with
the new amount and the old total, commit — the screen is now inconsistent — run
the effect, set state, render again, commit again. Two commits and a visibly
wrong intermediate frame, per character.

## Hint 2

The reason this pattern is so common is that it feels like "keeping things in
sync", and effects are advertised as the synchronisation tool. They are — for
synchronising with things *outside* React. Two pieces of React state never need
synchronising, because one of them should not exist.

## Hint 3

The test for whether a value should be state: could you recompute it from other
state and props at any moment and get the same answer? If yes, it is derived,
and storing it creates a second source of truth that can drift. Keep the amount;
compute the total. If it were genuinely expensive, the answer is `useMemo` —
still derived, still one commit — never state plus an effect.

## Exercise 8 — an external store as a trigger

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Export three things.

`createBoardStore()` returns an object with:

- `subscribe(listener: () => void): () => void` — registers a listener and
  returns a function that removes it;
- `getSnapshot(): { title: string; cards: string[] }` — returns the current
  state object, and returns **the same reference** until something changes it;
- `addCard(text: string): void`;
- `rename(title: string): void`.

`useBoardSlice<T>(store, selector)` reads a slice through
`useSyncExternalStore`.

`CardCount({ store, onRender })` renders `Cards: <n>` in a `role="status"`
paragraph and calls `onRender()` at the top of its body.

The gate mounts `CardCount`, calls `addCard` twice — the paragraph must reach
`Cards: 2` — then calls `rename("Roadmap")` three times and requires that
`onRender` was **not** called again. Unmounting must remove the listener; the
gate calls `addCard` afterwards and requires that the listener count is zero.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers ex8
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the failure this hook was invented to prevent. Before React 18 the
usual bridge to an outside store was `useEffect` plus `setState`. Under
concurrent rendering that can **tear**: one component reads the store during a
render that gets interrupted, another reads it after a write, and both commit in
the same paint showing different values from the same source.

## Hint 2

`useSyncExternalStore` fixes that by making React read the snapshot itself, at
the moments it chooses, and by re-reading before committing. The price is the
contract: `getSnapshot` must be cheap, must be free of side effects, and must
return a value that is stable while nothing has changed.

## Hint 3

That last clause is where people get it wrong. Returning
`state.cards.filter(...)` builds a new array on every call, so React sees a new
snapshot every time, re-renders, calls it again, and in development throws
"The result of getSnapshot should be cached". Select a primitive, or cache the
derived object inside the store so the same reference comes back.

## Challenge — a render budget

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. Export `AnalyticsBoard({ rows, onShellRender,
onFilterRender, onChartRender })` where `rows` is `{ id: string; label: string
}[]` and the three spies are `() => void`.

On screen:

- a `role="status"` paragraph reading `Refreshes: <n>`, starting at `0`, and a
  button reading `Refresh` that adds one up to a cap of `3`;
- an input labelled `Filter`, and a paragraph reading `Matches: <n>`;
- a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per row whose `label` contains the filter text,
  case-insensitively, showing the label.

Each of the three components calls its spy at the top of its body: the shell
(refresh area), the filter bar, and the chart (the list).

The budget the gate enforces:

| Interaction | shell | filter | chart |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| type one character in `Filter` | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| press `Refresh` (below the cap) | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| press `Refresh` at the cap of `3` | 0 | 0 | 0 |

`memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` are not allowed. Every row of that table is
achievable with tree shape and the equality bailout alone.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra01_render_triggers challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Take the table one row at a time and name the mechanism each row needs. Row two
and row three are about the refresh count; row one is about which components sit
in which subtree. Nothing in the table needs a hook you have not already used in
this sector.

## Hint 2

The chart must re-render when the filter changes, so the chart has to be inside
the filter's subtree, not beside it. The shell must not re-render either of
them, so neither can be inside the shell's subtree — which leaves exactly one
arrangement:

```tsx
<Shell onRender={onShellRender}>
  <FilterPanel … />
</Shell>
```

with `AnalyticsBoard` itself holding no state.

So: `Shell` owns the refresh count and renders `{children}`; `FilterPanel` owns

`setRefreshes((n) => Math.min(n + 1, 3))`. The decision left to you is where the

lessons.title: V3·RA2 — useEffect: dependencies, cleanup, and the effects you should delete
lessons.summary: Most effects in a codebase should not exist. This sector separates the ones that genuinely synchronise with the outside world from the derivations, resets and event handlers in disguise, then makes the survivors honest: real dependencies, per-run cleanups, and cancellation that survives out-of-order replies.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RA2 — useEffect: dependencies, cleanup, and the effects you should delete

`06_effects` taught you the mechanism: an effect runs after commit, its cleanup
runs before the next run and on unmount, and the dependency array is a claim
about what the body reads. That is the whole API. This sector is about
*judgement* — which effects should exist at all, and how the ones that survive
stop being a source of bugs.

The reason this needs its own sector is that the failure modes are silent. An
effect with a lying dependency array does not crash; it shows the wrong number.
An effect that should have been a derivation does not crash; it renders twice
and flashes for one frame. An effect racing itself does not crash; it shows you
the results of the query you typed two keystrokes ago, occasionally, on a slow
connection. None of these appear in a test that only checks the happy path.

## Concept — the one question

Before writing an effect, answer this: **what outside-of-React thing is this
keeping in step with the component's props and state?**

If there is an answer — the document title, a WebSocket, a `matchMedia` query, a
third-party chart instance, a server — write the effect. If there is no answer,
you are about to write one of these four, and each has a better form:

| What you were about to do | What it should be |
| --- | --- |
| Compute a value from props/state and store it | Compute it during render |
| Reset state because a prop changed | A `key` on the component |
| Do something because the user clicked | Code in the event handler |
| Tell the parent that state changed | Call the parent in the same handler |

`react.dev` calls this "You Might Not Need an Effect", and it is worth
re-reading annually. Each row costs a render pass, and rows one and two also
produce a committed frame in which the UI is internally inconsistent.

## Concept — the cleanup belongs to its own run

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const connection = connect(roomId);
  return () => connection.disconnect();
}, [roomId]);
```

When `roomId` changes from `"general"` to `"support"`, React runs the cleanup
created by the `"general"` render — which closed over `"general"`'s connection —
and *then* runs the new effect. Cleanups are not "the unmount handler"; they are
the undo for one particular run, and they see that run's values. Every
correctness property of effects follows from that pairing: a cleanup cancels its
own request, closes its own socket, clears its own timer.

## Concept — dependencies are values, compared by identity

React compares each dependency with `Object.is`. That is fine for strings and
numbers and catastrophic for objects created during render:

```tsx
function Chart({ options }: { options: { unit: string } }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    draw(options);            // runs forever if the parent writes
  }, [options]);              // <Chart options={{ unit: "px" }} />
}
```

Every render of the parent builds a new object, so the effect re-runs, and if it
sets state you have an infinite loop. The fix is not to remove `options` from the
array — that makes the array lie. The fix is to depend on the *primitives*
inside it, or to make the caller stop rebuilding it.

## Exercise 1 — the derivation

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `OrderSummary({ items, onEffect, onRender })` renders
`Items: <n>` and `Total: <n.nn>` in a `role="status"` paragraph. The stub keeps
the total in state and writes it from an effect. Remove the effect: the gate
requires `onEffect` to be called zero times and exactly one render per change of
`items`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the reset

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. Export `CommentBox({ postId })`, which owns its draft,
and `PostPage({ postId })`, which renders a heading and the comment box. Changing
`postId` must clear the draft, without an effect and without the parent storing
the draft.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — whose values does the cleanup see?

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `RoomPresence({ roomId, connect })` subscribes with
`connect(roomId)`, which returns `{ disconnect(): void }`, and renders
`In room: <roomId>` in a `role="status"` paragraph. When the room changes, the
gate requires the *previous* room's connection to be disconnected exactly once,
before the new one is opened.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the object in the dependency array

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `PollingStatus({ options, poll })` calls
`poll(options.url)` every `options.intervalMs` milliseconds and renders the
latest result in a `role="status"` paragraph. The parent passes a fresh
`options` object on every render. The gate re-renders the parent ten times with
structurally identical options and requires that exactly one interval was ever
started.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the race

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `CityWeather({ city, fetchWeather })` calls
`fetchWeather(city, signal)` and renders `<city>: <summary>` in a `role="status"`
paragraph. The gate changes the city from `Oslo` to `Lima`, resolves `Lima`
first and `Oslo` second, and requires the display to read `Lima`. It also
requires that the abandoned request's `AbortSignal` was aborted.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — the latest callback, without re-subscribing

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `TickReporter({ onTick, subscribe })` subscribes once
with `subscribe(handler)` — which returns an unsubscribe — and calls the
**current** `onTick` prop on every tick. The gate swaps `onTick` for a different
function between ticks and requires that the new one is called and that
`subscribe` was called exactly once.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — the notification that is an event

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `QuantityPicker({ onQuantityChange, label })` renders
`Quantity: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph and `Add` / `Remove` buttons, and
calls `onQuantityChange(next)` when the user changes the quantity. The gate
re-renders with a new `label` and requires that `onQuantityChange` was not
called; it also requires that a change at the floor of `0` — pressing `Remove`
when already at zero — does not call it either.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — skipping the first run

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `DraftAutosave({ draft, save })` calls `save(draft)`
1000 ms after the draft stops changing, but never for the initial value the
component mounted with. The gate mounts, advances the clock, requires no save,
then types and requires exactly one save with the final text.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex8
```

## Challenge — a live search that behaves

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `LiveSearch({ search, onSubscriptionCount })`
renders an input labelled `Search`, a `role="status"` paragraph reading
`Searching…`, `No results` or `Results: <n>`, and a `<ul>` of result labels.
`search(query, signal)` returns a promise. Requirements: debounce by 300 ms
using a timer that is cleared on every change; abort the superseded request;
never show the result of an abandoned query even if it resolves last; and show
nothing but `Results: 0` — not an error — for a query with no matches. An empty
query performs no search at all.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline challenge
```

## Review — three effects, one survivor

Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. `ProjectPanel({ project, onProjectOpen, track })`
has three effects: one derives the member count into state, one calls
`onProjectOpen` whenever `project` changes, and one calls `track("viewed",
project.id)` on mount and on every project change. Two of the three must be
deleted and the third must have an honest dependency array. The gate re-renders
with an unchanged `project` and requires that nothing fires.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline review1
```

# Reading — react/v3ra02_effect_discipline

## Notes

**An effect is a synchronisation, not a lifecycle hook.** The class-era question
was "when does this run" — mount, update, unmount. The hooks question is "what
does this keep in step with what". If you can name the outside system, the
effect is legitimate and its dependency array writes itself: the array is
whatever the outside system's configuration is made of. If you cannot name it,
you are looking at a derivation, a reset, or an event.

**Strict Mode's double invoke is a correctness test.** In development React
mounts, runs effects, runs cleanups, and runs effects again. An effect that
survives that is one whose cleanup genuinely undoes it, which is the same
property that makes it correct when a dependency changes. Effects that "only
work once" — an analytics ping with `[]`, an animation kicked off on mount — are
exactly the ones the double invoke exposes, and they are usually events wearing
an effect's clothes.

**Cleanups are per-run, and they are the only thing that makes effects
composable.** A cleanup closes over the values of the render that created it, so
it disconnects its own socket and cancels its own request. The corollary is that
you should never write a cleanup that reads "the current" anything: if it needs
the latest value it is not undoing its own run, and you have a bug waiting for a
fast enough user.

**The dependency array is the effect's inputs, not a tuning knob.** The lint
rule computes it correctly essentially always; where it is "wrong" is where it
is telling you something true that you do not like. The two honest responses to
an inconvenient dependency are: remove the read (updater form, a ref, a reducer),
or move the value out of the component (module scope, a stable prop). Silencing
the rule leaves a stale closure that nobody will find.

**Cancellation has two layers and you usually need both.** Aborting stops the
network work; the ignore flag stops the *state write*. An aborted `fetch`
rejects, so an unguarded `catch` renders an error for a request you cancelled on
purpose — and a promise that is not abortable at all can only be handled with
the flag.

**Timers are effects.** Every timer started in an effect must be cleared in its
cleanup, and the reason is not tidiness: the callback holds that render's
closure, so an uncleared timer keeps props and state alive and fires against a
component that is gone.

## ex1 — the effect that was a `const`

`total` is a pure function of `items`. Storing it means every change to `items`
renders with the stale total, commits, runs the effect, sets state, and renders
again. Between those two commits there is a real frame where the item count and
the total disagree, and on a slow device it is visible.

The version people defend is "but the calculation is expensive". Measure first;
if it genuinely is, `useMemo` is the answer — still derived, still one commit.

## ex2 — resetting by identity

An effect that clears the draft when `postId` changes renders once with the old
draft still on screen, commits, then resets. `key={postId}` on `CommentBox`
discards the fiber instead, so the new post gets a component that has never had
any state. One pass, no wrong frame, and it resets *everything* below rather
than the fields you remembered to name.

The design point worth arguing in review: the key goes on the child, in the
parent. `PostPage` knows a different `postId` is a different thing; `CommentBox`
should not have to know it is being reset.

## ex3 — cleanup ordering, observed

The gate can only see the ordering through the spy arguments, which is why the
exercise is shaped this way. Changing the room produces exactly:
`connect("general")`, then `disconnect` on that connection, then
`connect("support")`. Cleanup first, always, and the cleanup carries the old
value because it was created by the old render.

The trap is hoisting the connection into a `useRef` "so the cleanup can reach
it". Then the cleanup reads whatever the ref holds *now*, which after a fast
double change is the new connection — so you disconnect the one you just opened
and leak the one you meant to close. Let the closure do its job.

## ex4 — identity, not shape

`options` is rebuilt by the parent every render, so `[options]` re-runs the
effect every render, so the interval is cleared and restarted continuously — and
because the effect sets state, the parent re-renders and it never stops.

Depending on `[options.url, options.intervalMs]` is the fix, and it is honest:
those primitives are what the effect actually reads. `[JSON.stringify(options)]`
also works and is usually a smell — it hides which fields matter, it is O(size)
on every render, and it breaks on anything non-serialisable. Use it only when
the shape is genuinely dynamic, and leave a comment saying why.

The other legitimate fix lives in the caller: hoist the object to module scope
if it is constant, or `useMemo` it if it is not. Do that when several children
need it.

## ex5 — the race, and both layers of cancellation

Two requests are in flight; the second resolves first; the first overwrites it.
The user sees `Oslo` after asking for `Lima`, with no error anywhere.

The ignore flag is the part that is always required, because it is the only
thing that prevents the *state write*. The abort is the part that saves the
work, and it also changes the error handling: an aborted request rejects with an
`AbortError`, which is not a failure to report. Check `signal.aborted` — or the
ignore flag, which is equivalent here — before touching state in the `catch`.

## ex6 — the latest value without re-subscription

Putting `onTick` in the dependency array is correct and, if the parent creates
it inline, means unsubscribing and resubscribing on every render. For a DOM
listener that is cheap. For a WebSocket, a media session, or anything with a
handshake, it is unacceptable.

The pattern is a ref updated in an effect and read inside the subscription:

```tsx
const latest = useRef(onTick);
useEffect(() => { latest.current = onTick; });
useEffect(() => subscribe((n) => latest.current(n)), [subscribe]);
```

That is a hand-rolled `useEffectEvent`, the API React has been developing for
exactly this. What it is not is a way to make an inconvenient dependency go
away: it is only correct for a *callback* whose latest version you want. Store a
value in a ref and read it in an effect that should have re-run when it changed,
and you have re-created the stale-closure bug with extra steps.

## ex7 — the notification belongs to the click

Calling `onQuantityChange` from an effect keyed on the quantity means it fires
whenever the quantity is different from last render — including on mount, and
including when the parent re-rendered for an unrelated reason and the effect's
other dependencies moved. Calling it in the handler, right where the quantity
changes, means it fires exactly when the user changed something.

The floor case is the reason the handler version is strictly better: at zero,
`Remove` produces the same quantity, so nothing changed and nobody should be
told. In the handler you can compute the next value once and only notify if it
differs. From an effect you would be reconstructing that comparison from
history.

## ex8 — skipping the mount, honestly

The `didMount` ref works and the gate wants it, because a debounced autosave
genuinely should not fire for text the user never touched. Write it as a ref
initialised to `true` and flipped inside the effect, not as a state flag — a
state flag would cause an extra render.

Say the caveat out loud, though: "run on updates but not on mount" is almost
always a sign that the thing is reacting to a *user action*. Here it is
defensible because the trigger is "the value settled", which is a property of
the value and not of any one keystroke.

## challenge — all four disciplines at once

The debounce is a timer with a cleanup. The request is abortable. The state
write is guarded by an ignore flag. The dependency array is `[query, search]`
and nothing else, which is only possible because everything else the effect
needs is created inside it. And the empty query short-circuits before starting
anything, which is what stops the component firing a search on mount.

The ordering that trips people: clear the timer *and* abort in the same cleanup.
If you only clear the timer, an already-started request survives; if you only
abort, a pending timer fires a request for a query the user has replaced.

## review1 — deleting two thirds of the file

The member count is a derivation. The `onProjectOpen` call is a notification the
parent could have made itself — it is the one who changed `project` — and from
an effect it also fires on mount, which the parent did not ask for. The
analytics call is the survivor: it synchronises an outside system with "which
project is being viewed", it should fire on mount, and its dependencies are
`[track, project.id]` — the id, not the object, so a re-render with a
structurally identical project does not re-fire it.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — You Might Not Need an Effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)
- [react.dev — Lifecycle of Reactive Effects](https://react.dev/learn/lifecycle-of-reactive-effects)
- [react.dev — Removing Effect Dependencies](https://react.dev/learn/removing-effect-dependencies)
- [react.dev — Separating Events from Effects](https://react.dev/learn/separating-events-from-effects)
- [react.dev — Preserving and Resetting State](https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state)
- [MDN — `AbortController`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController)
- [MDN — `AbortSignal: abort` and `AbortError`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal)
