# Long reading — react/v3ra02_effect_discipline

## Where effects sit in the commit

React's commit is three sub-phases, and knowing which one your code runs in
explains every timing question you will ever have about effects.

**Before mutation.** React snapshots anything it needs from the DOM as it was.
This is where the class-era `getSnapshotBeforeUpdate` ran; there is no hook for
it, which is a deliberate omission.

**Mutation.** React applies the DOM operations. Immediately before doing so it
runs the *cleanups* of layout effects from the previous commit, and it detaches
refs that are about to change. This is why a `useLayoutEffect` cleanup can still
read the old DOM: it runs before the DOM is changed.

**Layout.** React attaches refs and runs `useLayoutEffect` bodies —
synchronously, before the browser has a chance to paint. If you set state here,
React will re-render and re-commit before yielding to the browser, so the user
never sees the intermediate state. That is exactly why measurement-and-adjust
code goes here, and why doing it in a passive effect flashes.

Then the browser paints. Then, on a scheduler callback, React flushes **passive
effects**: the previous commit's `useEffect` cleanups first, then the new
bodies. That is the whole ordering. Two consequences worth internalising: a
`useEffect` never blocks the first paint, and two effects in the same component
run in source order, with *all* cleanups in the tree running before *any* body.

There is one exception that surprises people: if an update originates from a
discrete input event — a click, a keypress — React flushes pending passive
effects synchronously before processing it, so that the handler does not run
against a tree whose effects have not been applied.

## Why the dependency array exists at all

It is worth understanding that the array is a workaround for JavaScript not
having reactive values. Svelte, Vue and Solid all track reads automatically,
because their compilers or their proxies can see which values a function
touched. React deliberately does not: it renders whole components, and functions
capture values by closure. Since the effect body is a closure over one render's
values, React has no way to know whether re-running it would produce anything
different — so you tell it.

That framing kills the two commonest misconceptions at once. The array is not a
performance optimisation, and it is not a list of "things that should trigger
this". It is a *declaration of the closure's inputs*, and the lint rule can
compute it exactly because it is a syntactic property of the body.

The API React has been developing to fill the remaining gap is `useEffectEvent`:
a way to extract the part of an effect that should always see the latest values
but should not cause re-subscription. It is still experimental at the time of
writing, and the hand-rolled `useLatest` ref in this sector is what everyone
uses in the meantime. The important thing is the *distinction* it encodes: a
value the effect reacts to belongs in the array, and a value the effect merely
reads at the moment something external happens does not.

## The history that explains the API's shape

`componentDidMount`, `componentDidUpdate` and `componentWillUnmount` split one
concept across three methods. A subscription's setup lived in one, its
reconfiguration in another — usually behind a hand-written
`if (prevProps.roomId !== this.props.roomId)` — and its teardown in a third,
hundreds of lines away. Bugs were guaranteed: the reconfigure branch and the
teardown drifted apart, and the mount and update paths did subtly different
things.

`useEffect` collapses all three into one place where setup and teardown are
adjacent and the reconfiguration condition is declarative. That is the whole
value proposition, and it is why "which lifecycle method is `useEffect`" is the
wrong question: it is none of them, because the decomposition changed.

React 18 added the Strict Mode double invoke specifically to force effects to be
resilient to being re-run, because concurrent features — and, later, activity
boundaries that unmount and remount subtrees while preserving state — mean React
reserves the right to run your effect more than once for reasons you did not
cause. An effect that only works the first time is not compatible with that
future.

## Two effects are usually better than one

A recurring temptation is to merge effects "to reduce overhead". The overhead is
a closure and an array comparison; it is not measurable. What merging does cost
you is precision: an effect whose dependency array is the union of two concerns
re-runs — and re-runs its cleanup — whenever either moves, so a room change tears
down a scroll listener that had nothing to do with rooms.

The rule is the same one that governs functions generally: **one effect, one
thing it keeps in step.** If you can describe an effect's job with the word
"and", it is two effects. This also makes review possible, because a reviewer can
check a four-line effect's array against its body at a glance and cannot do that
for a twenty-line one.

The ordering guarantee, if you need it: within a commit React runs every
cleanup in the tree before any body, and within one component effects run in
source order. Do not build on anything finer than that.

## Performance notes

**Effects are not free, but they are rarely the cost.** The expensive things are
what effects tend to do: network requests, subscriptions with handshakes, DOM
measurement that forces layout. An effect that re-runs unnecessarily because a
dependency is an unstable object is not "a bit wasteful"; it is a request per
render.

**Debouncing in an effect is the correct place for it.** A timer started in the
effect and cleared in the cleanup gives you debouncing with cancellation for
free, and it composes with the abort. Debouncing in the event handler needs a
ref to hold the timer and separate teardown on unmount.

**Do not batch work into fewer effects to save time.** Two effects with
different dependencies are cheaper *and* clearer than one with the union of
both, because each re-runs only when its own inputs move. Split by concern, not
by count.

**Layout effects block paint.** Anything slow in a `useLayoutEffect` is
directly visible as jank. Measure, adjust, and get out; do not fetch there.

## When not to use this

**Do not use an effect for data fetching in an application that has a framework
or a data library.** Everything in this sector — races, cancellation, dedup,
caching, retry, revalidation — is solved once, properly, in React Query, SWR, or
a router's loader. Hand-rolled fetching in a `useEffect` is correct for a
component library that must not take a dependency, for a genuinely one-off call,
and for learning what the libraries are doing. It is not the default for
product code, and an interviewer who asks you to write it is testing whether you
know the failure modes, not whether you would ship it.

**Do not use `useLayoutEffect` by default.** It runs before paint, so it blocks
it, and it does not run at all during server rendering — React warns about it,
loudly. Use `useEffect` and switch only when you can see a flash.

**Do not use the latest-value ref to escape a dependency you dislike.** It is
correct for callbacks. For a *value* the effect's behaviour depends on, the ref
means the effect silently keeps running with old logic, which is the exact bug
the dependency array exists to prevent, now invisible to the linter.

**Do not use a `didMount` ref as a habit.** Once or twice in a codebase it is a
pragmatic answer to "this genuinely reacts to changes only". Ten times, it means
your effects are event handlers and your components are fighting the model.

**Do not put an effect where a `key` belongs.** The reset-by-effect pattern is
so common that it is worth checking for by grep: any `useEffect` whose body is a
single setter back to an initial value is one of these.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — the derivation

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. Export `OrderSummary({ items, onEffect, onRender }: {
items: { id: string; price: number }[]; onEffect: () => void; onRender: () =>
void })`.

It renders a `role="status"` paragraph containing exactly
`Items: <n> · Total: <n.nn>` — the count, a middle dot with spaces around it,
and the summed price to two decimals.

Call `onRender()` at the top of the body. `onEffect` exists so the gate can
prove there is no effect left: it must be called **zero** times.

The gate renders with two items, then with three, and requires exactly two
renders total. The stub keeps `total` in `useState` and writes it from a
`useEffect`, which costs a second commit each time and leaves one frame in which
the count and the total disagree.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Ask whether the total can ever disagree with the items. It cannot — it is a pure
function of them. State exists for values React cannot recompute; anything you
can compute from props and other state during render is not state, it is a
`const`.

## Hint 2

Everything you need is in scope during render. This is the whole pattern:

```tsx
const visible = rows.filter((row) => !row.archived);
const anySelected = visible.some((row) => row.selected);
```

No hook, no dependency array, and no way for `visible` and `rows` to be out of
step, because there is nothing to keep in step.

## Hint 3

Delete the `useState` and the `useEffect` and compute the total in the body with
`reduce`, then format it with `toFixed(2)`. The decision left to you is whether
to sum in cents to avoid floating-point drift — for two decimals of currency
that is the professional answer, and the gate's numbers are small enough that
either passes.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write down the sequence of commits the stub produces for one change of `items`,
and mark the moment the DOM is wrong. Render (old total), commit — **the screen
now shows three items and the total of two** — effect, setState, render, commit.
Two commits and one lying frame, per change.

## Hint 2

The general rule this exercise teaches is about *sources of truth*. `items` is
one. `total` was a second, derived from the first, kept in step by hand. Any
time you have two pieces of state where one is a function of the other, you have
a synchronisation problem you invented.

## Hint 3

The objection is always "but it is expensive to recompute". Answer it with a
measurement, not a guess: summing a few hundred numbers is far below a frame. If
a derivation ever genuinely is expensive, the tool is `useMemo` — which is still
a derivation, still one commit, and still has a single source of truth — not
state written by an effect.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the reset

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. Export two components.

`CommentBox({ postId }: { postId: string })` owns its draft in `useState`,
renders an input labelled `Comment` and a paragraph reading
`Draft for <postId>: <n> characters`.

`PostPage({ postId }: { postId: string })` renders an `<h1>` with
`Post <postId>` and a `CommentBox` for that post.

Changing `postId` must give the user an empty comment box. The gate types
`looks good` on `post-1`, re-renders with `post-2`, and requires the input to be
empty and the paragraph to read `Draft for post-2: 0 characters`.

Constraints: no `useEffect` anywhere in the file; `CommentBox` must keep owning
its draft, so the parent may not store it and there is no setter prop.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are not resetting a value, you are saying that this is a different comment
box. React discards a component's state when it decides the component in that
position is not the same instance as before — and there is a prop that tells it
so.

## Hint 2

The same move, elsewhere:

```tsx
<AddressForm key={country} country={country} />
```

Switching country gives you a form that has never been filled in — every field,
every validation flag, every uncontrolled input inside it. You did not have to
enumerate them.

## Hint 3

Put `key={postId}` on the `CommentBox` element inside `PostPage`. The decision
left to you is *where* the key goes: on the child, in the parent, is the version
that keeps `CommentBox` ignorant of the fact that it is being reset. Be able to
say why that matters when a second caller appears.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Compare the two candidate mechanisms on what they throw away. A setter in an
effect changes one variable you named. A changed key throws away the fiber, and
with it the entire hook list of that component and everything below it.

## Hint 2

Now compare them on frames. The effect version renders with the old draft,
commits it — the user can see `post-2` in the heading and `looks good` in the
box — and only then resets. The key version never produces that frame, because
the old component is unmounted during the same commit that mounts the new one.

## Hint 3

The remaining question is whose knowledge the reset is. "A different post means
a different comment box" is a fact about the *page*, not about the box. Putting
the key in `PostPage` encodes it where it is true; putting an effect inside
`CommentBox` would make every future caller inherit a policy it did not choose.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — whose values does the cleanup see?

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Export `RoomPresence({ roomId, connect }: { roomId:
string; connect: (roomId: string) => { id: string; disconnect: () => void } })`.

It renders `In room: <roomId>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, and while mounted
it holds exactly one connection, for the current room.

The gate mounts with `general`, re-renders with `support`, and requires this
exact sequence of spy calls:

1. `connect("general")`
2. `disconnect()` on the connection whose `id` is the one `connect("general")`
   returned
3. `connect("support")`

Unmounting must disconnect the current connection, once. Re-rendering with an
unchanged `roomId` must do nothing at all.

Do not store the connection in a `useRef`. The exercise is about what a closure
already gives you.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The cleanup you return is a function created during the same run of the effect
body. Whatever local variables that body declared are still in scope for it —
and they are *that run's* variables, not the current ones. You do not need to
reach for the connection; you already have it.

## Hint 2

The shape, on a different resource:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const watcher = observe(path);
  return () => watcher.stop();
}, [path]);
```

`watcher` is a `const` local to one run. The cleanup for the `"/a"` run stops
`"/a"`'s watcher even though the component is now rendering `"/b"`.

## Hint 3

One effect, one `const` for the connection, a returned arrow that disconnects
it, and `[roomId, connect]` as the dependencies. The decision left to you is
whether `connect` belongs in the array — it does, it is a prop and could change
— and what that implies for a parent that creates it inline.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the wrong version, because you have probably written it:

```tsx
const connectionRef = useRef<Connection | null>(null);
useEffect(() => {
  connectionRef.current = connect(roomId);
  return () => connectionRef.current?.disconnect();
}, [roomId]);
```

It passes a slow test and fails a fast one. Work out the interleaving that
breaks it.

## Hint 2

Two rapid room changes. React runs the `general` cleanup, which reads
`connectionRef.current` — and if anything has already written the `support`
connection there, you disconnect the new one and leak the old. The ref reads
"now"; the cleanup needs "then".

## Hint 3

That is the whole principle: **a cleanup undoes its own run, so it must read its
own run's values, and a closure is the only thing that guarantees that.** Refs
are for values you deliberately want to be current. Everything an effect created
should be a `const` inside the effect.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the object in the dependency array

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. Export `PollingStatus({ options, poll }: { options: {
url: string; intervalMs: number }; poll: (url: string) => Promise<string> })`.

Every `options.intervalMs` milliseconds it calls `poll(options.url)` and renders
the resolved string in a `role="status"` paragraph, prefixed with `Status: `.
Before the first result it renders `Status: waiting`.

The parent writes `<PollingStatus options={{ url: "/health", intervalMs: 1000 }}
poll={poll} />`, so `options` is a **new object on every render**. The gate
re-renders the parent ten times with structurally identical options and requires
that exactly one interval was ever started — it counts `setInterval` and
`clearInterval` calls. Changing `url` or `intervalMs` must restart the interval,
once.

`JSON.stringify` in the dependency array is not accepted here; the fields are
known and finite.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

React compares dependencies with `Object.is`. Two objects with identical
contents written in two different renders are two different values, so
`[options]` says "re-run every time" — even though nothing meaningful changed.

## Hint 2

Depend on what the effect actually reads, which is not the object:

```tsx
const { host, port } = config;
useEffect(() => {
  const socket = open(host, port);
  return () => socket.close();
}, [host, port]);
```

Destructuring at the top of the component makes the real inputs visible and the
array honest.

## Hint 3

Pull `url` and `intervalMs` out of `options` above the effect and depend on
those two primitives plus `poll`. The decision left to you is what happens to a
result that arrives after the interval was replaced: the exercise does not
require cancellation, but decide whether a late resolution should be allowed to
write state, and be able to defend the answer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Trace the loop in the stub. New `options` object → effect re-runs → interval
restarted → a poll resolves → `setState` → parent re-renders → new `options`
object. There is no exit from that cycle, and on a real API it is a request
storm.

## Hint 2

There are three places the fix could live and it is worth knowing all of them.
In the child: depend on primitives. In the parent: `useMemo` the object, or
hoist it to module scope if it is constant. In neither: `JSON.stringify` the
object into the array.

## Hint 3

Rank them. Hoisting a constant is best when it is constant — no hook, nothing to
keep in step. Depending on primitives is best when the child cannot control its
callers, which is the case here and is why the exercise is written this way.
`useMemo` in the parent is right when several children need the same object.
`JSON.stringify` is last: it works, it hides which fields matter, it costs O(size)
every render, and it silently misbehaves on a `Date`, a `Map`, or a key order
change.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — the race

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. Export `CityWeather({ city, fetchWeather }: { city:
string; fetchWeather: (city: string, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<string> })`.

It renders `<city>: <summary>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, and
`<city>: loading` while a request for that city is in flight. A rejection that
is not an abort renders `<city>: unavailable`.

The gate:

1. mounts with `Oslo`, so a request for Oslo starts;
2. re-renders with `Lima` before Oslo resolves;
3. resolves `Lima` with `sunny`, then resolves `Oslo` with `rain`.

It then requires the paragraph to read `Lima: sunny` — not `Oslo: rain`, and not
`Lima: rain` — and requires that the signal handed to the Oslo call has
`aborted === true`. The word `unavailable` must not appear: an abort is not a
failure.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex5
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Separate the two things you are cancelling, because they need different
machinery. One is the *work*: bytes on the wire, a server doing a query. The
other is the *effect of the work*: a call to `setState`. Aborting handles the
first. Only the flag handles the second.

## Hint 2

The reason you cannot rely on the abort alone is timing and reach. A promise
that has already resolved cannot be aborted; a promise from a function that
ignores its signal cannot be aborted; and the microtask that calls your `.then`
may already be queued. The flag is checked at the last possible moment, right
before the write, so it is the one that is always correct.

## Hint 3

Now think about `catch`. `controller.abort()` causes the promise to reject with
an `AbortError` — you caused it, on purpose, and the user must not see it. Guard
the error branch with the same flag (or check `signal.aborted`) and return
without touching state. Forgetting this is why so many hand-written cancellation
implementations flash an error message every time the user types.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the latest callback, without re-subscribing

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export `TickReporter({ onTick, subscribe }: { onTick:
(tick: number) => void; subscribe: (handler: (tick: number) => void) => () =>
void })`.

It renders `Ticks seen: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, subscribes once,
and on every tick increments the counter and calls the **current** `onTick`.

The gate:

1. mounts, fires tick `1` — the first `onTick` is called with `1`;
2. re-renders with a *different* `onTick` function, fires tick `2` — the second
   `onTick` is called with `2` and the first is not called again;
3. requires `subscribe` to have been called exactly once across all of it;
4. unmounts and fires tick `3` — neither callback is called.

Putting `onTick` in the effect's dependency array satisfies points 1, 2 and 4
and fails point 3. That is the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You have two requirements pulling in opposite directions: always call the newest
`onTick`, and never re-subscribe. A dependency array can satisfy one or the
other. So the value has to reach the subscription by a route the dependency
array does not police.

## Hint 2

A ref is a mutable box whose identity never changes. Write to it in an effect
with no dependency array so it is refreshed after every commit, and read it
inside the long-lived callback:

```tsx
const latestQuery = useRef(query);
useEffect(() => {
  latestQuery.current = query;
});
```

Note where the write is. Writing a ref in the render body is not allowed —
a render can be discarded, and the write would not be.

## Hint 3

Two effects: one that keeps a ref pointing at the current `onTick`, and one
that subscribes with `[subscribe]` as its only dependency and calls
`ref.current(tick)` from the handler. The decision left to you is what the
subscription does about the counter — the updater form lets it avoid reading
state, which is what keeps that dependency array to one entry.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Classify the two values the effect touches. `subscribe` is something the effect
*reacts to*: a different subscribe function is a different subscription, so it
belongs in the array. `onTick` is something the effect merely *reads at the
moment an external event happens*. Those are different relationships, and React
only has one array for both.

## Hint 2

That distinction is exactly what the experimental `useEffectEvent` API exists to
express: a function extracted from an effect that always sees the latest props
and state but is not itself reactive. Until it ships, everyone hand-rolls it
with a ref, and knowing that it is a named concept rather than a hack is worth
as much as the code.

## Hint 3

The boundary matters more than the technique. This is correct for a *callback*
whose newest version you want. It is wrong for a *value the effect's behaviour
depends on* — hiding `roomId` in a ref would mean the subscription silently
keeps talking to the old room, which is the stale-closure bug with the linter
switched off.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — the notification that is an event

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. Export `QuantityPicker({ label, onQuantityChange }: {
label: string; onQuantityChange: (quantity: number) => void })`.

It renders the `label` in an `<h2>`, `Quantity: <n>` in a `role="status"`
paragraph starting at `0`, and buttons reading `Add` and `Remove`. `Remove` does
not go below zero.

`onQuantityChange(next)` is called when — and only when — the quantity actually
changes. The gate:

1. mounts and requires `onQuantityChange` **not** to have been called;
2. presses `Remove` at zero and requires it not to have been called;
3. presses `Add` twice and requires exactly two calls, with `1` and then `2`;
4. re-renders with a different `label` and requires no further calls.

There must be no `useEffect` in the file.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the four requirements as one sentence: the parent should hear about a
change exactly when the user causes one. An effect cannot express that, because
an effect only knows that a value is different from last render — not who made
it different, or whether anybody did.

## Hint 2

Compute the next value once, in the handler, and use it for both jobs:

```tsx
const setRating = (next: number) => {
  if (next === rating) return;
  setRatingState(next);
  onRatingChange(next);
};
```

One place decides what the new value is, so the state and the notification can
never disagree.

## Hint 3

Write a single private helper that takes the next quantity, returns early if it
equals the current one, and otherwise sets state and notifies. `Add` and
`Remove` both call it. The decision left to you is how the floor is applied —
clamping inside the helper keeps `Remove` trivial and makes requirement 2 fall
out of requirement "changes only".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enumerate every situation in which an effect with `[quantity]` fires. On mount,
because the effect always runs at least once. Whenever the quantity changes,
whoever changed it. And, if you also listed `onQuantityChange`, whenever the
parent re-created that function — which for an inline arrow is every render of
the parent, including the one caused by a new `label`.

## Hint 2

Requirements 1 and 4 exist to kill exactly those two false positives, and there
is no dependency array that removes them, because the effect genuinely has no
way to know the difference between "the user pressed Add" and "React ran me
again".

## Hint 3

The general principle: **effects describe a state of the world that should hold;
handlers describe things that happened.** "The parent has been told the current
quantity" is not a state of the world you can converge on — it is an event, and
events belong where they occur. The bonus is that the handler is the only place
that knows the *old* value and the *new* one at the same time, which is what
makes "only when it changed" cheap to express.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — skipping the first run

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Export `DraftAutosave({ draft, save }: { draft: string;
save: (draft: string) => void })`.

It renders `Saved: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph — the number of successful
saves — and calls `save(draft)` 1000 ms after the draft last changed. It must
never save the value the component mounted with, and it must never save an
intermediate value the user typed through.

The gate uses fake timers and:

1. mounts with `hello`, advances 5000 ms, and requires zero saves;
2. re-renders with `hello w`, then `hello wo`, then `hello wor` in quick
   succession, advances 1000 ms, and requires exactly one save, with
   `hello wor`;
3. unmounts with a pending timer and requires that no save happens afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three separate requirements, three separate mechanisms: "only after it settles"
is a timer plus a cleanup, "not on mount" is a piece of per-component memory
that is not state, and "not after unmount" is the same cleanup as the first one.

## Hint 2

Debouncing inside an effect is one of the places effects are genuinely elegant,
because the cleanup gives you the cancellation for free:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setTimeout(() => report(query), 500);
  return () => clearTimeout(id);
}, [query]);
```

Every change clears the pending timer before starting a new one, and unmounting
clears the last one.

## Hint 3

Add a ref initialised to `true`, and have the effect return early — after
flipping it to `false` — on its first run. The decision left to you is whether
the early return happens before or after the timer is scheduled, and what the
cleanup should be on that first run. Get that ordering wrong and requirement 1
passes while requirement 2 silently loses its first character.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Why a ref and not `useState(true)`? Because setting state schedules a render,
and the flag is not something the UI displays. A `useRef` is the right container
for per-instance memory that no render depends on — that is its entire purpose.

## Hint 2

Why not `[]` on a separate effect to set the flag? Because effect ordering would
put you at the mercy of source order, and because you would be encoding "have I
run before" in two places. One ref, read and written by the effect that cares,
is the whole implementation.

## Hint 3

Now the caveat worth carrying out of this exercise: "run on updates but not on
mount" is usually a smell. It means the effect is reacting to a *change* rather
than synchronising a *value*, and the honest form of "react to a change" is an
event handler at the place the change originated. It is defensible here because
the trigger is genuinely "this value has stopped moving", which is a property of
the value and not of any one keystroke — and because the component is not the
one changing it. If you find yourself writing the `didMount` ref more than twice
in a codebase, the effects are event handlers in disguise.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a live search that behaves

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. Export `LiveSearch({ search }: { search: (query:
string, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<{ id: string; label: string }[]> })`.

On screen:

- an input labelled `Search`;
- a `role="status"` paragraph reading `Type to search` for an empty query,
  `Searching…` while a request is in flight, `Results: <n>` once results have
  arrived, and `Search failed` for a genuine rejection;
- a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per result, showing the label.

The rules the gate enforces, with fake timers:

1. **Debounce.** Typing `reac` in four quick keystrokes and then advancing
   300 ms performs exactly one search, for `reac`.
2. **Abort.** When a pending request is superseded, its signal is aborted.
3. **No stale writes.** A superseded request that resolves *after* the current
   one must not change what is on screen.
4. **No phantom errors.** Aborting must never produce `Search failed`.
5. **Zero is not an error.** A query with no matches shows `Results: 0` and an
   empty list.
6. **Empty means idle.** Clearing the input performs no search, shows
   `Type to search`, and cancels anything pending.
7. **Unmount is clean.** Unmounting with a timer and a request outstanding
   leaves no timer running and no state written.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline challenge
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Work rule by rule, starting from the cleanup, because six of the seven rules are
about *undoing*. List everything one run of the effect creates: a timer, a
controller, and a claim on the component's state. The cleanup must retire all
three, and rules 2, 3, 6 and 7 are then satisfied by the same three lines.

## Hint 2

The most commonly shipped bug in this component is clearing the timer but not
aborting, or aborting but not setting the flag. Reason about each gap
concretely: if you only clear the timer, a request that already started runs to
completion and writes; if you only abort, a timer that has not fired yet still
launches a search for a query the user has replaced.

## Hint 3

Then check the two rules that are not about cancellation. Rule 5 fails when
people write `results.length > 0 ? … : "No results"` and lose the difference
between "searched and found nothing" and "have not searched yet" — which is what
the status union fixes. Rule 4 fails when the `catch` treats every rejection as a
failure; guard it with the same `ignore` flag, because you caused the abort.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review — three effects, one survivor

Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. `ProjectPanel({ project, onProjectOpen, track })`
is written and has three effects:

```tsx
useEffect(() => setMemberCount(project.members.length), [project]);
useEffect(() => onProjectOpen(project.id), [project, onProjectOpen]);
useEffect(() => track("viewed", project.id), [project, track]);
```

It renders an `<h2>` with the project name and `Members: <n>` in a
`role="status"` paragraph.

Two of those effects must be deleted outright and the third must be given an
honest dependency array. `onProjectOpen` must still be called when the user
opens a project — the panel renders a button reading `Open <name>` for that.

The gate:

1. mounts with `project` `p1` and requires exactly one `track("viewed", "p1")`
   and zero `onProjectOpen` calls;
2. re-renders with a **structurally identical but newly constructed** `project`
   object for `p1` and requires no further calls to either spy, and no extra
   render;
3. re-renders with `p2` and requires exactly one more `track("viewed", "p2")`;
4. clicks `Open p2` and requires exactly one `onProjectOpen("p2")`.

`project` is `{ id: string; name: string; members: string[] }`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra02_effect_discipline review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Take the effects one at a time and ask the sector's question of each: what
outside-of-React system is this keeping in step? Two of them cannot answer, and
the answers they *would* give ("the parent", "a state variable") are the two
tells for a derivation and an event.

## Hint 2

Requirement 2 is doing most of the work. A new object with identical contents is
a changed dependency, so anything keyed on `[project]` fires again. The effect
that survives must depend on the *identity of the thing being viewed*, which is
a string:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  track("viewed", project.id);
}, [track, project.id]);
```

## Hint 3

Delete the member-count state and compute `project.members.length` in the body;
delete the open-notification effect and call `onProjectOpen(project.id)` from
the button's `onClick`. The decision left to you is whether the analytics effect
should also depend on `project.name` — decide by asking what the effect
actually reads, and let the array say exactly that.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Classify before you edit. Effect one writes state from props: a derivation.
Effect two informs the component's own parent: an event, and one the parent
could have observed itself. Effect three talks to an analytics service that
knows nothing about React: a genuine synchronisation, and the only one of the
three that should fire on mount.

## Hint 2

Now look at what each deletion buys, concretely. Deleting the derivation removes
a `useState`, an effect, and a second commit per project change — which is why
requirement 2 says "no extra render" as well as "no calls". Deleting the
notification removes a spurious call on mount, which is the bug the gate's first
requirement is built around.

## Hint 3

Finally, the survivor's array. `[project, track]` re-fires whenever the parent
rebuilds the object, which for an object assembled in a parent's render is every
time. `[project.id, track]` says what the effect reads and nothing more. This is
the general repair for object dependencies: name the fields, not the container —
and if that feels awkward, it is usually telling you the effect wanted a
narrower prop in the first place.

lessons.summary: Refs are the part of React that is not declarative, and React 19 changed how they attach. This sector covers ref-as-a-prop, ref callbacks that return a teardown, measuring before paint without a flash, observers that clean up properly, and imperative handles narrow enough to be worth exposing.

# V3·RA3 — Refs, imperative handles and measuring the DOM

`08_refs_dom` gave you `useRef` for two jobs: reaching a DOM node to focus it,
and holding a value that must survive renders without causing one. Both are
still true and both are still the whole point. What has changed since most
tutorials were written is *how a ref gets attached*, and what happens when you
need more than "the node is there now".

React 19 made two changes that matter to everything below. `ref` is now an
ordinary prop, so `forwardRef` is no longer needed to pass one through a
component. And a ref *callback* may return a cleanup function, which replaces
the old convention of being called a second time with `null`.

## Concept — two jobs, one hook

```tsx
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);   // a DOM handle
const intervalRef = useRef<number | null>(null);   // a mutable box
```

Both are `{ current: T }`. The difference is who writes to `current`: React
does, if you pass the object as a `ref` prop, or you do, for anything else.

The rule that keeps refs safe is one line: **do not read or write a ref during
render.** A render can be discarded — thrown away by a concurrent update, or
double-invoked by Strict Mode — and a write that happened during it is not
undone. Refs are for the commit phase and for event handlers, which is exactly
where the interesting cases live.

The other half of the rule is a consequence: **changing a ref does not schedule
a render.** That is the feature. It is also the trap, because a value the UI
displays must be state, and a value the UI does not display should not be.

## Concept — the ref callback, and its teardown

You may pass a function instead of a ref object. React calls it with the node
when it attaches, and — since React 19 — calls the function it *returned* when
it detaches:

```tsx
<div
  ref={(node) => {
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(onResize);
    observer.observe(node);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }}
/>
```

Before React 19, the same code needed a `null` check and a place to stash the
observer between calls, because React called the callback twice: once with the
node and once with `null`. The cleanup form is strictly better — the observer is
a `const` in the closure of the attach, which is the same "cleanup undoes its own
run" property that makes effects composable.

One gotcha survives from the old API: an *inline* ref callback is a new function
every render, so React detaches and reattaches on every render of the parent.
That is usually harmless and occasionally expensive, and the fix is
`useCallback` — one of the few places it is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.

## Concept — measuring, and the flash

To measure you need a real node, which means you need to be after the commit.
`useEffect` is after the commit *and after paint*, so measure-then-adjust there
and the user sees one frame of the wrong layout. `useLayoutEffect` runs after
the commit and before paint, synchronously, and if you set state in it React
re-renders and re-commits before yielding to the browser. That is the whole
reason it exists, and it is the only reason to prefer it.

## Exercise 1 — a ref is not state

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `ClickAudit({ onRender, onReport })` renders a
`Record` button and a `Show total` button. `Record` increments a private tally
without re-rendering; `Show total` calls `onReport(tally)`. The gate presses
`Record` five times and requires `onRender` to have been called once.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the ref callback and its cleanup

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `HighlightBox({ visible, attach, onAttach, onDetach })`
renders a `<div>` when `visible` is true. On attach it calls `attach(node)` and
keeps whatever that returns; on detach it must call the teardown exactly once.
The gate toggles `visible` three times and requires attach and detach counts to
stay equal, and requires that re-rendering with an unchanged `visible` does not
re-attach.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — ref as a prop

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Export `SearchField({ label, ref })` — a labelled text
input that forwards `ref` to the `<input>` — and `SearchPanel()`, which renders
it and a `Focus search` button that focuses the field. No `forwardRef`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — measure before paint

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `FitLabel({ text, measure })` renders the text in a
`<span>` and sets a `data-fits` attribute on it to `yes` or `no`, based on
`measure(node)` returning a width and comparing it to `160`. The measurement and
the adjustment must both happen before the browser paints; the gate asserts that
no committed frame ever had the attribute missing or wrong.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — an observer that cleans up

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `SizeReporter({ createObserver, onSize })` renders a
`<div>` and a `role="status"` paragraph reading `Width: <n>`. It observes the
div with `createObserver(callback)` — which returns
`{ observe(node), disconnect() }` — and reports each new width. The gate
unmounts and requires exactly one `disconnect`, and requires that a re-render
does not create a second observer.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a narrow imperative handle

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export `TranscriptLog({ lines, ref })` exposing a
handle of exactly `{ focus(): void; scrollToEnd(): void; visibleCount(): number
}` via `useImperativeHandle`, and `TranscriptScreen()` which renders it with
`Focus log`, `Jump to end` and `Count visible` buttons. The raw DOM node must
not be reachable from the handle.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — gesture state that is not UI state

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `DragMeter({ onDrag, onRender })` renders a `<div>`
with `role="slider"` that reports a horizontal drag distance through
`onDrag(delta)` on every pointer move, using refs to remember where the drag
started. A whole drag — down, three moves, up — must produce exactly zero
re-renders.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — a map of nodes

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `StepList({ steps, scrollTo })` renders one `<li>` per
step with a button reading `Go to <label>`, keeps a `Map` from step id to node,
and calls `scrollTo(node)` for the right one when a button is pressed. Removing
a step must remove its entry from the map.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex8
```

## Challenge — a measured popover

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `Popover({ label, content, measure, onAttach,
onDetach })` renders a trigger button and, when open, a panel positioned above
or below the trigger depending on measured space, with focus moved into the
panel. Three ideas at once: a ref callback with cleanup, measurement before
paint, and an imperative handle exposing `open()` and `close()`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement challenge
```

## Review — the leak and the illegal read

Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. `ViewportBadge` is written and wrong in two ways:
it reads a ref during render, and it creates an observer it never disconnects.
Fix both without changing what is on screen.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement review1
```

# Reading — react/v3ra03_refs_and_measurement

## Notes

**A ref is an escape hatch with a contract.** The contract is: React does not
know when it changes, so nothing that the render output depends on may live in
one. Break that and you get a component that shows a stale value until something
unrelated happens to re-render it — a bug that is intermittent by construction,
because it depends on what else is going on in the app.

**Do not read or write refs during render.** Under concurrent rendering a render
can be started, interrupted and thrown away; state written to a ref during it is
not rolled back. Strict Mode's double render makes the same point in
development: a ref incremented in the body counts twice. Writes belong in
effects, in ref callbacks, and in event handlers.

**`ref` is a prop in React 19.** `function Field({ ref }: { ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement> })`
is all it takes. `forwardRef` still works and is deprecated in spirit; its
existence was a workaround for `ref` and `key` being reserved, and only `key`
still is. For library authors the practical consequence is that
`ComponentPropsWithRef` and plain prop spreading now do the obvious thing.

**Ref callbacks may return a teardown.** React calls the returned function when
the node detaches or when the callback's identity changes. The old two-call
protocol — once with the node, once with `null` — still fires for callbacks that
return nothing, so both styles work; do not mix them in one callback. The
teardown form is better for the same reason effect cleanups are: the thing you
created is a `const` in the same closure as the thing that undoes it.

**Ref callback identity matters.** An inline arrow is a new function each
render, so React detaches and reattaches the node every time the parent renders.
For a plain assignment that is invisible. For a callback that starts an observer
or measures, it is real work on every keystroke elsewhere in the parent, and
`useCallback` is the fix — one of the few places it changes behaviour rather
than just allocations.

**Layout effects run before paint.** Order within one commit: React mutates the
DOM, runs the previous layout-effect cleanups, attaches refs, runs
`useLayoutEffect` bodies, and only then lets the browser paint. Setting state in
a layout effect causes a synchronous re-render before paint. That is why it is
the right place to measure and adjust — and why anything slow in it is directly
visible as jank.

**Measurement forces layout.** `getBoundingClientRect`, `offsetWidth` and
friends flush pending style and layout work. Reading them in a loop over many
nodes, interleaved with writes, produces layout thrashing. Batch: read
everything, then write everything.

## ex1 — the tally that is not on screen

The whole exercise is deciding which container a value belongs in. The tally is
never rendered — only reported on demand — so putting it in state would cost a
render per click for no visible change. `useRef` is the container for
per-instance memory that no render reads.

The mirror-image mistake is worth naming because it is far more common: keeping
a value in a ref that the UI *does* show. It works until you notice the screen
lags one interaction behind, which is the signature of exactly this bug.

## ex2 — attach and detach, paired

The gate counts attaches and detaches because pairing is the property that
matters. Return the teardown from the ref callback and the pairing is
structural: the thing that undoes the attach is created by the attach.

The second requirement — no re-attach on an unrelated re-render — is about the
callback's identity, not about `visible`. An inline arrow makes React tear down
and set up on every render. `useCallback` with the right dependencies keeps the
same function, so React leaves the node alone.

## ex3 — a prop like any other

Typing is the part people get wrong. `ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement>` is the prop
type — `Ref<T>`, which covers both a callback and a `RefObject<T>`, not
`RefObject<T>` alone, because a caller may legitimately pass either. Then spread
or pass it straight to the `<input>`.

`SearchPanel` holds `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)` and calls
`ref.current?.focus()` in the button handler. The `?.` is not defensive
programming, it is the type telling the truth: before the first commit, and
after unmount, `current` is `null`.

## ex4 — the flash you would otherwise ship

Measure in `useEffect` and the sequence is commit, paint, measure, set state,
commit, paint. There is one painted frame with the wrong attribute. On a fast
machine you will not see it; on a slow one, or under a `content-visibility`
boundary, it is a visible jump.

`useLayoutEffect` moves both steps before paint. The cost is real — you are
blocking the browser — so the discipline is to do the minimum: one read, one
write, nothing asynchronous, and nothing that could loop. The classic loop is
measuring, setting state, and having that state change the size you measured.

## ex5 — one observer, cleaned up

Two failure modes and the exercise checks both. A missing `disconnect` leaks the
observer, which holds the callback, which holds the component's closure — so the
whole subtree stays in memory and the callback keeps firing into a component
that no longer exists.

Creating the observer on every render is the other one, and it is why the
observer belongs in a ref callback (or an effect with the right dependencies)
rather than in the body. The gate re-renders without changing anything and
requires the observer count to stay at one.

## ex6 — a handle you would be happy to support

`useImperativeHandle(ref, factory, deps)` replaces what the parent sees. Exposing
`{ focus, scrollToEnd, visibleCount }` rather than the node is the entire point:
it is a public API, it can be implemented differently later, and it prevents a
caller from reaching in and setting `style.display` on your internals.

Two details. The dependency array is real — a factory closing over `lines` with
`[]` returns a handle that keeps reporting the first render's count, which is a
stale closure with a nicer name. And `useImperativeHandle` should be rare: if a
parent needs to change what a child *shows*, that is a prop; the handle is for
verbs the DOM itself has — focus, scroll, play, select.

## ex7 — refs during a gesture

A drag produces a pointer event every few milliseconds. If the start position
lives in state, every move re-renders the component for a value nobody is
displaying. Refs make the whole gesture cost zero renders, and the component
only re-renders if you decide to show something.

The detail that makes it correct rather than merely fast is `setPointerCapture`.
Without it, moving the pointer outside the element stops delivering events to it
and the drag ends silently wherever the user left the box. With it, the element
receives every move and the `pointerup` until you release.

## ex8 — a map, and its removals

One ref callback shared by every row, closing over the id, storing the node in a
`Map` held in a ref. The teardown deletes the entry — which is the part people
forget, and the reason the old `null`-based protocol produced so many leaks: a
map that grows one detached DOM node per removed row is a memory leak with no
symptom until the tab has been open for an hour.

A `Map` and not an array because rows have ids, not positions, and positions
change.

## challenge — three mechanisms in one component

The panel's node arrives through a ref callback that both stores it and starts
whatever the popover needs; the placement decision is a measurement made before
paint, so the panel never appears in the wrong place first; and `open` / `close`
are exposed through an imperative handle because they are verbs, not state the
parent should own.

The ordering that matters: the panel must be in the DOM to be measured, so the
first commit renders it — invisible or with no placement class — the layout
effect measures and sets the placement, and React re-commits before paint.

## review1 — two bugs, two rules

The read during render is `heightRef.current` in the body. It works, until a
render is discarded and the value belongs to a render that never committed.
Move the read into the layout effect and put anything the UI shows into state.

The leak is an observer created in an effect whose cleanup returns nothing.
Return `() => observer.disconnect()`; and while you are there, check the
dependency array, because an observer recreated on every render is the same bug
in a hurry.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Referencing values with refs](https://react.dev/learn/referencing-values-with-refs)
- [react.dev — Manipulating the DOM with refs](https://react.dev/learn/manipulating-the-dom-with-refs)
- [react.dev — `useImperativeHandle`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useImperativeHandle)
- [react.dev — `useLayoutEffect`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect)
- [React 19 — ref as a prop and ref cleanup functions](https://react.dev/blog/2024/12/05/react-19)
- [MDN — `ResizeObserver`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ResizeObserver)
- [MDN — `Element.setPointerCapture()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/setPointerCapture)

# Long reading — react/v3ra03_refs_and_measurement

## What a ref actually is

`useRef(initial)` allocates one object — `{ current: initial }` — on the fiber's
hook list at mount and returns the same object on every subsequent render. That
is the entire implementation. There is no subscription, no proxy, no
notification. `useRef` is `useState` with the setter removed and the object
identity guaranteed.

The `ref` *prop* is a separate mechanism that happens to use the same object
shape. During the commit phase React walks the effect list and, for every host
component whose ref changed, detaches the old one and attaches the new one. If
the ref is an object, "attach" means assigning `current`; if it is a function,
attach means calling it with the node. Detaching means assigning `null` or
calling the stored cleanup.

The ordering inside a commit is fixed and worth memorising, because every
"the node is null" question is answered by it:

1. Mutation phase: DOM operations; previous layout-effect cleanups; **refs
   detached** (old callbacks torn down).
2. Layout phase: **refs attached**; `useLayoutEffect` bodies.
3. Browser paint.
4. Passive phase: previous `useEffect` cleanups, then new `useEffect` bodies.

So a ref is always populated by the time any effect runs, and always `null`
during render — including the first render, which is why every `ref.current`
access is optional-chained.

## The road to ref-as-a-prop

`ref` and `key` were special-cased on the props object from the beginning:
React pulled them out before your component ever saw them. That was fine for
host elements, where React itself consumes the ref, and a problem for component
elements, where the ref had nowhere to go. `forwardRef` was the workaround — a
wrapper that accepted the extracted ref as a second argument.

It worked and it was ugly. It doubled the generic parameters of every typed
component, it made prop spreading subtly wrong, it needed
`ComponentPropsWithRef` versus `ComponentPropsWithoutRef` as a distinction
nobody could remember, and it broke the mental model that a component is a
function of its props.

React 19 stopped extracting `ref` from props for function components. It is now
an ordinary prop with an ordinary name, defaultable, spreadable and typeable.
`forwardRef` still exists for compatibility and its wrapper is now a no-op layer
you can delete during any refactor. `key` remains special, because it is
consumed by reconciliation before the component exists at all.

The ref-callback cleanup arrived in the same release for a related reason. The
old protocol — call with the node, later call with `null` — could not express
"undo what this attach did", so everybody stored the observer, listener or
subscription somewhere outside the callback and hoped the two calls stayed in
step. Returning a teardown makes the pairing local, which is the same design
that makes `useEffect` cleanups work. One consequence to know: because a
returned function is now meaningful, a ref callback written as a concise arrow
body — `ref={(node) => (map.current[id] = node)}` — now accidentally "returns"
the assignment. React tolerates non-function return values, but the lint rules
flag it, and you should write a block body.

## Measurement, layout and the browser

`getBoundingClientRect()` is not a read of a stored number. It forces the
browser to flush any pending style recalculation and layout so that the answer
is correct — which is why the pattern

```js
for (const node of nodes) {
  const width = node.getBoundingClientRect().width;
  node.style.height = `${width / 2}px`;
}
```

is quadratic in practice: each write invalidates layout and each read forces it
again. The fix is always the same shape — collect every measurement, then apply
every mutation — and it applies exactly as much inside React as outside it.

`useLayoutEffect` is where measurement belongs because React guarantees that any
state you set inside it is rendered and committed before the browser paints. The
mechanism is that React flushes the resulting synchronous re-render inside the
same task. That guarantee is also the cost: the browser is waiting. Anything
that takes more than a millisecond or two in a layout effect is directly visible
as a stutter, and anything asynchronous in one is a mistake, because the await
lands after paint anyway.

The modern alternative to measuring on every render is to let the platform tell
you: `ResizeObserver` for size, `IntersectionObserver` for visibility,
`matchMedia` for breakpoints. All three are subscriptions, so all three want a
cleanup, and all three are better handled with a ref callback than with an
effect plus a stored node — because the callback fires exactly when the node
exists and its teardown fires exactly when it goes away.

## Gestures, and the render budget of a drag

A pointer drag delivers an event every few milliseconds — on a 120 Hz display,
faster than you can usefully render. If the transient values of a gesture live
in state, every one of those events schedules a render, and the component
re-runs to produce output that is usually identical, because most gestures do
not display their raw coordinates.

The professional shape is: refs for everything transient, direct DOM writes for
anything that must follow the pointer, and exactly one state update at the
boundary — when the gesture ends, or when a value the user actually reads has
settled. That is not a micro-optimisation; it is the difference between a drag
that tracks the pointer and one that lags behind it on a mid-range phone.

`setPointerCapture` is the other half of a correct drag, and it is a browser
feature rather than a React one. It redirects all subsequent pointer events for
that pointer id to the capturing element until `pointerup`, so a fast drag that
leaves the element still delivers moves and still delivers the release that
tears the gesture down. Without it, the gesture ends silently and the component
is left believing a drag is still in progress — which is why a stuck slider is
almost always a missing capture rather than a React bug.

## Performance notes

**Refs make gestures cheap.** A drag, a resize handle, a canvas pointer tool:
none of them need a render per event. Keep the transient values in refs, write
directly to `style` or to a canvas, and render only at the boundaries — start,
end, or when a value the user reads has settled.

**Ref callbacks that do work must be memoized.** Otherwise you pay setup and
teardown per render of the parent, which turns an unrelated keystroke into
observer churn.

**`useImperativeHandle` has a dependency array and it is not decorative.** The
handle object is rebuilt when the array changes, and the parent's ref is
reassigned. Closures inside a handle built with `[]` capture the first render.

**Measurement in a layout effect blocks paint; measurement in an observer does
not.** If the adjustment does not have to be correct in the first painted frame,
an observer is cheaper. If it does — a tooltip that would otherwise appear in
the wrong place — the layout effect is the price of correctness.

## When not to use this

**Do not use a ref to avoid thinking about state.** "Put it in a ref so it does
not re-render" is correct only when nothing renders it. If you find yourself
adding a `forceUpdate` to make a ref-held value show up, you wanted state.

**Do not use an imperative handle where a prop works.** A parent that needs the
child to show a different thing should pass a different prop. Handles are for
verbs the DOM owns — `focus`, `scrollIntoView`, `play`, `select` — and every
handle you export is API you now have to keep working.

**Do not use `useLayoutEffect` by default.** It does not run during server
rendering — React warns loudly — and it blocks paint. Start with `useEffect` and
move only when you can see the flash.

**Do not reach into another component's DOM.** A ref that escapes the component
that rendered the node turns an implementation detail into a contract. If a
parent needs to act on a child's internals, the child should offer a narrow
handle, and if that feels heavy, that is a signal the boundary is wrong.

**Do not hand-roll what the platform observes.** Polling `offsetWidth` in an
interval, or measuring on every render "just in case", is both slower and less
correct than a `ResizeObserver` — which fires for content changes, zoom, font
loading and container queries that your render has no way of knowing about.

## Exercise 2 — the ref callback and its cleanup

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. Export `HighlightBox({ visible, attach, label }: {
visible: boolean; attach: (node: HTMLDivElement) => () => void; label: string })`.

When `visible` is true it renders a `<div>` with `data-testid="box"` containing
the `label`; when false it renders nothing but the label in a paragraph.

be called exactly once when the node goes away. Use the React 19 ref-callback
cleanup form — no `null` check, no stored node.

The gate:

1. mounts visible, toggles `visible` three times, and requires the attach count
   and the teardown count to be equal at every step;

   re-attach happened.


exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Requirement 1 is about the shape of the callback. Requirement 2 is about its
*identity*: React tears down and re-runs a ref callback whenever the function
you pass is not the same function as last time, and an arrow written inline in
the JSX never is.

## Hint 2

A ref callback in React 19 looks like an effect:

```tsx

  ref={(node) => {
    node.play();
    return () => node.pause();
  }}
/>
```

structural rather than remembered.

## Hint 3

Write the callback with `useCallback` so its identity survives a `label` change,
and return `attach(node)` directly from it. The decision left to you is the
dependency array: `attach` belongs in it, `label` does not, and being able to
explain that difference is the exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the API that this replaced, because the contrast is the lesson:

```tsx
ref={(node) => {
  if (node) teardownRef.current = attach(node);
  else teardownRef.current?.();
}}
```

Two branches, a ref to carry the teardown between two separate calls, and a
silent leak if the two ever get out of step.

## Hint 2

The React 19 form removes the carrying. The teardown is created inside the same
closure as the attach, so it cannot refer to a later node, and React is the one
holding it. This is the same reason `useEffect` cleanups are reliable, applied
one phase earlier — refs are attached during the layout phase, before any effect
runs.

## Hint 3

Now the identity requirement. React compares the ref callback with the previous
one; a different function means "the ref changed", so it detaches, then attaches.
For a callback that only assigns, that is free. For one that starts an observer,
a subscription or an animation, it is real work on every unrelated render — which
is why `useCallback` here is load-bearing and not decoration.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — ref as a prop

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Export two components.

`SearchField({ label, ref }: { label: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement> })`
renders a `<label>` bound to an `<input>` by `htmlFor`/`id`, and forwards `ref`
to the input.

`SearchPanel()` renders `<SearchField label="Search" ref={…} />` and a button
reading `Focus search` that focuses the field, plus a `role="status"` paragraph
reading `Ready`.

Constraints: no `forwardRef`, and the prop must be typed `Ref<HTMLInputElement>`
rather than `RefObject<HTMLInputElement>`.

The gate clicks `Focus search` and asserts the input is the active element. It
also renders `SearchField` with a **ref callback** rather than a ref object, and
requires that to work too — which is what the `Ref<T>` type is for.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

In React 19 there is nothing to do to "forward" a ref through a function
component. `ref` arrives in props like `label` does. The only interesting part
is the type, and the gate's last requirement tells you which type it has to be.

## Hint 2

`Ref<T>` is the union of every legal thing a caller can put in a `ref` prop —
a `RefObject<T>`, a callback, or `null`. Declaring `RefObject<T>` compiles for
the object case and rejects the callback case:

```tsx
<SearchField label="Search" ref={(node) => node?.select()} />
```

## Hint 3

Declare `ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement>` and pass it straight to the `<input>`; in
`SearchPanel`, hold `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)` and call
`inputRef.current?.focus()` in the button handler. The decision left to you is
whether the `id` is hard-coded or generated — `useId` is the correct answer for
anything that might be rendered twice on a page, and the gate accepts either.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

It is worth knowing what you are *not* writing, because you will meet it in
every codebase older than 2025:

```tsx
const SearchField = forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, { label: string }>(
  function SearchField({ label }, ref) { … },
);
```

Two generic parameters in the wrong order, a second positional argument that is
not a prop, and a wrapper object that is not a plain function.

## Hint 2

That existed because React extracted `ref` from props before your component ran.
React 19 stopped doing that for function components, so `ref` is now spreadable,
defaultable and typeable like anything else. `key` is still extracted, because
reconciliation consumes it before the component exists.

## Hint 3

The remaining subtlety is `null`. `ref.current` is `null` before the first
commit and again after unmount, and TypeScript will tell you so. The `?.` in
`inputRef.current?.focus()` is the type being honest, not defensive coding —
resist the urge to write `!` there, because the one time it is `null` is the one
time it matters.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — measure before paint

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. Export `FitLabel({ text, measure }: { text: string;
measure: (node: HTMLSpanElement) => { width: number } })`.

It renders the text in a `<span>` carrying `data-fits="yes"` when
`measure(node).width` is at most `160`, and `data-fits="no"` otherwise. The
attribute must be correct in the **first painted frame** for every value of
`text`.

The gate wraps the commit phases so it can see what was committed and when. It
requires:

- the measurement to happen in the layout phase, not the passive phase — no
  committed frame may ever be painted with a missing or wrong `data-fits`;
- exactly one measurement per change of `text`;
- no measurement at all when the component re-renders with the same `text`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You need a real node, so you must be after the commit. You need the correction
to be invisible, so you must be before the paint. There is exactly one hook in
that window.

## Hint 2

`useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously after React has mutated the DOM and before
the browser paints, and state set inside it is rendered and committed in the
same task:

```tsx
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const node = boxRef.current;
  if (!node) return;
  setOverflowing(node.scrollHeight > node.clientHeight);
}, [children]);
```

The user never sees the intermediate frame.

## Hint 3

Hold the span with `useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null)`, measure in a
`useLayoutEffect` keyed on `[text, measure]`, and keep the result in state so
the attribute follows it. The decision left to you is the initial value: there
is no measurement before the first layout effect, so pick a starting state and
be able to say why it cannot produce a wrong painted frame.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the `useEffect` version first and describe the frames. Commit with no
attribute, **paint**, effect runs, measure, set state, commit with the
attribute, paint. The user saw one frame of unstyled text. On a fast machine
that is invisible; on a slow one it is the flash every layout-shift metric
punishes.

## Hint 2

`useLayoutEffect` is the same hook moved one phase earlier: React runs it after
refs are attached and before it hands control back to the browser, and it
flushes the resulting re-render before painting. That is the only difference,
and it is the only reason to use it.

## Hint 3

The costs are real, so know them. It blocks paint, so anything slow in it stutters
visibly; it does not run during server rendering, and React warns; and a
measure-then-set-state that changes what you measured is an infinite loop. Keep
it to one read and one write, and make sure the state you set cannot change the
width you measured.
