exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — an observer that cleans up

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. Export `SizeReporter({ createObserver, label }: {
createObserver: (onEntry: (width: number) => void) => { observe: (node:
Element) => void; disconnect: () => void }; label: string })`.

It renders a `<div data-testid="panel">` containing the `label`, and a
`role="status"` paragraph reading `Width: <n>` starting at `Width: 0`.

On attach it creates one observer, observes the div, and updates the paragraph
from every reported width. The gate:

1. mounts, reports `320`, and requires `Width: 320`;
2. re-renders with a different `label` and requires that `createObserver` has
   still been called exactly once;
3. unmounts and requires exactly one `disconnect`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex5
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Take the leak seriously by describing what it holds. The observer holds your
callback; the callback closes over the component's scope; that scope holds
props, state and the setter. So one missing `disconnect` retains the whole
subtree, and the callback keeps firing into a component React has forgotten.

## Hint 2

The second requirement is a different failure with the same symptom. If the
observer is created in the render body, or in an effect with a dependency array
that moves, you get a new observer per render — several live observers on the
same node, several callbacks, several copies of the closure. The counter in the
gate exists to catch exactly that.

## Hint 3

Compare the two places the setup could live. An effect can do it, but it needs
the node, which means an extra ref and an implicit assumption that the node
exists by the time effects run. A ref callback is handed the node at exactly the
moment it attaches and torn down at exactly the moment it detaches — no
assumption, no second container, and it works for a node that appears and
disappears with a condition.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a narrow imperative handle

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export two components.

`TranscriptLog({ lines, ref })` renders a `<ul>` with `tabIndex={-1}` and one
`<li>` per line, and exposes through `ref` a handle of exactly:

```ts
type TranscriptHandle = {
  focus: () => void;
  scrollToEnd: () => void;
  visibleCount: () => number;
};
```

`visibleCount()` returns the current number of lines. The DOM node must **not**
be reachable from the handle — no `node`, no `element`, no `current`.

`TranscriptScreen({ lines, onCount })` renders the log plus three buttons:
`Focus log`, `Jump to end` and `Count visible`, the last of which calls
`onCount(handle.visibleCount())`.

The gate renders with three lines, adds a fourth, clicks `Count visible`, and
requires `4`. Getting `3` means the handle closed over a stale render.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`useImperativeHandle(ref, factory, deps)` replaces what the parent sees in
`ref.current` with whatever the factory returns. So the question is what the
factory should return — and the constraint says: three functions and nothing
else.

## Hint 2

The shape, on a different component:

```tsx
useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
  play: () => videoRef.current?.play(),
  seek: (seconds: number) => {
    if (videoRef.current) videoRef.current.currentTime = seconds;
  },
}), []);
```

Notice that the internal `videoRef` never leaves the component. What escapes is
a vocabulary, not a node.

## Hint 3

Keep a private `useRef<HTMLUListElement>(null)` for the list, and build the
handle from it. The decision left to you is the dependency array, and the gate's
last requirement is the clue: `visibleCount` reads `lines`, so `[]` would freeze
it at the first render's value.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about it as publishing an API rather than as wiring. Every method on the
handle is something you have promised to keep working, and every method you did
*not* add is freedom to change the markup later. `{ focus, scrollToEnd,
visibleCount }` says nothing about `<ul>`; returning the node says everything.

## Hint 2

That is also the practical argument against the shortcut people reach for —
`useImperativeHandle(ref, () => listRef.current!, [])`. It compiles, it "works",
and it means a caller can set `style.display = "none"` on your internals, read
`children`, or depend on the tag name. You have made your DOM structure a
contract.

## Hint 3

Now the staleness. The factory is a closure like any other, so `visibleCount`
captures the `lines` of whichever render built the handle. With `[]` that is the
first one, forever — a stale closure with a formal-sounding name. List what the
factory reads, exactly as you would for an effect. If that makes the handle
rebuild often, that is fine: rebuilding a small object is cheap, and the
alternative is being wrong.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — gesture state that is not UI state

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. Export `DragMeter({ onDrag, onRender }: { onDrag:
(delta: number) => void; onRender: () => void })`.

It renders a `<div role="slider" data-testid="track">` containing the text
`Drag me`. Pointer handling:

- `pointerdown` records the pointer's `clientX` and captures the pointer on the
  element;
- each `pointermove` **while dragging** calls `onDrag(clientX - start)`;
- `pointerup` ends the drag and releases the capture;
- `pointermove` when not dragging calls nothing.

Call `onRender()` at the top of the body. The gate performs a full gesture —
down at `100`, moves at `130`, `160`, `90`, then up — and requires
`onDrag` to have been called with `30`, `60`, `-10`, and `onRender` to have been
called exactly **once**.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two values have to survive between events: whether a drag is in progress, and
where it started. Neither of them appears on screen. Put them in state and every
pointer move costs a render for a number nobody displays.

## Hint 2

Refs are the right container, and reading them inside an event handler is
always legal — handlers run long after the commit:

```tsx
const startY = useRef(0);
const onDown = (e: React.PointerEvent) => {
  startY.current = e.clientY;
};
```

## Hint 3

Use two refs — a boolean for "dragging" and a number for the start — or one ref
holding `number | null`, which collapses the two into a single state. Add
`event.currentTarget.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId)` on the way down and
release it on the way up. The decision left to you is which of those two
representations to use; one of them makes "not dragging" unrepresentable as a
half-state.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the capture, because it is the part that makes the component correct
rather than merely cheap. Without `setPointerCapture`, moving the pointer
outside the element stops delivering `pointermove` to it, so the drag ends
silently wherever the user left the box — and you never receive the
`pointerup` that would have cleaned up.

## Hint 2

With capture, the element receives every subsequent move and the `pointerup`
regardless of what is under the cursor, and the browser releases the capture
automatically on `pointerup`. Calling `releasePointerCapture` yourself is still
worth doing so the code says what it means.

## Hint 3

Now the render budget. The gate asks for exactly one render across the whole
gesture, which tells you that *nothing* about the drag may be state. If the
component later needs to show the live value, the professional answer is not to
promote the refs to state — it is to write to the DOM directly during the drag
and commit one piece of state when the gesture ends.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — a map of nodes

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Export `StepList({ steps, scrollTo, onRegistrySize }: {
steps: { id: string; label: string }[]; scrollTo: (node: HTMLLIElement) =>
void; onRegistrySize: (size: number) => void })`.

It renders a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per step showing the label, and above it one
button per step reading `Go to <label>`. Pressing a button calls `scrollTo` with
that step's `<li>` node.

It also renders a button reading `Report registry`, which calls
`onRegistrySize` with the number of nodes currently registered.

The gate renders three steps, presses `Go to Second` and asserts `scrollTo`
received the second `<li>`, then re-renders with only the first and third steps,
presses `Report registry`, and requires `2`. A registry that still holds the
removed node fails.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra03_refs_and_measurement ex8
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Name the failure the gate is checking for. A map that gains an entry when a row
mounts and never loses one when it unmounts holds a **detached DOM node** for
every row the user has ever removed. Nothing breaks; memory grows; and the
symptom is a tab that gets slower over an afternoon.

## Hint 2

Under the pre-React-19 protocol this was easy to get wrong, because the removal
lived in the `else` branch of a `null` check that people forgot to write. The
cleanup form makes the removal adjacent to the insertion, so a reviewer can see
both in one glance.

## Hint 3

The other design choice worth defending is `Map` over an array. Rows have ids,
and ids survive reordering; array indices do not, so an array-of-refs quietly
associates node 2 with row 3 the moment somebody sorts the list. Any time you
are tempted to key a registry by position, ask what happens when the list is
reordered.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Break it into the three mechanisms the sector taught and solve them separately:
something that runs when the panel node appears, something that decides the
placement before paint, and something that publishes two verbs to the parent.
None of them interacts with the others as much as it first looks.

## Hint 2

The ordering that makes requirement 1 possible is worth writing down before you
code:

1. `open` becomes true, so React renders the panel with a provisional placement;
2. React commits — the node now exists and can be measured;
3. a layout effect measures both nodes and sets the placement;
4. React re-renders and re-commits **before** the browser paints.

So the first painted frame already carries the corrected attribute. The
provisional value in step 1 is never seen.

## Hint 3

Hold the trigger and the panel in two refs, run one `useLayoutEffect` keyed on
`[open]` that measures and sets the placement, and expose `{ open, close }` with
`useImperativeHandle`. The decision left to you is where the focus moves happen:
opening's focus can go in the same layout effect, but returning focus to the
trigger on close cannot — work out why, and pick a place for it that runs after
the panel is gone.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Requirement 2 is the one that will fail first, so design for it. A measurement
"once per open" means the layout effect's dependency array contains the open
flag and nothing that changes for unrelated reasons — so `measure` and `label`
need thinking about. Ask what the effect actually reads.

## Hint 2

Requirement 4 is the one people get subtly wrong. If you call
`trigger.focus()` in the close handler *before* the state update commits, the
panel is still in the DOM and may take focus back; if you call it from a layout
effect keyed on `[open]`, it also runs on mount, focusing the trigger when
nobody asked. Both bugs are about *when*, not about *what*.

The cleanest resolution is to make the effect distinguish "closed after having
been open" from "closed on mount" — the `didMount` ref from the effects sector
is one honest way, and moving the focus call into the close path is another.

## Hint 3

Accessibility is not decoration here and the gate reads it: `aria-expanded` on
the trigger, `role="dialog"` on the panel, `Escape` closing, focus moving in and
back. A popover that measures beautifully and traps the user's focus in the
document body is not finished. Wire the `Escape` handler on the panel rather
than on `document` if you can — a listener scoped to the node dies with the
node, and one on `document` needs a cleanup you can forget.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two faults, two rules from this sector, and they are almost opposites. One value
is in the wrong container; one subscription is missing its undo. Fix them
independently — trying to solve both with one change is how people end up with
a `forceUpdate`.

## Hint 2

For the first: the paragraph displays the height, so the height is state. A ref
schedules nothing, so the number on screen is whatever it was at the last render
caused by something else — which is why the bug looks intermittent.

For the second: an effect with no dependency array runs after every commit, and
one that returns nothing cleans up nothing.

## Hint 3

Move the height to `useState`, and move the observer into a memoized ref
callback that observes on attach and returns a disconnect. The decision left to
you is whether to keep an effect at all — the sector argues the ref callback is
the better home because it is handed the node instead of assuming one exists,
and you should be able to say why `frameRef.current!` in the current code is a
lie waiting to happen.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Diagnose the staleness precisely rather than by feel. The observer writes
`heightRef.current`; nothing schedules a render; so the DOM keeps whatever
number was interpolated at the last render. The next unrelated render picks up
the current value — so the component is not "always wrong", it is "right
whenever something else happened", which is the hardest class of bug to
reproduce.

## Hint 2

Now the second fault, and note that it has *two* halves people usually fix only
one of. The missing cleanup leaks the observer. The missing dependency array
creates a new observer after every commit — so by the tenth render there are ten
observers on one node, ten callbacks, and ten copies of the closure. The gate's
"called once" assertion is aimed at that half.

## Hint 3

Finally, the `!`. `frameRef.current!` asserts that the node exists when the
effect runs, which happens to be true today and is a promise about ordering that
the code has no way to keep if the section ever becomes conditional. A ref
callback removes the question: it is called *with* the node, so there is nothing
to assert and nothing to be wrong about.

lessons.title: V3·RA4 — useReducer and modelling state transitions
lessons.summary: A reducer is not a fancier setter — it is a place to write down what your state is allowed to do. This sector covers discriminated action unions, lazy initialisation, purity, making impossible states unrepresentable, undo, guarded transitions, and why a stable dispatch is worth more than it looks.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RA4 — useReducer and modelling state transitions

`09_context_reducer` and `d17_reducers` gave you the mechanics: a reducer is
`(state, action) => nextState`, `useReducer` returns the state and a `dispatch`,
and dispatching is how you ask for a change. That is the API and it takes ten
minutes to learn.

What takes longer is knowing when it is worth it, and what a good reducer looks
like. The honest answer to the first question is: **when the transitions matter
more than the values.** A checkbox has one transition and belongs in `useState`.
A checkout flow has fifteen, half of which are invalid from most states, and
writing those fifteen as scattered `setX` calls across eight handlers means the
rules exist only as an emergent property of the code.

## Concept — actions are facts, not commands

```tsx
type Action =
  | { type: "added"; item: Item }
  | { type: "removed"; id: string }
  | { type: "quantityChanged"; id: string; quantity: number }
  | { type: "cleared" };
```

Two conventions in that snippet are load-bearing.

**Past tense.** `added`, not `add`. An action describes something that happened
in the user's world; the reducer decides what that means for the state. Command
names — `setTotal`, `incrementAndValidate` — put the decision at the call site,
which is exactly the coupling the reducer was supposed to remove.

**A discriminated union.** Every variant has a literal `type`, and its payload
lives on the variant that needs it. That lets TypeScript narrow inside the
`switch`, so `action.quantity` exists only in the branch where it means
something, and it lets you get **exhaustiveness checking**:

```tsx
default: {
  const impossible: never = action;
  throw new Error(`Unhandled action: ${JSON.stringify(impossible)}`);
}
```

Add a variant to the union and forget the case, and that line stops compiling.
That single trick is most of the reason reducers scale better than setters.

## Concept — the reducer must be pure

React may call your reducer more than once for the same action: Strict Mode
double-invokes it in development, and concurrent rendering may replay updates
during a re-render. So a reducer that reads `Date.now()`, generates an id, calls
an API, or mutates its input is not merely unfashionable — it produces different
answers on different runs.

The rule that follows is mechanical: **impurity goes into the action.** The
handler that knows the current time puts it in the payload; the reducer only
computes.

## Concept — make impossible states impossible

```tsx
// Sixteen combinations, twelve of which are nonsense.
{ isLoading: boolean; isError: boolean; data: Row[] | null; error: string | null }

// Four states, each carrying exactly what it has.
type State =
  | { status: "idle" }
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "success"; rows: Row[] }
  | { status: "failure"; message: string };
```

The second version cannot represent "loading and also an error", cannot be asked
for `rows` while loading, and turns a family of runtime bugs into compile
errors. A reducer is where this shape pays off most, because the transitions
between the variants are written down in one place.

## Concept — `dispatch` is stable

React guarantees that the `dispatch` returned by `useReducer` is the same
function for the life of the component. That is worth more than it sounds: a
memoized child that receives only `dispatch` never re-renders, a context whose
value contains only `dispatch` never invalidates its consumers, and an effect
that dispatches needs no dependency on it. `useState`'s setter has the same
guarantee, but a `dispatch` covers many operations where setters proliferate.

## Exercise 1 — the exhaustive switch

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. Build `cartReducer` over a discriminated union and a
`CartPanel` that dispatches it, with a `never` check in the default branch.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling ex1

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `SignupForm({ onSubmit })` keeps field values and

Errors are never stored.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — a stable dispatch

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `CounterBoard({ onControlsRender })` renders a memoized

re-render `Controls`, without a single `useCallback`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — composing reducers

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `boardReducer` delegates per-card actions to a
`cardReducer` that knows nothing about the board, and returns the same board
object when the targeted card did not change.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling ex8
```

## Challenge — a checkout machine

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. A guarded state machine for checkout: actions
that are invalid in the current state return **the same state object** so React
bails out, totals are derived, and every accepted transition is reported to an
injected `onTransition`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling challenge
```

## Review — three faults in one reducer

Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. A reducer that mutates its input, has a
command-shaped action carrying a pre-computed result, and returns a fresh object
for a no-op. Fix all three; the gate measures renders as well as values.

```

# Reading — react/v3ra04_reducer_modelling

## Notes

**A reducer separates *what happened* from *what that means*.** With setters,
every handler both decides the event and computes the consequence, so the rules
live in eight places. With a reducer, handlers report events and one function
owns every rule. The test for whether you have done it properly: can a reviewer
learn the entire behaviour of the state by reading one function? If they still
have to read the handlers, the actions are commands.

**The `never` check is the point.** Exhaustiveness is what makes reducers
maintainable at the fifteen-action size. Assigning `action` to a `never` in the
default branch turns "somebody added a variant and forgot a case" from a runtime
surprise into a type error, and it costs one line.

**Reducers must be pure, and React means it.** Strict Mode calls your reducer
twice per dispatch in development. Concurrent rendering may replay queued
updates when a render is discarded and redone. So `Math.random()`, `Date.now()`,
mutation of `state`, and API calls inside a reducer all produce results that
depend on how many times React happened to run it.

**Returning the same object is a real feature.** `Object.is(next, current)`
being true means React bails out — no render, no commit. So a guard that returns
`state` for an invalid transition is not merely tidy; it is the difference
between a no-op and a wasted commit. Return `state` itself, not a structurally
identical copy.

**Lazy initialisation is the third argument.** `useReducer(reducer, arg, init)`
calls `init(arg)` once, at mount. Writing `useReducer(reducer, expensive())`
calls `expensive()` on every render and throws the result away every time but
the first — which is invisible in a profiler unless you go looking.

**`dispatch` is stable for the life of the component.** Pass it instead of a
bundle of callbacks and you get memoization for free: the memoized child's props
never change identity, so nothing needs `useCallback`.

**`useReducer` is not a state manager.** It is local state with a better shape.
It does not share anything between components on its own — that is
`v3ra05_context_composition` — and it does not persist, cache or synchronise.

## ex1 — the union and the switch

Two things make this more than boilerplate. The past-tense names force you to
describe the user's world rather than the state's implementation, which means
the action set survives a redesign of the state. And the payload-per-variant
shape means TypeScript narrows: `action.id` exists in `removed` and not in
`cleared`, so a typo is a compile error rather than an `undefined`.

The `never` line is the part people leave out because it looks like ceremony.
It is the whole safety property: without it, an unhandled action silently
returns the current state, which reads as "the button does nothing" and takes an
afternoon to find.

## ex2 — the third argument

`useReducer(reducer, savedFilters, parseFilters)` calls `parseFilters` once.
Written as `useReducer(reducer, parseFilters(savedFilters))`, the parse runs on
every render — including the hundreds caused by typing in a field elsewhere —
and every result but the first is discarded.

The same argument applies to `useState(expensive())` versus
`useState(() => expensive())`, and it is worth internalising as "an initial
value is an *argument*, and arguments are evaluated eagerly". The lazy forms
exist because that is almost never what you want for anything costly.

## ex3 — impurity belongs in the action

The reducer must be a function in the mathematical sense: same inputs, same
output. `Date.now()` and `crypto.randomUUID()` break that, and the symptom under
Strict Mode is two notes with different ids for one click — or, worse, one note
whose id changes between the render that created it and the render that displays
it.

The fix is a discipline, not a workaround: the handler is where the outside
world is allowed in, so the handler stamps the time and mints the id and puts
both in the payload. A pleasant side effect is that the reducer becomes trivially
testable — no fake timers, no mocked crypto, just values in and values out.

## ex4 — flags to variants

Count the states the boolean version can represent and then count the ones that
make sense. `isLoading && isError` is representable and meaningless.
`data !== null && isLoading` is representable and ambiguous. Every one of those
is a branch somebody will eventually have to write a defensive check for.

The union version replaces the checks with narrowing: inside
`state.status === "success"`, `state.rows` exists and is not nullable, and
outside it, it does not exist at all. The UI stops asking "which flags are set"
and starts asking "which state am I in", which is also how you would describe
the component to a designer.

## ex5 — history as data

`{ past, present, future }` is the smallest complete model of undo, and the
interesting rule is the third one: **a new edit clears the future.** Without it,
redo after an edit replays a branch of history that no longer exists, which
users experience as text appearing from nowhere.

The two no-ops matter for the same reason as the guards elsewhere: undo with an
empty `past` must return the *same* state object so React bails out. Returning
`{ ...state }` there means a commit for nothing and, in a memoized tree, a wave
of re-renders.

## ex6 — validate, do not store

Errors are a pure function of the values, so storing them creates a second
source of truth that can disagree — and the way it disagrees is always the same:
the user fixes a field and the error stays. Derive during render and the bug is
unrepresentable.

What *is* state is `touched`. "Has the user visited this field" is genuinely
extra information that cannot be recomputed from the values, which is exactly
the test for whether something belongs in the reducer. That distinction — values
and touched in the reducer, errors derived — is the shape of every good form in
React, with or without a library.

## ex7 — the free memoization

`Controls` takes `dispatch` and nothing else. `dispatch` is guaranteed stable, so
the memo comparison passes on every render of the parent and `Controls` never
re-renders — and you wrote no `useCallback` at all.

This is the strongest practical argument for reducers in a performance-sensitive
tree. The `useState` equivalent needs a `useCallback` per handler, each with a
dependency array to keep honest, and one inline arrow anywhere in the JSX undoes
the lot.

## ex8 — reducers compose

The board reducer handles board-level actions itself and delegates card-level
ones to `cardReducer(card, action)`, which knows nothing about boards. Two
benefits: `cardReducer` is unit-testable in isolation, and the board's `map` can
compare the returned card with the old one and return the *same board object*
when nothing changed.

That last part is the detail worth stealing. A `map` that always allocates a new
array means every card-level dispatch invalidates every memoized card. Returning
`state` unchanged when the targeted card is unchanged makes no-ops genuinely
free.

## challenge — guards, and the bailout

A state machine is a reducer plus the discipline that each action is only
meaningful in some states. `{ type: "paid" }` while `status` is `"cart"` is not
an error to throw — the user double-clicked, or a stale event arrived — it is
simply nothing, and the correct response is `return state`.

Deriving the totals rather than storing them keeps the machine honest: there is
no transition that can forget to update a total, because there is no total to
update. And reporting transitions through an injected callback is how you get
an audit log without putting a side effect in the reducer — the reducer stays
pure, and the effect that reports lives outside it.

## review1 — the three classic faults

The mutation (`state.items.push(...)`) means React compares the array with
itself, sees no change, and skips the render. The command-shaped action
(`{ type: "setTotal", total }`) means the total was computed at the call site, so
two callers can compute it differently and the reducer cannot enforce anything.
The no-op that returns a fresh object costs a commit every time the user presses
a disabled-in-effect button. Each is a different lesson and each has a one-line
fix.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — `useReducer`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useReducer)
- [react.dev — Extracting State Logic into a Reducer](https://react.dev/learn/extracting-state-logic-into-a-reducer)
- [react.dev — Choosing the State Structure](https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure)
- [react.dev — Keeping Components Pure](https://react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure)
- [TypeScript — Discriminated unions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#discriminated-unions)
- [TypeScript — Exhaustiveness checking](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#exhaustiveness-checking)
- [Making impossible states impossible](https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure#avoid-contradictions-in-state)

# Long reading — react/v3ra04_reducer_modelling

## What `useReducer` does under the hood

`useState` is implemented in terms of `useReducer`. Internally React has one
update mechanism: each state hook owns a circular linked list of pending
updates, each carrying a lane (a priority) and either a value or a function.
`useState`'s reducer is a built-in one called `basicStateReducer` that returns
`typeof action === "function" ? action(state) : action` — which is exactly why
the updater form of a setter exists and why it behaves like a tiny reducer.

`useReducer` simply lets you supply that function. Everything else — queueing,
lanes, batching, the eager bailout — is identical. Two consequences follow.

First, **your reducer runs during render**, not when you dispatch. Dispatching
appends to the queue and schedules work; React processes the queue at the start
of the next render of that component, applying each pending action in order.
That is why a reducer must be pure, why reading state immediately after
dispatching gives you the old value, and why React can throw away a render and
replay the queue without harm.

Second, **the eager bailout applies**. If the queue was empty, React computes
the next state immediately and, if `Object.is` says it equals the current one,
schedules nothing at all. A reducer that returns `state` for a guarded
transition therefore costs a function call and nothing else — no render, no
commit, no effects.

`dispatch` is created once and stored on the hook, which is where its stability
guarantee comes from. It is not memoized; it is genuinely the same function.

## Where this shape came from

The reducer pattern predates React's version of it. `Array.prototype.reduce`
gave the name; Elm gave the architecture — a model, a set of messages, and an
`update : Msg -> Model -> Model` — and Redux brought that into JavaScript in
2015, at a moment when Flux's multiple stores and dispatcher were proving hard
to reason about.

Redux was, for several years, how large React applications managed state, and
it accumulated a reputation for boilerplate that Redux Toolkit later fixed.
`useReducer` arrived with hooks in 2019 as the *local* version of the same idea:
the same discipline, the same testability, none of the global store, middleware
or devtools.

That distinction still trips people up in interviews. `useReducer` gives you the
pattern; Redux (or Zustand, or Jotai, or a context-plus-reducer of your own)
gives you the *sharing*. If your reducer's state needs to be read by components
in three different branches of the tree, `useReducer` alone will not do it, and
the next sector is about the composition that will.

The TypeScript half of the story matters as much. Discriminated unions with
literal `type` fields, narrowing inside a `switch`, and exhaustiveness via
assignment to `never` are what turn a reducer from "a big switch" into a
checkable specification. In a JavaScript codebase, a reducer is a convention. In
a TypeScript one, it is enforced.

## Modelling notes

**Prefer variants to flags.** The number of representable states of a record of
`n` booleans is `2^n`, and the number that are meaningful is usually `n + 1`.
Every gap is a place a defensive check will eventually be written, and defensive
checks are where behaviour hides.

**Put the payload on the variant that has it.** `{ status: "success"; rows:
Row[] }` means `rows` is non-nullable exactly where it exists. Hoisting `rows`
to the top level as `Row[] | null` re-introduces the nullability everywhere.

**Normalise collections when they are looked up by id.** A `Record<string,
Card>` plus an array of ids makes "update one card" a single-key change rather
than a `map` over everything, which preserves the identity of untouched entries
and keeps memoized children still.

**Do not store what you can derive.** Totals, counts, sort orders, validity,
"can I submit". Each is a function of the state, and each stored copy is a
transition that can forget to update it.

**Keep the reducer honest about its own scope.** A reducer that reaches for
`props` is a reducer that is not a function of `(state, action)`. If a
transition needs a prop, pass it in the action.

## State machines, and how far to take them

A reducer with guards is a finite state machine written by hand: a set of
states, a set of events, and a transition function that is total — every
(state, event) pair has an answer, and for most pairs the answer is "nothing
happens". That totality is the property that makes machines pleasant to work
with, because "what happens if the user double-clicks Pay" stops being a
question you have to think about and becomes a row in a table you already wrote.

Formal libraries — XState is the well-known one — add things a hand-written
reducer does not have: hierarchical and parallel states, entry and exit actions,
delayed transitions, and a visualiser that renders the machine as a diagram
non-engineers can review. That last one is genuinely valuable on a flow with
regulatory or commercial consequences, because it turns the implementation into
an artefact a product owner can check.

The cost is a dependency, a new vocabulary, and a layer of indirection that
smaller flows do not repay. The honest boundary is roughly: fewer than about six
states and a handful of guards, a plain reducer with a `switch` on `status` is
clearer than any library; more than that — especially with nesting, timeouts or
cancellation — and you are re-implementing a machine library badly.

What survives at every size is the discipline, not the tool: switch on the
state first, list the events each state accepts, and return the current state
for everything else.

## Performance notes

**Bailouts are the reducer's cheapest optimisation.** Returning `state` for
no-ops means a component with a memoized subtree does no work at all when the
user presses a button that is currently meaningless.

**Preserve identity through delegation.** A parent reducer that always builds a
new array over its children invalidates every memoized child on every action.
Compare the sub-reducer's result with the previous value and reuse the array
when nothing moved.

**Lazy init matters more than it looks.** Parsing saved state, building an index,
seeding a large structure — all of it happens on every render if you write it as
the second argument, and none of it shows up in a profiler as anything but "this
component is slow".

**One dispatch beats five setters.** Not because of batching — React batches
either way — but because five setters is five queues, five comparisons, and five
opportunities for two of them to be updated in different places.

## When not to use this

**Do not use a reducer for one boolean.** `useState` exists, and
`dispatch({ type: "toggled" })` is not clearer than `setOpen(!open)` when there
is one transition.

**Do not use a reducer as a global store.** It is local state. Sharing it needs
context, and context has its own cost model — that is the next sector, and
"reducer plus context" is a pattern with real limits, not a free Redux.

**Do not put async in the reducer.** Reducers are synchronous and pure. The
request goes in an effect or a handler, and the reducer receives
`{ type: "loadSucceeded", rows }` when it lands. The moment you want middleware,
you want a library.

**Do not model everything as a machine.** A form with eight independent fields
has no interesting transitions; a reducer there is a hundred lines that a record
and one `fieldChanged` action would have handled — and if you find yourself
writing one action per field, that is the signal.

**Do not reach for a reducer to fix re-renders alone.** The stable `dispatch` is
a genuine benefit, but restructuring your tree — colocation, pass-through — is
usually the larger win, and it is available without changing your state shape at
all.

is really a decision about the action set: if a case in the switch needs

## Hint 2

The narrowing you get from a literal `type` field is the reason to write it this

```tsx
switch (action.type) {

    return { items: state.items.filter((item) => item.id !== action.id) };
}
```

exactly where they are meaningful.

## Hint 3

serialised action. The decision left to you is where the "quantity of zero
removes the line" rule lives: inside `quantityChanged`, or by having the handler
dispatch `removed` instead. One of those keeps the rule enforceable from every
call site — pick that one and be able to say why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the naming convention, because it shapes everything else.
`{ type: "add" }` is an instruction to the reducer; `{ type: "added" }` is a
report of something that happened. The second leaves the reducer free to decide
what it means — which is the entire reason the pattern exists.

## Hint 2

Test the convention against a change: suppose adding an item must now also clear
a coupon. With `added`, that is a line in one case. With `add`, every caller that
"adds" must remember to also clear, because the action told the reducer what to
do rather than what happened.

## Hint 3

Then look at the `never` check as a maintenance device rather than a type trick.
In six months somebody adds `{ type: "restored"; items: Item[] }` to the union.
Without the check, the switch falls through, the reducer returns the current
state, and the feature "does nothing" with no error anywhere. With it, the file
does not compile until the case is written.

The gate:

## Hint 1

`useReducer(reducer, initialState)` takes a *value*. Arguments are evaluated
before the call, so `useReducer(reducer, parseFilters(saved))` runs the parse on
every render and throws away every result but the first.

## Hint 2

There is a third parameter for exactly this:

```tsx
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, savedFilters, parseFilters);
```

React calls `parseFilters(savedFilters)` once, at mount. The same idea appears
in `useState(() => expensive())`, and for the same reason.

## Hint 3

Use the three-argument form, and notice that `Reset` needs the starting value —
which the reducer cannot recompute without parsing again. The state shape in the
prompt is the hint: carry the parsed starting point *in the state*, put there

## Hint 1

Make the cost visible before you fix it. Put a counter in `parseFilters` and
type into any input elsewhere on the page — every keystroke that re-renders this
component runs the parse. The profiler will not show it as anything but "this
component is slow", because the work is inside the hook call, not in a child.

## Hint 2

The general rule is that **an initial value is an argument, and arguments are
eager**. That is why every "initial" API in React has a lazy variant:
`useState(() => …)`, `useReducer(r, arg, init)`, `useMemo(() => …, [])`. When
you see an expensive expression sitting directly in one of those positions, it
runs on every render.

## Hint 3

Now the `Reset` design, which is the part with a real choice in it. The reducer
needs a starting point to return to and must not recompute it, so it has to be
data the reducer already holds. Putting it in the state — written once by the

nullable. Now count how many of those combinations describe a situation that can
actually occur. Every gap between those two numbers is a defensive check

Put the payload on the variant that owns it, and keep genuinely global fields at
the top level of each variant:

  | { status: "failure"; attempts: number; message: string };

## Hint 3

Write actions for `loadStarted`, `loadSucceeded` and `loadFailed`, and render by

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Attack the "second press while loading" requirement first, because it exposes
why the boolean version is hard. With flags, the guard is
`if (isLoading) return;` at the call site — one line, in one handler, that a
second caller will forget. With a union, `loadStarted` while `status` is
`"loading"` can `return state`, and the rule is enforced for every caller for
ever.

## Hint 2

Then notice what the union does to the render. The flag version is a chain of
questions — is it loading, is there an error, is `rows` null — whose order
encodes precedence that nobody wrote down. The union version is a switch on one
field, and the exhaustiveness check means a new variant cannot be forgotten in
the UI either.

## Hint 3

Finally, be honest about the field that is *not* per-variant. `attempts` is
meaningful in all four states, so repeating it in each variant is correct but
noisy; the alternative is `{ attempts: number } & (…union of the rest…)`, which
TypeScript narrows just as well. Either is defensible. What is not defensible is
hoisting `rows` out of `success` to avoid the repetition — that puts the
nullability back everywhere and undoes the whole exercise.

## Exercise 5 — undo and redo

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. Export `historyReducer` and `DocumentEditor`.

```ts
type History = { past: string[]; present: string; future: string[] };

type HistoryAction =
  | { type: "edited"; text: string }
  | { type: "undone" }
  | { type: "redone" }
  | { type: "reset"; text: string };
```

`DocumentEditor({ initialText })` renders a textarea labelled `Document` bound
to `present`, buttons reading `Undo`, `Redo` and `Reset`, and a `role="status"`
paragraph reading `History: <past> back, <future> forward`.

The rules:

- `edited` pushes the old `present` onto `past`, sets the new `present`, and
  **clears `future`**;
- `edited` with text equal to the current `present` returns the same state
  object;
- `undone` with an empty `past` returns the same state object; so does `redone`
  with an empty `future`;
- `reset` discards all history.

`Undo` and `Redo` are disabled when they would do nothing.

The gate types three edits, undoes twice, edits again, and requires that `Redo`
is then disabled — the future was discarded by the new edit.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Draw the three lists as a single timeline with a cursor: `past` is everything
behind the cursor, `present` is under it, `future` is ahead. Undo moves the
cursor back one position; redo moves it forward; an edit writes at the cursor
and truncates everything ahead of it.

## Hint 2

Undo is three simultaneous moves, and writing them as one object literal keeps
them honest:

```tsx
case "undone":
  if (state.past.length === 0) return state;
  return {
    past: state.past.slice(0, -1),
    present: state.past[state.past.length - 1],
    future: [state.present, ...state.future],
  };
```

Redo is the mirror image. Write it from the timeline, not by copying and
editing this one.

## Hint 3

For `edited`, push the old present onto `past` and set `future: []`. The
decision left to you is whether every keystroke should be its own history entry
— it is what the gate tests and it is not what a real editor does. Be able to
say how you would coalesce runs of typing into one entry, and what extra state
that would need.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the rule people forget, because it is the one users notice:
**a new edit clears the future.** Without it, the redo stack still describes a
timeline that was abandoned, so pressing `Redo` after typing replaces the user's
text with something they never wrote — appearing, from their side, out of
nowhere.

## Hint 2

Then look at the two no-ops. Undo with an empty `past` must return `state`
itself, not `{ ...state }`. The difference is not tidiness: `Object.is` on the
same object means React schedules nothing, while a structural copy means a
render and a commit for a button press that did nothing — and in a memoized tree
that ripples outward.

## Hint 3

Finally, the invariant worth stating out loud, because it is what makes this
model correct rather than merely working: **`past`, `present` and `future`
always describe one timeline, and every action moves the cursor or truncates.**
If you can write down an action that leaves the three lists describing two
different documents, that action is wrong. The `reset` case is a good test of
it: discarding history entirely is a legitimate move, and discarding only
`past` would not be.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a form reducer, with derived validation

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export `signupReducer` and `SignupForm`.

The reducer state is `{ values: { email: string; password: string; confirm:
string }; touched: { email: boolean; password: boolean; confirm: boolean } }`,
with actions `fieldChanged`, `fieldBlurred` and `submitted`.

`SignupForm({ onSubmit })` renders three inputs labelled `Email`, `Password` and
`Confirm password`, a `Create account` button, and — for each field that is
**touched and invalid** — a paragraph with `role="alert"` containing the message.

The rules:

- `Email` must contain an `@`; message `Email needs an @`;
- `Password` must be at least eight characters; message
  `Password needs 8 characters`;
- `Confirm password` must equal `Password`; message `Passwords must match`;
- pressing `Create account` marks every field touched, and calls
  `onSubmit(values)` only when all three are valid.

**No error message may be stored in the reducer.** The gate inspects the state
and fails if it finds any of the three strings in it. It also types a valid
email into an invalid one and requires the alert to disappear on the same
commit.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Split the state into two questions. "What did the user type" cannot be
recomputed from anything — that is state. "Is this field valid" is a function of
what they typed — that is not. The `touched` flags are the interesting case:
decide which side they fall on before writing anything.

## Hint 2

Derive the errors during render, from the values, into a plain object:

```tsx
const errors = {
  email: values.email.includes("@") ? null : "Email needs an @",
  password: values.password.length >= 8 ? null : "Password needs 8 characters",
};
const isValid = Object.values(errors).every((error) => error === null);
```

Nothing to keep in step, and no way for a fixed field to keep showing its old
message.

## Hint 3

Keep `values` and `touched` in the reducer; compute `errors` and `isValid` in
the body; render an alert only where `touched[field] && errors[field]`. The
decision left to you is what `submitted` does in the reducer — it clearly marks
everything touched, but whether it also decides validity is a design question,
and one answer keeps the reducer ignorant of the validation rules.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Consider the specific bug the "no stored errors" rule prevents, because it is
the one every hand-rolled form has shipped at least once. Errors written by a
blur handler, values changed by a keystroke: the user fixes the field and the
message stays, because nothing recomputed it until the next blur.

## Hint 2

That is a two-sources-of-truth problem, and the general repair is always the
same — delete the derived copy. Once `errors` is computed during render there is
no code path in which the message and the value can disagree, so the gate's
"disappears on the same commit" requirement is satisfied by construction rather
than by remembering to revalidate.

## Hint 3

Now justify `touched`, which is the field that genuinely *is* state.
"Has the user visited this input" cannot be recomputed from the values — an
empty email is invalid whether or not it has been touched, and the whole point
of the flag is to avoid shouting at somebody before they have typed. That is the
test for what belongs in the reducer: **information the user's history carries
that the current values do not.**

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a stable dispatch

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. Export `counterReducer`, `Controls` and
`CounterBoard`.

`Controls` is wrapped in `memo` and its props are exactly
`{ dispatch: Dispatch<CounterAction>; onRender: () => void }`. It renders
buttons reading `Increment`, `Decrement` and `Reset`, and calls `onRender()` at
the top of its body.

`CounterBoard({ onControlsRender })` renders `Count: <n>` in a `role="status"`
paragraph, a `Doubled: <n>` paragraph, and `Controls`.

The gate presses each button twice — six presses — and requires `onRender` to
have been called **exactly once**.

Constraints: no `useCallback` and no `useMemo` anywhere in the file. If you find
yourself wanting one, the point of the exercise has not landed yet.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`memo` compares each prop with `Object.is`. Two of `Controls`'s props are
functions, and functions are compared by identity. So the whole exercise is:
where do those two functions come from, and are they the same object on every
render of the board?

## Hint 2

React guarantees the identity of the `dispatch` it hands you:

```tsx
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initial);
// `dispatch` is the same function for the lifetime of the component.
```

That is a documented guarantee, not an implementation detail — the same one
`useState` gives its setter.

## Hint 3

Pass `dispatch` straight through, and let `Controls` build its own actions. The
decision left to you is what `Controls` is allowed to know: passing `dispatch`
means the child names the actions, which couples it to the action union. Be able
to argue that trade against the `useState` alternative, where you would need one
memoized callback per button and a dependency array on each.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the `useState` version in your head and count what it costs. Three
handlers, so three `useCallback`s, so three dependency arrays; and if any of
them reads the current count, the updater form is needed or the array names the
state the callback is about to replace — the classic self-defeating
`useCallback`.

## Hint 2

Now count the reducer version: zero hooks beyond `useReducer`, zero dependency
arrays, and nothing that a future edit can silently break. The child's props
cannot lose their identity because neither of them was ever created during a
render.

## Hint 3

That is the strongest practical argument for reducers in a performance-sensitive
tree, and it generalises beyond this component: a context whose value is only
`dispatch` never invalidates its consumers; an effect that dispatches needs no
dependency on the dispatch; and a deep tree can be given the ability to change
state without being given anything that changes. The next sector builds on
exactly that property.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — composing reducers

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Export `cardReducer`, `boardReducer` and `Board`.

```ts
type Card = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean; votes: number };
type BoardState = { name: string; cards: Card[] };
```

`cardReducer(card: Card, action: CardAction): Card` handles `toggled`,
`renamed` and `upvoted` and knows nothing about boards.

`boardReducer(state: BoardState, action: BoardAction): BoardState` handles
`boardRenamed` and `cardAdded` itself, and delegates any action carrying a
`cardId` to `cardReducer`.

`Board({ initialState, onCardsIdentity })` renders the board name in an `<h2>`,
one row per card with its title, `done`/`to do`, the vote count, and buttons
reading `Toggle <title>`, `Upvote <title>`. It calls
`onCardsIdentity(state.cards)` at the top of its body so the gate can compare
array identity across renders.

The requirement that makes this an exercise: **when a delegated action does not
change the targeted card, `boardReducer` must return the same `BoardState`
object** — and when it does change one card, the `cards` array must be new but
every untouched card object must be the same object as before.

The gate dispatches `toggled` for a card id that does not exist, and requires
the state object to be identical. It then dispatches `upvoted` on card 2 and
requires cards 1 and 3 to be reference-identical to their previous selves.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling ex8
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the identity requirements are really protecting. In a memoized list,
every card that gets a new object identity re-renders. A `map` that rebuilds all
of them means upvoting one card redraws a hundred — the exact cost the memo was
added to avoid, arriving through the state layer instead of the props layer.

## Hint 2

So the rule generalises beyond this exercise: **a reducer over a collection
should preserve the identity of everything it did not touch.** That is also why
normalising by id — `Record<string, Card>` plus an array of ids — is the standard
move once collections get large: changing one entry is a single-key spread and
nothing else moves.

## Hint 3

The second benefit of delegation is the one you will feel in review.
`cardReducer` is a pure function from a card and an action to a card, so its
tests need no board, no React and no fixtures beyond one object. When the card
rules get complicated — and they always do — that boundary is what stops the
board reducer becoming a two-hundred-line switch nobody wants to change.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a checkout machine

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. Export `checkoutReducer` and `Checkout`.

```ts
type Line = { id: string; name: string; unitPence: number; quantity: number };

type CheckoutState =
  | { status: "shopping"; lines: Line[] }
  | { status: "reviewing"; lines: Line[] }
  | { status: "paying"; lines: Line[] }
  | { status: "paid"; lines: Line[]; reference: string }
  | { status: "failed"; lines: Line[]; message: string };
```

Actions: `lineAdded`, `lineRemoved`, `reviewRequested`, `backToShopping`,
`paymentStarted`, `paymentSucceeded` (carrying `reference`),
`paymentFailed` (carrying `message`).

The guards — an action that is not legal in the current state returns **the same
state object**:

| From | Legal actions |
| --- | --- |
| `shopping` | `lineAdded`, `lineRemoved`, `reviewRequested` (only with at least one line) |
| `reviewing` | `backToShopping`, `paymentStarted`, `lineRemoved` |
| `paying` | `paymentSucceeded`, `paymentFailed` |
| `paid` | nothing |
| `failed` | `backToShopping`, `paymentStarted` |

`Checkout({ catalogue, pay, onTransition })` renders a `role="status"` paragraph
naming the state, one `Add <name>` button per catalogue entry, the lines, a
`Total: £<n.nn>` paragraph, and whichever of `Review`, `Back`, `Pay` and
`Try again` the current state permits. `pay()` returns a promise of a reference
string.

Two more requirements:

1. **Totals are derived, never stored.** The gate inspects the state for any
   numeric total and fails if it finds one.
2. `onTransition(fromStatus, action.type, toStatus)` is called for every
   **accepted** transition and never for a rejected one — and the reducer must
   stay pure, so this cannot be called from inside it.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the table as the specification it is. Each row is a `case` on
`state.status`, not on `action.type` — switching on the state first and the
action second is what makes the guards obvious and what makes an illegal pairing
fall through to a single `return state`.

## Hint 2

Two nested switches, or one switch plus a legality check. The shape that reads
best:

```tsx
switch (state.status) {
  case "paying":
    if (action.type === "paymentSucceeded")
      return { status: "paid", lines: state.lines, reference: action.reference };
    if (action.type === "paymentFailed")
      return { status: "failed", lines: state.lines, message: action.message };
    return state;                       // anything else is not legal here
  …
}
```

Note `reviewRequested` has an extra condition — an empty cart cannot be
reviewed — and the same `return state` handles it.

## Hint 3

For requirement 2, the reducer cannot call `onTransition` without becoming
impure, so the reporting has to happen where the *result* is visible: compare
the status before and after. The decision left to you is where that comparison
lives — an effect keyed on the status can see a change but not which action
caused it, so you will need to carry something. Work out the smallest thing that
is enough.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the guards, because they are the reason this is a machine rather than
a bag of state. `paymentStarted` while already `paying` is not an error to
throw — the user double-clicked, or a retry fired — and it is not a state change
either. It is *nothing*, and `return state` says so in a way React understands:
`Object.is` is true, so no render, no commit, no effects.

## Hint 2

Then the derived total. Storing `totalPence` would mean every transition that
touches `lines` must remember to recompute it, and one that forgets produces a
checkout that charges the wrong amount — the worst class of bug in this domain.
Derive it in the component from `state.lines` and the arithmetic cannot drift
from the data.

Work in pence, not pounds. `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3`, and money in floating point
is an outage waiting for a big enough order.

## Hint 3

Now requirement 2, which is a genuine design problem rather than a trick. You
need to know *which* action was accepted, and only the dispatch site knows that
— but the dispatch site does not know whether the reducer accepted it. The
smallest honest answer is to wrap `dispatch` in a function that captures the
current status, dispatches, and lets an effect compare; or to have the component
hold the last accepted action in the state itself. Both are defensible; a
`console.log` inside the reducer is not, and neither is calling `onTransition`
from a handler that has not checked whether anything changed.

exercises.prompt:
## Review — three faults in one reducer

Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. `playlistReducer` is written, compiles, and is
wrong three times over:

```tsx
export function playlistReducer(state: PlaylistState, action: PlaylistAction) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "trackAdded":
      state.tracks.push(action.track);        // 1
      return state;
    case "setDuration":
      return { ...state, totalSeconds: action.totalSeconds };   // 2
    case "shuffleToggled":
      return { ...state, shuffle: !state.shuffle };
    case "cleared":
      return { ...state, tracks: [] };        // 3
  }
}
```

`PlaylistPanel({ tracks, onPanelRender })` renders `Tracks: <n>`,
`Total: <n>s` and `Shuffle: on|off` in a `role="status"` region, plus
`Add <title>` buttons, a `Shuffle` button and a `Clear` button.

The three faults, and what the gate checks:

1. **The mutation.** Adding a track changes nothing on screen. Fix it and the
   count must follow.
2. **The command-shaped action.** `setDuration` carries a total computed by the
   caller, so two callers can disagree and the reducer enforces nothing. The
   total must be derived instead, and `setDuration` must disappear from the
   union — the gate fails if the state contains a stored total.
3. **The no-op that allocates.** `Clear` on an already-empty playlist must
   return the same state object; the gate presses it three times on an empty
   playlist and requires `onPanelRender` not to be called again.

Add the `never` check while you are there.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra04_reducer_modelling review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three faults, three separate rules from this sector, and they do not interact.
Fix them one at a time and re-read the gate's three requirements after each —
resist the urge to rewrite the file in one go.

## Hint 2

For the first, the array in state must be replaced, not written to:
`{ ...state, tracks: [...state.tracks, action.track] }`. For the third, compare
before allocating: `state.tracks.length === 0 ? state : { ...state, tracks: [] }`.

## Hint 3

The second is the design fault rather than the mechanical one. Delete
`totalSeconds` from the state and the `setDuration` variant from the union, and
compute the total in the component from `state.tracks`. The decision left to you
is where the summing lives — inline in the JSX, a `const` in the body, or a
small exported helper that a test can call — and only one of those is easy to
assert on without rendering.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Diagnose fault 1 rather than pattern-matching it. `push` changes the array
React is already holding, then `return state` hands back the same reference, so
`Object.is` is true and React schedules nothing. The data changed and the screen
did not, which is why this bug survives review: the state really is correct.

## Hint 2

Fault 2 is the one worth arguing about in a real review, because it compiles and
"works". `{ type: "setDuration", totalSeconds }` means the arithmetic happened at
the call site — so a second caller can compute it differently, a caller can
forget to send it after adding a track, and the reducer has no way to notice. An
action should be a *fact about what happened*; the consequence is the reducer's
job.

The general test: if you removed the field from the payload, could the reducer
still compute the result? If yes, the field should not be in the payload.

## Hint 3

Fault 3 looks like a micro-optimisation and is not. In a memoized tree a fresh
state object on a no-op invalidates every consumer of that state — so a button
that does nothing costs a full re-render of everything below it. `return state`
is the reducer's way of telling React "nothing happened", and it is the same
mechanism as the `Object.is` bailout on a setter.

lessons.title: V3·RA5 — Context, provider composition and the re-render trap
lessons.summary: Context solves prop drilling and creates a re-render problem in its place. This sector covers the throwing hook, memoized values, splitting state from dispatch, composing providers without a JSX pyramid, scoped overrides, selector-based subscriptions, `use(Context)` in a branch, and the identity pitfalls.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RA5 — Context, provider composition and the re-render trap

`09_context_reducer` and `d16_context` gave you a provider, a `useX()` hook that
throws when it is missing, and the idea that context removes prop drilling. All
true. This sector is about what happens next: when there are five providers,
when the value is an object, and when the profiler shows forty components
re-rendering because a theme toggled.

The thing to understand first is what context actually is. **It is not a store.**
It has no subscription granularity, no selectors, and no way for a consumer to
say "only wake me for this field". It is a way of passing a value down the tree
without threading it through props — and the propagation rule is blunt:

> When a provider's `value` is not `Object.is`-equal to its previous value,
> **every consumer of that context below it re-renders**, regardless of which
> part of the value they read.

That single sentence explains every context performance problem you will ever
see, and most of the design decisions below.

## Concept — React 19 syntax, and the throwing hook

```tsx
const ThemeContext = createContext<Theme | null>(null);

export function useTheme(): Theme {
  const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
  if (theme === null) throw new Error("useTheme must be used inside ThemeProvider");
  return theme;
}
```

Two things. In React 19 you render `<ThemeContext value={theme}>` directly —
`.Provider` is no longer required, and is deprecated. And the default value is
`null` on purpose: a "sensible default" turns a missing provider into a
component that silently renders with the wrong data, whereas `null` plus a
throwing hook turns it into an error with a name, at the exact component that
needed it. Consumers also get a non-nullable type for free.

## Concept — the re-render trap

```tsx
// Every render of the provider produces a new object.
<SessionContext value={{ user, signOut }}>{children}</SessionContext>
```

That object is rebuilt whenever anything re-renders `SessionProvider` — including
a parent re-rendering for a completely unrelated reason. `Object.is` fails, and
every consumer in the subtree re-renders. `useMemo` on the value is the minimum
fix:

```tsx
const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, signOut }), [user, signOut]);
```

The better fix is often structural. If half your consumers only ever call
`signOut` and never read `user`, they are being woken for a value they do not
use — and the answer is two contexts.

## Concept — split the value that changes from the value that does not

`dispatch` from `useReducer` is stable for the life of the component. Put it in
its own context and its consumers never re-render at all, while the state
context wakes only the components that read state. That pairing — one context
for the data, one for the actions — is the standard shape for a context-plus-
reducer feature, and it is why the previous sector spent an exercise on
`dispatch` identity.

## Concept — composing providers without a pyramid

Five providers nested by hand is eleven lines of closing tags and a merge
conflict waiting to happen. A `compose` helper turns the list into data:

```tsx
const providers = [ThemeProvider, SessionProvider, ToastProvider];
```

Ordering still matters — a provider that *reads* another must be inside it — and
making the list explicit makes that dependency visible rather than accidental.

lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/v3ra05_context_composition

## Notes

**Context propagates by value identity, not by field.** A provider whose value
changed wakes every consumer beneath it. There is no partial subscription, and
`memo` on a consumer does not help — context propagation bypasses the memo
check, because the consumer's *context* changed even though its props did not.
That surprises people, and it is the single most important fact in this sector.

**`memo` stops prop propagation, not context propagation.** A memoized component
between the provider and a consumer does prevent the *parent's* re-render from
reaching down. It does nothing about the consumer's own context subscription.
So the classic "wrap it in memo and it will be fine" reflex fails here, and the
fix has to be about what is in the value.

**The default value is a trap unless it is `null`.** `createContext("light")`
means a component rendered outside a provider silently gets `"light"` — a bug
that survives to production looking like a styling glitch. `createContext<T |
null>(null)` plus a hook that throws gives you a stack trace pointing at the
component that needed the provider, and gives every consumer a non-nullable type.

**React 19 renders the context itself.** `<ThemeContext value={x}>` replaces
`<ThemeContext.Provider value={x}>`. `.Provider` still works and is deprecated;
`Context.Consumer` has been deprecated for longer and has no reason to exist in
a hooks codebase.

**`use(Context)` is a hook that is allowed in a branch.** It is the one
exception React has carved out, and it exists because the alternative — reading
a context you might not need, above an early return — is a real cost in some
trees. It still may not be called inside a loop, a `try` block, or after an
`await`.

**Two contexts beat one wide one.** Splitting by change frequency is the highest
leverage move available: state versus actions, session versus theme, "the thing
that changes on every keystroke" versus "the thing that changes twice a day".

## ex1 — the shape every context should have

Three exports and no shortcuts: the context (not exported, usually — nobody
outside should be reading it directly), the provider, and the hook. The hook is
the API; the context is the implementation.

The throwing check is the part that earns its keep. It converts "why is the
label in English" into an error naming the missing provider, and it narrows
`Theme | null` to `Theme` for every consumer, so the rest of your code has no
`?.` in it.

## ex2 — the object that is rebuilt

The provider re-renders for reasons that have nothing to do with the session —
its parent rendered — and the value literal is rebuilt, and every consumer wakes.
`useMemo(() => ({ user, signOut }), [user, signOut])` fixes it, on one condition:
`signOut` must itself be stable, or the memo's dependency changes every render
and you have moved the problem one level down.

That is worth generalising. **Memoizing a value only helps if its dependencies
are themselves stable.** A chain of `useMemo`s over unstable inputs is a chain of
no-ops, and it is one of the commonest reasons "I memoized it and nothing
changed".

## ex3 — the split that costs nothing

`dispatch` never changes, so a `TodoDispatchContext` never invalidates. Its
consumers — every button, every menu item, every keyboard shortcut — re-render
only when their own parents do. The state context wakes the components that
actually display something.

The measurable outcome is that a page with one list and twenty action buttons
goes from twenty-one consumers waking on every keystroke to one. And it costs
you two `createContext` calls and one extra provider.

## ex4 — providers as data

The `compose` helper is four lines, and its real value is not brevity. It makes
the *order* explicit and reviewable, which matters because the order encodes a
dependency: a provider that calls `useTheme()` in its own body must be nested
inside the theme provider, and in a hand-nested pyramid that constraint is
invisible until someone reorders two lines and the app throws.

Write the list top-to-bottom as outermost-to-innermost and put a comment on any
entry whose position is load-bearing.

## ex5 — the nearest provider wins

A consumer reads the closest provider above it. That is what makes scoped
overrides work — a `compact` density inside a sidebar, a different locale inside
a preview pane — and it is a genuinely useful pattern that people forget context
supports at all.

The thing to watch is that the inner provider is a *different value*, not a
different context. Consumers do not know which provider answered them, so the
override is invisible from below, which is exactly what you want for theming and
exactly what makes debugging harder if you overuse it.

## ex6 — putting a store in context

The trick is to publish something whose *identity never changes* — a store object
— and let each consumer subscribe to the slice it cares about with
`useSyncExternalStore`. The context value is constant, so context propagation
never fires; the re-renders come from the subscription instead, which does have
granularity.

That is, in outline, how every state library that "solves context re-renders"
works. Building it once by hand is worth doing, because afterwards the trade-off
is obvious: you have gained selector-level subscriptions and given up the ability
to read the state during render without subscribing.

## ex7 — the conditional read

```tsx
if (!enabled) return <Placeholder />;
const theme = use(ThemeContext);
```

`useContext` there is a rules-of-hooks violation: the hook list is positional, so
a call that sometimes does not happen shifts every later hook. `use` is exempt
because React tracks context reads separately from the hook list.

The remaining restrictions are worth naming: not in a loop, not inside
`try`/`catch` — and the second one matters, because `use` on a promise throws to
the nearest Suspense boundary, so catching it locally would swallow the
mechanism. That is the next sector.

## ex8 — two ways to have no context at all

`const Ctx = createContext(null)` inside a component body creates a **new
context object on every render**. Providers and consumers then refer to
different objects, so every consumer falls back to the default and the provider
appears to do nothing. Contexts belong at module scope, always.

The second fault is subtler and more common in real code: two `<SessionProvider>`
elements in different branches of the tree are two independent pieces of state.
Nothing warns you. Whether that is a bug or a feature depends on whether you
meant to scope it, which is why "there is exactly one of these, near the root"
is worth writing down.

## challenge — the budget

Every clause maps to one of the moves above: theme and session are separate
contexts because they change at different rates; state and actions are separate
because actions never change; the values are memoized because the providers
re-render for unrelated reasons; and the composition is a list so the ordering
dependency is visible. Nothing in the budget requires `memo`.

## review1 — reading a context profile

Three of the five consumers wake for nothing, and each has a different cause: an
unmemoized value object, a consumer that reads a context it does not need, and a
provider mounted so high that unrelated renders reach it. The diagnostic
question for each is the same one: *what changed, and did this component read
it?*

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Passing Data Deeply with Context](https://react.dev/learn/passing-data-deeply-with-context)
- [react.dev — Scaling Up with Reducer and Context](https://react.dev/learn/scaling-up-with-reducer-and-context)
- [react.dev — `createContext`](https://react.dev/reference/react/createContext)
- [react.dev — `useContext`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useContext)
- [react.dev — `use`](https://react.dev/reference/react/use)
- [react.dev — `useSyncExternalStore`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore)
- [React 19 — `<Context>` as a provider](https://react.dev/blog/2024/12/05/react-19)
