# V3·RA5 — Context and provider composition (archive)

## The propagation rule

One sentence, and everything else is a consequence:

> A provider whose `value` is not `Object.is`-equal to its previous value
> re-renders **every** consumer of that context in its subtree, whatever part of
> the value they read.

Consequences worth stating separately:

- **`memo` does not stop it.** A memoized component whose props did not change
  still re-renders if it consumes a context whose value changed. Context
  propagation is a separate path from prop propagation.
- **Reading one field costs the same as reading all of them.** There is no
  selector. A component that only uses `value.locale` wakes when `value.user`
  changes.
- **The provider's own re-renders are what rebuild the value.** Which means an
  unrelated parent render is enough to invalidate everything below.

## Worked example — the standard shape

```tsx
import { createContext, useContext, useMemo, useState } from "react";
import type { ReactNode } from "react";

type Session = { user: string | null; signOut: () => void };

const SessionContext = createContext<Session | null>(null);

export function useSession(): Session {
  const session = useContext(SessionContext);
  if (session === null) {
    throw new Error("useSession must be used inside a SessionProvider");
  }
  return session;
}

export function SessionProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const signOut = useCallback(() => setUser(null), []);
  const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, signOut }), [user, signOut]);

  return <SessionContext value={value}>{children}</SessionContext>;
}
```

Three things are deliberate. The context is not exported — the hook is the API.
The default is `null`, so a missing provider is an error rather than a silently
wrong render. And `signOut` is memoized, because `useMemo` over an unstable
dependency is a no-op with extra steps.

## Worked example — state and actions, separately

```tsx
const TodosContext = createContext<Todo[] | null>(null);
const TodosDispatchContext = createContext<Dispatch<TodoAction> | null>(null);

export function TodosProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [todos, dispatch] = useReducer(todosReducer, []);
  return (
    <TodosContext value={todos}>
      <TodosDispatchContext value={dispatch}>{children}</TodosDispatchContext>
    </TodosContext>
  );
}
```

`dispatch` is stable for the life of the component, so `TodosDispatchContext`
never invalidates — every button, menu item and shortcut handler that only needs
to *cause* a change stops re-rendering entirely. No `useMemo` is needed on
either value: one is an array the reducer manages, the other never changes.

## Worked example — composing providers

```tsx
type Wrapper = ({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) => ReactNode;

export function composeProviders(providers: Wrapper[]): Wrapper {
  return function Composed({ children }) {
    return providers.reduceRight<ReactNode>(
      (acc, Provider) => <Provider>{acc}</Provider>,
      children,
    );
  };
}

// Outermost first. SessionProvider reads the theme, so it must be inside it.
const AppProviders = composeProviders([ThemeProvider, SessionProvider, ToastProvider]);
```

`reduceRight` so the array reads outermost-to-innermost, which is how people
read a nested JSX tree. The order is now a line of code somebody can review
rather than an accident of indentation.

## Worked example — a store in context

```tsx
const StoreContext = createContext<Store | null>(null);   // identity never changes

export function useStoreSlice<T>(select: (state: State) => T): T {
  const store = useStore();
  return useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, () => select(store.getSnapshot()));
}
```

The context value is the store object, created once, so context propagation
never fires. Each consumer subscribes to the slice it reads, so a change to one
field wakes only the components that select it. Return primitives from
selectors, or cache derived objects in the store — a fresh array from a selector
re-renders forever.

## Worked example — a scoped override

```tsx
<DensityProvider density="comfortable">
  <main>…</main>
  <aside>
    <DensityProvider density="compact">…</DensityProvider>
  </aside>
</DensityProvider>
```

A consumer reads the *nearest* provider above it, so nesting a second one is the
entire mechanism — same context object, different value. Rows inside the aside
have no branch for it and would behave identically if the panel became
comfortable tomorrow.

The same property that makes this safe makes it hard to debug: a value with no
visible source. "Why is this row compact" is answered by walking the tree in
DevTools, not by reading the component, which is the standing argument for
reserving context for genuinely ambient concerns.

## Common mistakes

- **An inline object as the value.** Rebuilt every render; every consumer wakes.
- **`useMemo` over an unstable dependency.** A no-op with ceremony.
- **A non-null default value.** A missing provider becomes a silent wrong render.
- **`createContext` inside a component.** A new context per render; consumers
  fall back to the default and the provider appears inert.
- **Two provider instances that were meant to be one.** Two independent states,
  no warning.
- **Expecting `memo` to stop context propagation.** It does not.
- **One wide context for everything.** Couples the change rate of your fastest
  value to the render cost of your whole tree.
- **A selector returning a new array through `useSyncExternalStore`.** Infinite
  re-render, and React will tell you the snapshot should be cached.
- **`Context.Consumer` in new code.** Deprecated; the hook is the API.
- **Putting a provider high just in case.** The higher it is, the more unrelated
  renders rebuild its value.

## Interview answer

> **"What is the downside of context, and how do you deal with it?"**
>
> Context has no subscription granularity. When a provider's value changes by
> `Object.is`, every consumer in the subtree re-renders, whichever field they
> read — and `memo` does not help, because context propagation is a separate
> path from props.
>
> Three moves, in order of how much they buy. First, memoize the value, because
> an inline object literal is rebuilt whenever the provider re-renders for any
> reason at all — and check that the memo's own dependencies are stable, or you
> have moved the problem rather than fixed it. Second, split by change rate: one
> context for state and one for `dispatch`, which is stable, so every component
> that only causes changes stops re-rendering entirely. Third, if you genuinely
> need per-field subscriptions, put a *store* in the context — its identity never
> changes, so context propagation never fires — and have consumers subscribe with
> `useSyncExternalStore` and a selector. That last step is, in outline, what
> every state library is doing.
>
> The other thing I would say is that context is for values that are genuinely
> ambient — theme, locale, session, a router. Threading a prop through two
> components is not prop drilling, it is just props.

## Check yourself

1. State the propagation rule exactly. What does `memo` do about it?
2. Why is `null` the right default value, and what does the throwing hook buy?
3. What is the React 19 provider syntax, and what is deprecated?
4. Your value is `useMemo`'d and consumers still wake on every render. Why?
5. Why does splitting `dispatch` into its own context cost nothing?
6. Write `composeProviders`. Why `reduceRight`?
7. When is the ordering of composed providers load-bearing?
8. How does a nested provider override an outer one, and how would a consumer
   know which answered?
9. How does putting a store in context restore per-field subscriptions? What do
   you give up?
10. Why is `use(Context)` allowed in a branch when `useContext` is not?
11. Where may `use` still not be called?
12. What happens if `createContext` is called inside a component body?
13. Two `<SessionProvider>` elements in one app. Bug or feature?
14. When would you not use context at all?

# Long reading — react/v3ra05_context_composition

## How context propagation actually works

A context object is a pair of value slots and a bookkeeping structure. When
React renders a provider, it pushes the new value onto the context's stack and
compares it with the previous one using `Object.is`. If they are equal, React
can take a fast path: the subtree has no context work to do, and if nothing else
scheduled anything, whole branches are skipped.

If they differ, React walks the subtree looking for consumers. This is the part
worth understanding, because it explains the `memo` surprise. During the walk,
React does **not** stop at a memoized component whose props are unchanged; it
descends through it, because a consumer further down has a *dependency on this
context* recorded on its fiber. When it finds one, it schedules work on that
fiber and marks the path from the provider to it as having pending work.

So there are two independent propagation paths in React: one down through props
and elements, which `memo` and element identity can interrupt, and one from a
provider to its registered consumers, which nothing can interrupt except the
value not changing. Every context performance technique is therefore about the
value: make it change less often, make it smaller, or make it never change at
all and move the notification elsewhere.

The consumer registration itself is cheap — `useContext` records a dependency on
the fiber and returns the current value — which is why reading five contexts in
one component is not a problem. What is a problem is one context that changes
five times as often as it needs to.

## A short history of "how do I share state"

The original context API was undocumented and unstable, and everybody used
Redux instead, partly for the store and partly because passing a value down
without props was otherwise painful. React 16.3 shipped the modern
`createContext` with a render-prop `Consumer`; hooks made `useContext` the
obvious way to read it; and React 19 removed the last of the ceremony by letting
the context object itself be the provider element.

Along the way the community learned the lesson this sector teaches, mostly the
hard way. "Context plus reducer replaces Redux" was a widely repeated claim
around 2019, and it is true for the *shape* of the problem and false for the
*performance* of the solution: Redux's `connect`, and later `useSelector`,
always had selector-level subscriptions, which context does not. That gap is why
Zustand, Jotai, Valtio and Redux Toolkit all still exist, and why every one of
them is built on either `useSyncExternalStore` or something equivalent.

`useSyncExternalStore` itself was added in React 18 for a related but distinct
reason: with concurrent rendering, a store read during an interrupted render
could disagree with the same store read after it resumed, so two components
could commit different values from the same source in one paint. That is called
**tearing**, and the hook exists to let React re-read the snapshot at the right
moments and force a synchronous re-render if it changed. Using it for
selector-based context subscriptions is a happy side effect of a correctness
API.

`use` arrived in React 19 as a different kind of primitive: not a hook in the
positional sense, but a first-class operator for reading a resource — a context
or a promise — that is allowed to appear conditionally. It is the first genuine
exception to the rules of hooks, and it is exempt because React does not need a
stable call index to resolve a context or a promise.

## Design notes

**Context is for ambient values.** Theme, locale, session, feature flags, a
router, a design-system density setting. The test: would you be annoyed to pass
this through five components as a prop *every time*, in every feature? If the
answer is "only in this one screen", it is a prop.

**Passing a prop through two levels is not prop drilling.** Context has a real
cost in indirection — a value with no visible source — and paying it to avoid
writing `theme={theme}` twice is a bad trade.

**Colocate providers.** Mount a provider at the lowest node that contains all
its consumers. A provider at the root re-renders whenever the root does, and its
value is rebuilt every time; the same provider mounted inside a feature is
insulated from everything above it.

**One context, one concern.** Merging theme and session into an `AppContext`
because "they are both global" ties the change rate of the faster one to the
render cost of both.

**Prefer composition to configuration.** Providers that each own one thing, in a
list you can read, beat one provider taking eight props.

## The order to fix things in

A context performance investigation has a natural order, and doing it backwards
wastes the most time.

**Colocate first.** Find the value in the context that changes most often and
ask how many components read it. A draft string read by one editor, a hover
state read by one row, a scroll offset read by one panel — none of those belong
in a shared value at all, and removing them removes the loudest source of
invalidation without touching anything else.

**Split second.** Group what remains by change rate and by reader set. State and
actions is the standard split and the one that pays most, because the actions
half never changes. Theme and session is another: two values that are both
"global" but move on completely different timescales.

**Memoize third.** Only now is `useMemo` on the value the right move, and only
where the provider genuinely re-renders for reasons unrelated to its own value.
Check the memo's dependencies before you trust it.

**Reach for a store last.** Selector subscriptions are the answer to a measured
problem with a genuinely hot value that many components read different parts of.
Reached for first, it is a large amount of machinery in front of state that
`useState` was handling correctly.

## Performance notes

**The value's stability is the whole game.** An unmemoized object is the default
state of a hand-written provider and is almost always the cause when a profiler
shows a wide, shallow flash of re-renders.

**A memo chain is only as stable as its weakest dependency.** `useMemo(() => ({
user, signOut }), [user, signOut])` is a no-op if `signOut` is an inline arrow.
Check the leaves before blaming the root.

**Stable contexts are free.** A context whose value never changes — a store, a
`dispatch`, a set of constants — costs one `Object.is` per provider render and
wakes nobody.

**Splitting beats memoizing.** Two contexts with narrow values usually beat one
memoized wide value, because the memo only avoids *unnecessary* changes while
the split also avoids *irrelevant* ones.

**Measure with the Profiler's "why did this render".** It names context as a
cause explicitly, which distinguishes it from a parent render and saves an hour
of guessing.

## When not to use this

**Do not use context for high-frequency values.** Mouse position, scroll offset,
an animation clock, the contents of a text input. Every consumer re-renders on
every change, and the tree cannot keep up. Those belong in a store with
selectors, in a ref plus direct DOM writes, or colocated with the one component
that needs them.

**Do not use context as a cache for server data.** Requests, caching,
revalidation, retries and deduplication are a solved problem in React Query, SWR
or a router loader, and a hand-rolled context cache will reimplement half of one
badly.

**Do not use context to avoid thinking about component boundaries.** A component
that reaches for five contexts is often one that should have been given props by
a smaller parent.

**Do not reach for a store in context on day one.** It is the right answer when
you have measured a real problem with a genuinely hot value. Reached for early,
it costs you the ability to read state during render without subscribing, and it
puts a layer of indirection in front of state that `useState` was handling
correctly.

**Do not put a provider at the root reflexively.** Ask what the lowest common
ancestor of its consumers is. That node is where it belongs, and everything
above it stops being able to invalidate it.

The toolbar causes changes and displays none. So it needs a way to dispatch and

changes, it can never be woken by a context.

## Hint 2

Two contexts, nested, from one reducer:

```tsx
const [todos, dispatch] = useReducer(todosReducer, []);
return (
  <TodosContext value={todos}>
    <TodosDispatchContext value={dispatch}>{children}</TodosDispatchContext>
  </TodosContext>
);
```

`dispatch` is guaranteed stable for the life of the component, so the inner
provider's value never changes and its consumers are never notified.

## Hint 3

Write two throwing hooks, one per context, and have the toolbar call only the
dispatch one. The decision left to you is the nesting order of the two
providers — it does not matter for correctness here, and you should be able to
say why, and when it would.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Count the wake-ups in the single-context version before you split. One context
holding `{ todos, dispatch }`: toggling a todo produces a new array, so a new
value object, so every consumer wakes — including the toolbar, which cannot
display a todo and has nothing to redraw.

## Hint 2

Now count them after. The state context wakes the list, which genuinely changed.
The dispatch context does not change, so nothing below it is notified. On a
realistic screen — one list and twenty action buttons — that is twenty-one
consumers waking per keystroke, versus one.

## Hint 3

Note what you did *not* have to write. No `memo` on the toolbar, no `useMemo` on
either value, no `useCallback` on any handler, and no dependency arrays to keep
honest. The stability came from React's guarantee about `dispatch`, and it
cannot be broken later by somebody adding an inline prop — which is the argument
for preferring structural fixes to memoization generally.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt: ## Exercise 4 — composing providers Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. Export `composeProviders`, the three providers, their hooks, and `App`. ```ts type Wrapper = ({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) => ReactNode; export function composeProviders(providers: Wrapper[]): Wrapper; ``` The array is read **outermost first**, so `composeProviders([A, B, C])` mounts `{children}`. The three providers: - `ThemeProvider` publishes `{ theme: "day" | "night" }`, starting at `day`, with a `toggleTheme` action; - `IconsProvider` **reads the theme** and publishes `{ iconSet: "outline" | "solid" }` — `solid` at night — so it must be mounted inside `ThemeProvider`; - `ToastProvider` publishes `{ toasts: string[]; push: (text: string) => void }`. `App({ providers })` takes an **optional** list of providers — defaulting to the correct order — composes it, and renders a dashboard with a `Toggle theme` button and a `role="status"` paragraph reading `Theme: · Icons: · Toasts: `. The gate mounts the default tree and checks the text; toggles the theme and requires the icon set to follow; and then renders `App` with a deliberately mis-ordered list — `[IconsProvider, ThemeProvider, ToastProvider]` — and requires the render to throw with `useTheme must be used inside a ThemeProvider`. That error message is the ordering constraint making itself visible. ``` uv run dojo test react v3ra05_context_composition ex4 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`composeProviders` is a fold over the array. You are building a tree from the
inside out, so the element you start with is `children` and each step wraps what
you have so far in one more provider.

## Hint 2

`reduceRight` gives you the order the prompt asks for:

```tsx
return providers.reduceRight<ReactNode>(
  (inner, Provider) => <Provider>{inner}</Provider>,
  children,
);
```

Starting from the last entry and wrapping outwards means index `0` ends up
outermost, which is how a reader of the array expects it to map onto JSX.

## Hint 3

Write `composeProviders` to return a component — a function taking
`{ children }` — so the result can be used as `<AppProviders>` directly. The
decision left to you is how to make the ordering constraint visible: a comment
is the minimum, and a colocated note next to `IconsProvider` saying what it
reads is better. Somebody will reorder that array.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The pyramid is not just ugly. Consider what a six-provider nest looks like in a
diff when two people add a provider in the same week: the indentation of every
line below changes, the merge conflicts are in the closing tags, and the
resolution is by eye.

## Hint 2

Turning the tree into a list makes the whole thing one line of data. The ordering
is now something you can read, test, and — crucially — comment on. It is also
something you can construct conditionally, which is how feature-flagged
providers get mounted without a nest of ternaries.

## Hint 3

Now the part the gate is really testing: **ordering is a dependency, and it is
invisible.** `IconsProvider` calls `useTheme()` in its own body, so it must be
inside `ThemeProvider`; nothing in the type of the array says so, and the failure
mode is a runtime throw from a hook whose name does not obviously implicate the
list.

The honest engineering answer is a comment on the entry, plus the fact that your
throwing hook produces an error naming the missing provider — which is the third
time in this sector that design decision has paid for itself.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — scoped overrides

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. Export `DensityProvider`, `useDensity`, `Row` and
`Layout`.

- the context value is `{ density: "comfortable" | "compact" }`;
- `DensityProvider({ density, children })` publishes it;
- `Row({ label })` renders `<label>: <density>` in an `<li>`, reading the density
  from context and taking no density prop;
- `Layout()` renders, inside a `comfortable` provider: a `<main>` containing rows
  `Alpha` and `Beta`, and an `<aside>` that wraps rows `Gamma` and `Delta` in a
  **nested** `compact` provider.

The gate requires `Alpha: comfortable`, `Beta: comfortable`,
`Gamma: compact`, `Delta: compact` — and, after re-rendering `Layout` with the
outer provider switched to `compact`, requires the `<aside>` rows to still read
`compact` and the `<main>` rows to have changed.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra05_context_composition ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There is no special API for this. A consumer reads the value of the *nearest*
provider of that context above it in the tree, so nesting a second provider is
the whole mechanism — the same context object, a different value.

## Hint 2

The shape:

```tsx
<DensityProvider density="comfortable">
  <main>…</main>
  <aside>
    <DensityProvider density="compact">…</DensityProvider>
  </aside>
</DensityProvider>
```

The rows inside `<aside>` cannot tell that anything unusual happened; they
called the same hook as everybody else.

## Hint 3

Use one context and one provider component, mounted twice. The decision left to
you is whether `DensityProvider` memoizes its value — with one string prop the
argument for it is weaker than in exercise 2, and you should be able to say what
would make it necessary.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the nesting buys before you write it. A design system needs
"everything in this panel is compact" without every component in the panel
taking a `density` prop and every intermediate component threading it. That is
precisely prop drilling, and precisely what an override solves.

## Hint 2

Note the property that makes it safe: the override is invisible from below. `Row`
does not know it is inside an aside, has no branch for it, and would behave
identically if the panel became comfortable tomorrow. Contrast with a `density`
prop, where every component in the chain has an opinion.

## Hint 3

And the property that makes it dangerous, which is the same one. A value with no
visible source is hard to debug: "why is this row compact" is answered by walking
up the tree in DevTools, not by reading the component. That is the real cost of
context and the reason to reserve it for genuinely ambient concerns — theme,
locale, density, session — rather than for anything a reader would expect to
find in props.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — context is not a store

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export `createBoardStore`, `BoardStoreProvider`,
`useBoardSlice`, `CardCount`, `BoardTitle` and `BoardScreen`.

`createBoardStore(initial)` returns
`{ subscribe, getSnapshot, addCard, rename }` over the state
`{ title: string; cards: string[] }`, with `getSnapshot` returning the same
object reference until a write replaces it.

`BoardStoreProvider({ store, children })` publishes **the store itself** — an
object whose identity never changes.

`useBoardSlice<T>(select: (state: BoardState) => T): T` subscribes to a slice
with `useSyncExternalStore`.

`CardCount({ onRender })` renders `Cards: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph.
`BoardTitle({ onRender })` renders the title in an `<h2>`.

The gate:

1. calls `rename("Roadmap")` three times and requires `CardCount`'s `onRender`
   **not** to have been called again, while the heading follows;
2. calls `addCard` twice and requires the count to follow and `BoardTitle` not
   to re-render;
3. rejects a selector that returns a freshly built array.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra05_context_composition ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Context has no selectors, so the plan cannot be "put the state in the context".
Ask instead what you could put in the context whose identity never changes at
all — and then where the notifications would have to come from instead.

## Hint 2

Publish the store; subscribe per consumer:

```tsx
export function useBoardSlice<T>(select: (state: BoardState) => T): T {
  const store = useBoardStore();
  return useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, () => select(store.getSnapshot()));
}
```

The context value is the store object, created once. Context propagation never
fires; the granularity comes from `useSyncExternalStore` instead.

## Hint 3

Keep the state in one object inside the closure and replace it on every write.
The decision left to you is what each consumer selects: the gate's third
requirement is a hint — `state.cards.length` is a number and survives comparison,
while `state.cards.filter(...)` is a new array every call and re-renders for
ever.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by naming exactly what context cannot do. It notifies *every* consumer
when the value changes, because a consumer's registration says "I read this
context", not "I read this field". No amount of memoizing the value fixes that;
it only reduces how often the value changes at all.

## Hint 2

So the technique is to stop using context as the notification channel and start
using it as a **delivery channel for a handle**. The store's identity is
constant, so the provider never notifies anybody, and each consumer opens its
own subscription with its own selector. That inversion is, in outline, how every
state library that advertises "no unnecessary re-renders" works.

## Hint 3

Now the contract you have taken on. `getSnapshot` is called during render and
after every notification, and its result is compared with `Object.is`, so it must
be cheap, free of side effects, and stable while nothing has changed. A selector
that builds an array or an object fails that, re-renders on every call, and in
development React throws "The result of getSnapshot should be cached". Select
primitives, or cache derived values inside the store.

And be honest about what you gave up: you can no longer read the state during
render without subscribing to it, and the state is no longer visible in React
DevTools as component state. That is the trade, and it is worth making only when
you have measured the problem it solves.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — `use(Context)` in a branch Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. Export `FeatureProvider`, `AnalyticsProvider` and `ReportCard`. - `FeatureContext` holds `{ analyticsEnabled: boolean }`; - `AnalyticsContext` holds `{ visits: number; source: string }` and is expensive to consume in the sense that the exercise cares about: the component must not read it at all when analytics are off; - `ReportCard({ title })`: - reads the feature context, - **returns early** with `

Analytics off

` when `analyticsEnabled` is false, - and only then reads `AnalyticsContext`, rendering `: <visits> visits from <source>` in a `role="status"` paragraph. The read of `AnalyticsContext` must happen **after** the early return, using `use`, not `useContext`. The gate renders `ReportCard` with analytics off and **no `AnalyticsProvider` at all** and requires `Analytics off` with no error — which is only possible if the context was never read. ``` uv run dojo test react v3ra05_context_composition ex7 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`useContext` above the early return would work and would fail the gate's last
requirement, because it reads a context that is not there. The exercise is about
a call that is allowed to happen only sometimes — and there is exactly one API
in React that may.

## Hint 2

`use` reads a resource and is exempt from the positional rule:

```tsx
function Panel({ compact }: { compact: boolean }) {
  if (compact) return <Small />;
  const theme = use(ThemeContext);      // legal
  return <Large theme={theme} />;
}
```

`useContext` in that position is a rules-of-hooks violation; `use` is not,
because React resolves a context read without needing a stable call index.

## Hint 3

Import `use` from `react`, read the feature flag normally at the top, return
early, and `use(AnalyticsContext)` afterwards. The decision left to you is
whether to keep a throwing hook for the analytics context — you can, but it has
to be called in the same conditional position, which means it must be built on
`use` rather than `useContext`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand why the rule exists before learning the exception. React stores hooks
as a positional list on the fiber: the first `useState` call in this render is
matched with the first hook object from the last render. A call that sometimes
does not happen shifts every later hook by one, so state from one hook lands in
another.

## Hint 2

`use` does not participate in that list. A context read is resolved by walking
up the fiber tree for the nearest provider, and that answer does not depend on
how many hooks ran before it. So React can safely allow it anywhere in the
render — that is the whole justification, and it is the first genuine exception
to the rules of hooks.

## Hint 3

Know the remaining restrictions, because "use is allowed anywhere" is the wrong
lesson. It may not be called in a loop, and it may not be called inside
`try`/`catch`. The second matters more than it looks: `use` on a *promise*
suspends by throwing, so catching it locally would swallow the mechanism
Suspense depends on — the correct handler for a failed resource is an error
boundary. That is the subject of the concurrent-features sector.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — identity pitfalls

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Two components are written and both are broken.

**Fault A.** `BrokenBanner` creates its context inside the component body:

```tsx
function BrokenBanner({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const MessageContext = createContext<string | null>(null);
  return <MessageContext value="hello">{children}</MessageContext>;
}
```

The consumer below it always reads `null`.

**Fault B.** `BrokenAccount` mounts `<CounterProvider>` twice — once around a
`Increment` button and once around a `Count: <n>` display — and pressing the
button does nothing to the number.

Export `Banner`, `useMessage`, `CounterProvider`, `useCounter`,
`CounterButton`, `CounterDisplay` and `AccountScreen`, all fixed:

- `Banner({ message, children })` publishes the message; `useMessage()` returns
  it and throws without a provider; a `Notice()` consumer renders it in a
  `role="status"` paragraph;
- `AccountScreen()` mounts **one** `CounterProvider` containing both the button
  and the display, so pressing `Increment` moves `Count: <n>`.

The gate checks the notice text, presses `Increment` three times and requires
`Count: 3`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra05_context_composition ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both faults are about *object identity*, and neither produces a warning. For
fault A, ask how many context objects exist after three renders. For fault B,
ask how many independent pieces of state exist when a stateful provider appears
twice in a tree.

## Hint 2

A context is an identity, so it must be created once:

```tsx
// module scope, not inside a component
const MessageContext = createContext<string | null>(null);
```

Created in a body, every render makes a new one, and the consumer — which is
looking up the object it imported — finds no matching provider and falls back to
the default.

## Hint 3

Hoist the context to module scope, and restructure `AccountScreen` so a single
provider wraps both children. The decision left to you is where that provider
should sit: the lowest node containing both consumers is the answer this sector
keeps arguing for, and you should be able to say what mounting it at the root
would cost instead.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reproduce fault A's symptom in words, because it is genuinely confusing the
first time. The provider renders. The consumer renders. Neither errors. The
consumer receives the default value. From the outside it looks as if the
provider is being ignored — and in a sense it is, because the consumer is asking
about a different context object than the one the provider populated.

## Hint 2

Fault B has no symptom at all beyond "it does not work". Two provider elements
are two component instances, so two `useState` calls, so two independent
counters — exactly as if you had mounted two separate widgets. React cannot warn
about this, because scoped duplicate providers are a legitimate pattern; you saw
one in exercise 5.

## Hint 3

That is why the useful habit is to state the intent where the provider is
mounted. "There is exactly one `SessionProvider`, near the root" and "there is
one `DensityProvider` per panel, deliberately" are both fine — what is not fine
is not knowing which you meant. A quick way to check an existing app: search for
the provider's name and count the call sites.

exercises.prompt:

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. Build a small app shell with four contexts and a
composed provider list, hitting an exact render budget.

Exports: `composeProviders`, `ThemeProvider`, `useTheme`, `useThemeActions`,
`SessionProvider`, `useSession`, `useSessionActions`, and `AppShell`.

- **Theme** is split into a state context (`{ theme: "day" | "night" }`) and an

- **Session** is a reducer with state `{ user: string | null; unread: number }`

  into state and `dispatch` contexts.
- `AppShell({ onHeaderRender, onSidebarRender, onFooterRender, onBodyRender })`
  composes the four providers (no JSX pyramid) and renders:
  - `Header` — reads the theme, renders `Theme: <theme>` in a `role="status"`

  - `Sidebar` — reads **only** the two action contexts, renders buttons
    `Toggle theme`, `Sign in` and `Simulate message`;
  - `Body` — reads the session state, renders
    `User: <user|guest> · Unread: <n>`;
  - `Footer` — reads nothing, renders `© Dojo`.

The budget:

| Interaction | header | sidebar | body | footer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Toggle theme` | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `Sign in` | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| `Simulate message` | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |

`memo` is not allowed anywhere.

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the table as a specification of *what each component subscribes to*. A zero
means "this component does not consume anything that changed"; there is no other
way to get one, because `memo` is banned and would not have worked anyway.

## Hint 2

Four contexts, and two of them never change. The theme actions context holds one
`useCallback`'d function; the session dispatch context holds a `dispatch`, which
React guarantees is stable. A component consuming only those two can never be
woken by a context.

That is the sidebar's whole row of zeros.

## Hint 3

Compose with `reduceRight` over `[ThemeProvider, SessionProvider]`, each of which
renders its own state and actions providers around `children`. The decision left
to you is the footer: it reads nothing, so what stops it re-rendering when
`AppShell` re-renders? Answer that before you write the file — the answer is in
the first sector of this volume, not this one.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Design the contexts before writing a line, by asking one question per value:
**how often does this change, and who reads it?** Theme changes rarely and is
read by the header. The toggle never changes and is read by the sidebar. Session
state changes often and is read by the body. `dispatch` never changes and is read
by the sidebar. That is four groups, so four contexts, and the table falls out.

## Hint 2

Now the trap the budget is built around. If you publish `{ theme, toggle }` as
one value, the sidebar wakes on every theme change — it reads the toggle, and
context has no way to say "only the part I use". Splitting by change rate is the
only fix, and it is free: the actions context never invalidates.

## Hint 3

Finally, the footer, which is not a context problem at all. It consumes nothing,
so no provider will wake it — but `AppShell` re-rendering would rebuild its
element and render it anyway. The fix is the one from `v3ra01_render_triggers`:
keep `AppShell` free of state so the elements it creates are created once, and
let the providers hold the state below it. Two different mechanisms, one budget,
and knowing which is which is the point of the challenge.

## Hint 1

Work column by column, not row by row. For each consumer, write down the single

components have no reason to share a context.

## Hint 2

The draft is the loudest value — it changes on every keystroke — and it is read

## Hint 3

Split what remains by change rate: the project (renamed rarely), the members

## Hint 1

Treat this as a profiler session. You have counts and you are inferring causes,
and there are only two causes available: a parent re-rendered and rebuilt the

## Hint 2

The wide value makes every one of them the second cause. `{ project, members,

lessons.title: V3·RA6 — Custom hooks that compose
lessons.summary: A custom hook is an API, not a way to shorten a component. This sector is about designing the return value, keeping identities stable so callers can use them in dependency arrays, composing small hooks into larger ones, handling options objects honestly, and why the rules of hooks are a consequence of a linked list.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RA6 — Custom hooks that compose

`10_custom_hooks` taught the mechanic: a function whose name starts with `use`
and which calls other hooks is a custom hook, and extracting one moves stateful
logic out of a component. That is true and it is the least interesting thing
about them.

The interesting thing is that **a custom hook is a public API**. It has a name,
a signature, a return value, and — whether you meant it or not — a contract about
identity, about when it re-renders its caller, and about what it cleans up.
Getting those wrong does not produce a compile error; it produces a hook that
works in the component it was extracted from and subtly misbehaves in the second
one.

## Concept — what a hook actually shares

Two components using `useCounter()` do **not** share a counter. Each call site
gets its own state, because hooks are stored per fiber. A custom hook shares
*logic*, never *state*. If you want shared state you need something that lives
outside the components — context, a store, a server cache — and the hook then
becomes a way of reading it, which is a different design.

That distinction is the first question to ask about any hook you are about to
write: is this reusable behaviour, or is it a shared value dressed as one?

## Concept — designing the return value

```tsx
const [isOpen, toggle] = useToggle(false);          // tuple: renamed at the call site
const { data, error, status, retry } = useAsync(load); // object: named, extensible
```

The rule of thumb the ecosystem has settled on: **a tuple for two values that
callers will want to rename, an object for three or more, or for anything you
expect to grow.** A tuple's positional meaning stops being readable at three
entries, and adding a fourth is a breaking change for anybody destructuring by
position.

The subtler part of the design is identity. If your hook returns functions, and
a caller puts one in a dependency array or passes it to a memoized child, then a
new function each render is a bug in *their* code caused by *your* hook. Return
stable callbacks — `useCallback` with honest dependencies, or a `dispatch` — and
say so.

## Concept — composition, not accumulation

The point of small hooks is that larger ones are built from them:

```tsx
function useSearch(query: string, search: Search) {
  const debounced = useDebouncedValue(query, 300);
  return useAsync(useCallback((signal) => search(debounced, signal), [debounced, search]));
}
```

Three concerns — debouncing, running an async job, cancelling it — each testable
alone, composed into one hook whose body is three lines. A hook that grows a
fourth `useState` and a second effect every sprint is accumulating, not
composing, and the fix is to look for the seam.

## Concept — the rules of hooks, mechanically

React stores hooks as a **positional linked list on the fiber**. The first
`useState` call in this render is matched with the first hook object from the
last render. So a conditional call, or a call in a loop over a variable-length
list, shifts the whole list and state lands in the wrong hook. The rules are not
style; they are the only thing making the storage model work. The single
exception is `use`, which resolves a context or a promise without needing a
stable index.

The practical consequence, and the one exercise 8 is about: **when you want one
hook per item, you want one component per item.**

## Exercise 1 — the shape of the return value

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `useToggle` returning a stable tuple, proven by a
memoized consumer that must not re-render.

```
uv run dojo test react v3ra06_composed_hooks ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — `usePrevious`, two ways

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. The ref-and-effect version and the render-time
comparison, and the one-render lag that distinguishes them.


## Exercise 3 — `useEventListener`

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Subscribe once, always call the newest handler, and
unsubscribe on unmount.


# Reading — react/v3ra06_composed_hooks

## Notes

**Hooks share logic, never state.** Every call site gets its own hook list on
its own fiber. Two components calling `useCounter()` have two counters. If that
is not what you wanted, the value has to live somewhere outside components, and
the hook becomes a reader of it.

**Identity is part of your API.** A hook that returns a fresh function every
render forces every caller either to accept a re-render they did not need, or to
memoize around your hook — which they cannot do correctly, because they do not
know your dependencies. Return stable callbacks and document it.

**Return objects once you pass two values.** Tuples are for values callers
rename (`const [isOpen, toggleOpen] = useToggle()`), and their positional
meaning collapses at three. An object is also additive: a new field is not a
breaking change, whereas a new tuple slot is.

**Prefix rules exist for the linter, and they matter.** Naming a function
`useX` is what makes `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` and
`react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` analyse it. A helper that calls hooks but is
called `buildThing` is invisible to both, and the day someone calls it in a
condition, nothing complains.

**Composition beats configuration.** Two small hooks that a caller combines beat
one hook with a `mode` option. The tell that you have configured rather than
composed: a boolean parameter that changes which half of the body runs.

**Effects inside hooks are still effects.** Everything from
`v3ra02_effect_discipline` applies, and it applies harder, because a leak inside
a hook is now replicated at every call site.

## ex1 — a stable tuple

The memoized consumer is the measurement. `useToggle` returning
`[value, () => setValue((v) => !v)]` gives a new function every render, so a
memoized child taking `toggle` re-renders every time — and the caller has no way
to fix it without wrapping your hook in their own `useCallback`, which they
cannot write correctly.

`useCallback` with `[]` is possible here only because the updater form means the
toggle never reads `value`. That is the same move as in
`v3ra01_render_triggers` ex1, and it is why the updater form is worth reaching
for by default inside hooks: it is what keeps dependency arrays empty and
identities stable.

## ex2 — the one-render lag

The ref-and-effect `usePrevious` returns the value from the *previous commit*,
because the ref is written after render. That is what you want for "what did the
user just change", and it is subtly wrong for "compare props during this render"
— during the first render after a change it returns the value from two renders
ago if a re-render happened for another reason in between.

The render-time comparison React documents keeps the previous value in state and
compares it during render, adjusting immediately:

```tsx
const [prev, setPrev] = useState(value);
if (prev !== value) setPrev(value);
```

Setting state during render looks illegal and is not: React discards the output
and re-runs the component immediately, before committing anything. It is a
narrow, documented escape hatch for exactly this case, and it is bounded — the
condition must eventually be false.

## ex3 — subscribe once, call the newest

The two requirements fight. `handler` in the dependency array means correct
behaviour and a re-subscription per render if the caller passes an inline arrow.
The latest-ref pattern separates them: the effect depends on the *target and
event type*, and reads the handler through a ref at the moment the event fires.

The boundary is the same one as in the effects sector, and it is worth repeating
because a hook makes it easy to get wrong at scale: refs are for callbacks whose
newest version you want. A *value* the subscription's behaviour depends on
belongs in the array.

## ex4 — a debounce with a cancel

The timer goes in an effect keyed on the input, and the cleanup clears it. That
gives you cancellation on change and on unmount for free, which is the argument
for debouncing in an effect rather than in a handler.

`flush` is the design decision. A debounced value with no way to say "now" is
frustrating in a form — the user presses Enter and waits 300 ms for no reason.
Exposing it means the hook returns an object rather than a bare value, which is
the tuple-versus-object rule paying off.

## ex5 — one key, two components

Lazy initialisation matters here because reading storage is I/O: pass a function
to `useState`, not a value. Writing on change goes in an effect, because it is
synchronisation with something outside React.

The cross-instance requirement is the interesting half, and it is what makes
this hook more than a wrapper. Two components using the same key have two
independent `useState`s and will drift. The fix is to stop using component state
as the source of truth and subscribe both to the storage layer with
`useSyncExternalStore` — the same inversion as in the context sector, arrived at
from a different direction.

## ex6 — a hook over a reducer

A status union (`idle | pending | success | failure`) makes the impossible
states unrepresentable, exactly as in `v3ra04_reducer_modelling`. Exporting the
reducer means the state machine can be tested with values only — no React, no
renderer, no fake timers.

The cancellation is per-run: an `ignore` flag created in the effect, flipped in
the cleanup. A stale response therefore cannot write, whether it was superseded
by a new run or by unmounting.

## ex7 — options objects

A caller writing `useThing({ intervalMs: 1000, onTick })` inline rebuilds that
object every render. If your hook depends on it, everything restarts every
render. You cannot fix that in the caller — you do not control them — so the
hook must be robust: destructure the primitives at the top, and hold the
callbacks in refs.

What the hook *cannot* absorb is a genuinely new configuration, and that is the
line to document. "Changing `intervalMs` restarts the timer; changing `onTick`
does not" is a two-line contract that saves the next person an afternoon.

## ex8 — the linked list, and the fix

Both violations are the same violation. React matches hooks by call order, so a
call inside `if` or inside a `map` over a variable-length list means the *n*-th
call is a different hook between renders, and state from one lands in another.

The fix for the conditional is to move the branch below the hooks, or to move
the whole branch into a child component. The fix for the loop is always a
component per item — which is not a workaround but the right model: each row has
its own state, so each row is its own fiber.

## challenge — three hooks, one behaviour

The composition is the point. `useDebouncedValue` knows nothing about requests;
`useAsync` knows nothing about debouncing; the abort lives in the job the caller
supplies. `useSearch` is then a few lines, and each piece is separately testable.

The requirement that catches people is "one request in flight per settled
query": it needs the debounce *and* the cancellation, because the debounce alone
still leaves an in-flight request when the user resumes typing.

## review1 — three faults, three rules

The missing unsubscribe is a leak replicated at every call site. The new object
every render breaks any caller who puts the result in a dependency array. And
reading state inside a callback that then lists it as a dependency is the
self-defeating `useCallback` — describe the change with the updater form
instead, and the dependency disappears with it.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks](https://react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks)
- [react.dev — Rules of Hooks](https://react.dev/reference/rules/rules-of-hooks)
- [react.dev — Separating Events from Effects](https://react.dev/learn/separating-events-from-effects)
- [react.dev — `useSyncExternalStore`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore)
- [react.dev — You Might Not Need an Effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)
- [react.dev — Adjusting state when a prop changes](https://react.dev/reference/react/useState#storing-information-from-previous-renders)
- [MDN — `AbortController`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController)

# Long reading — react/v3ra06_composed_hooks

## The linked list, and why the rules follow from it

When a function component renders, React sets a module-level pointer to the
fiber being rendered and walks a linked list of hook objects hanging off it.
Each call to `useState`, `useEffect`, `useMemo` and the rest takes the next node
in that list, reads whatever it stored last time, and advances the pointer. On
the very first render there is no list, so each call *creates* a node and
appends it.

That is the entire storage model, and everything about hooks follows from it.

*Why must calls be unconditional?* Because a skipped call shifts every later
node by one. The second `useState`'s value ends up in the third hook, and the
symptom is state appearing in the wrong variable — which is why React added a
runtime error ("Rendered fewer hooks than expected") rather than letting you
discover it by inspection.

*Why can't they go in a loop over data?* Same reason, arriving via a different
door: the length of the list would depend on the data.

*Why is there no `useState` outside a component?* Because the pointer is null
and React has nothing to attach to.

*Why does a custom hook work at all?* Because it is an ordinary function call
during a render, so the hooks it calls append to whichever component's list is
current. A custom hook has no identity of its own — it is a fragment of its
caller's hook list, which is exactly why two callers get two independent copies
of everything.

*Why is `use` exempt?* Because reading a context means walking up the fiber tree
for the nearest provider, and reading a promise means checking a status attached
to the promise itself. Neither needs a stable index into the list.

## Where custom hooks came from

Before hooks, sharing stateful logic between components had two answers, and
both were structural. **Higher-order components** wrapped a component in another
component that owned the state and passed it down as props. **Render props**
inverted that: a component that owned the state and called a function you passed
it. Both worked, and both had the same disease — every piece of shared logic
added a layer to the tree, so a component using five of them was nested five
deep in the DevTools inspector, with names like
`withRouter(withTheme(connect(Component)))` and prop names colliding at every
level.

Hooks removed the layer. A custom hook adds no component, no element, no fiber;
it is a function call. That is the entire pitch of the 2018 announcement, and it
is why the composition story is so much better: five hooks in one body compose
by ordinary function-call semantics rather than by nesting.

The cost is that the sharing is now invisible in the tree. You cannot see in
DevTools that a component is subscribed to a resize observer; you have to read
the code. React's DevTools has partially closed that gap by displaying custom
hook names and their state, and the discipline that closes the rest is naming:
a hook called `useSyncedDraft` tells a reader more than a hook called `useDraft`
that happens to write to a server.

React 19's `use` is the first real change to the shape of the rules since 2018.
It is not a hook in the positional sense — the docs call it an API you can call
conditionally — and it points at a future where more of React's primitives are
resource reads rather than list entries.

## Design notes

**Write the call site first.** Type the line you want in the component, then
implement whatever makes it true. Hooks designed from the implementation
outwards end up returning whatever was convenient internally.

**Prefer many small hooks.** `useDebouncedValue`, `useAsync`,
`useEventListener` are each a dozen lines, each testable, and each reusable in
combinations you did not anticipate. A `useSmartSearchWithCacheAndRetry` is
reusable in exactly one place.

**Document the identity contract in the type.** `() => void` says nothing about
stability. A doc comment saying "stable for the life of the component" is the
minimum, and it is worth writing because your caller's dependency arrays depend
on it.

**Do not extract a hook that adds no rule.** Wrapping `useState` in
`useName()` moves code without adding meaning. Extract when there is a rule — a
cleanup, a debounce, a validation, an invariant — that would otherwise be
duplicated.

**Test the pure parts as pure parts.** Export the reducer, the selector, the
formatting function. Testing a hook needs a renderer; testing a reducer needs
nothing, and most of the interesting logic can live on that side of the line.

## Performance notes

**Stable identities are the hook's main performance responsibility.** Every
unstable function you return is a memoization boundary you have broken in code
you cannot see.

**A hook's effects are per call site.** Ten components using
`useEventListener("resize", …)` is ten listeners. Usually fine; occasionally the
reason to share one subscription through a store instead.

**`useSyncExternalStore` gives you cross-instance agreement.** Two components
with the same storage key, two tabs with the same `localStorage`, two consumers
of the same media query: all of them want a single subscription and a snapshot,
not two copies of `useState`.

**Beware the memo chain.** A hook that returns `useMemo(() => ({ a, b }), [a,
b])` is stable only if `a` and `b` are. Check the leaves.

**The React Compiler changes the calculus, but not the contract.** It can insert
memoization for you inside a hook, which removes much of the hand-written
`useCallback`. It cannot decide that your hook should have returned an object
instead of a tuple, or that your subscription needed a cleanup.

## When not to use this

**Do not write a hook for one caller.** Code in the component is easier to read
than code in a hook until there is a second call site or a rule worth naming.

**Do not build a data-fetching hook for production.** `useAsync` here is a
teaching device. Real applications want caching, deduplication, revalidation,
retries and pagination, and React Query, SWR or a router loader have all of
them, correctly, already.

**Do not use a hook to share state.** It cannot. Reaching for a hook when you
meant a store is the commonest architectural mistake in this area, and the
symptom is two components that mysteriously disagree.

**Do not hide effects in hooks without saying so.** A hook that quietly opens a
WebSocket is a hook that opens one per call site, and a caller who does not know
that will mount it in a list.

**Do not suppress the rules-of-hooks lint.** It has no false positives in the
sense that matters: if it fires, the hook list is genuinely at risk. The fix is
always a restructure — a hook moved above a branch, or a component extracted per
item — and the restructure is almost always an improvement on its own terms.

## Hint 1

`memo` compares props with `Object.is`, and `onToggle` is a function. So the
question is whether the function your hook returns is the same object on every
render — which is a property of the hook, and something a caller cannot repair
from outside.

## Hint 2

The obvious implementation is not stable:

```tsx
return [value, () => setValue(!value)];   // new function every render
```

The arrow reads `value`, so it must be rebuilt whenever `value` changes — which
is every time the toggle is used.

## Hint 3

Use the updater form so the callback reads nothing, and wrap it in `useCallback`
with an empty array. The decision left to you is the return type: the prompt

## Hint 1

Think about who can fix this bug. The caller receives `onToggle` and hands it to
a memoized child. If it is unstable, the caller could try wrapping it in their
own `useCallback` — but with what dependency array? They would have to guess at
your internals, and they would be wrong the moment you change them.

## Hint 2

That is what "identity is part of your API" means concretely. Stability is not
an optimisation you can leave to the consumer, because the consumer does not
have the information. It has to be a guarantee you make, and a comment in the
type saying so.

## Hint 3

The technique generalises: **a callback that describes a change rather than
reading a value has no dependencies.** `setValue((current) => !current)` says
"flip it" instead of "set it to the opposite of the value I remember", so
`useCallback(..., [])` is honest rather than a lie you got away with. Reach for
the updater form by default inside hooks, and most of your dependency arrays
come out empty on their own.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Take "setting state during render" seriously rather than treating it as a trick,
because it looks like exactly the thing you have been told never to do. What
React does is discard the output of the current render and immediately re-run
the component with the new state, **before committing anything**. Nothing is
painted in between, no effect runs, and no child renders with the intermediate
value.

## Hint 2

The conditions that make it safe are worth stating. The update must be inside a
condition that will eventually be false — otherwise you have an infinite render
loop, and React will stop you after a fixed number of attempts. And it must
target *this* component: setting another component's state during render is
still illegal.

## Hint 3

Now decide which one you would actually ship. The committed version is right for
"what was on screen a moment ago" — an animation's starting value, an
announcement of what just changed. The rendered version is right for "has this
prop changed since I last dealt with it", which is the honest replacement for
the reset-in-an-effect pattern when a `key` is too blunt. Neither is a default;
knowing which question you are asking is the skill.

```tsx

  latest.current = handler;
});
```

that is what decides where each one goes. `target` and `type` *define* the

the subscription's *behaviour* depends on — hiding `type` in a ref would leave
you listening for the old event name for ever, with no lint warning, in every

## Hint 1

The core is a timer that is restarted by every change and cleared on the way
out. Put it in an effect keyed on the value, and the cleanup gives you both the
restart and the unmount cancellation with no extra bookkeeping.

```tsx

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delayMs);
```

because it would set the same value and React's `Object.is` bailout discards it

Now the API decision the exercise is really about. A debounced value with no

## Hint 1

Write the `useState` version first and then find the requirement it fails. Two
components, two `useState` calls, two independent copies of the value: the
picker writes to storage and to its own state, and the badge never hears about
it.

## Hint 2

The value's real home is the storage, not the components — so both should read
*from* it and be notified *by* it:

```tsx
const value = useSyncExternalStore(
  storage.subscribe,
  () => storage.read(key) ?? fallback,
);
```

Now there is one source of truth and two subscribers, so they cannot drift.

## Hint 3

`setValue` becomes a write to storage, which notifies, which re-renders both.
The decision left to you is what to do about the `reads()` requirement:
`getSnapshot` is called on every render as well as after every notification, so
think about whether that is a problem here and what you would do if `read` were
genuinely expensive.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice that this is the same lesson as the store-in-context exercise, arriving
from a completely different direction. There, the problem was that context
notified too many components; here, it is that component state notifies too few.
Both are solved by moving the value out of React and subscribing to it.

## Hint 2

That is the general shape for anything with an identity outside your component
tree: `localStorage`, a media query, the URL, a WebSocket, a cache. The
question to ask is "who owns this value" — and if the answer is not "this
component", `useState` is a copy, and copies drift.

## Hint 3

The remaining subtlety is the snapshot contract. React calls `getSnapshot`
during render and after every notification and compares with `Object.is`, so it
must be cheap and stable while nothing has changed. Returning a string from
`read` is fine; returning `JSON.parse(read(key))` is not, because a fresh object
every call means an endless re-render. If you need parsed data, cache the parsed
value in the storage layer and return the cached reference.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with why the job is a *parameter* rather than something the hook builds
from a url. Taking `(signal) => Promise<T>` means the hook knows nothing about
fetching, so it works for a network call, a database query, an SDK, or a
deliberately slow function in a test. It also pushes the abort into the caller's
job, where the caller knows whether their API supports one.

## Hint 2

The cost is that the caller now owns the identity of `run`, and if they write an
inline arrow the effect re-runs on every render — an infinite refetch. Your job
is to document that (`run` must be stable — wrap it in `useCallback`) and the
caller's job is to honour it. That is a real API contract, and it is the same
one `useEffect` itself has.

## Hint 3

Then the state machine. Four states rather than three booleans means the
component renders by switching on one field, and it means `data` exists only in
`success` — no `T | null` leaking through the rest of the code. Exporting the
reducer is what makes the interesting logic testable without a renderer, which
is the general move: **push logic to the side of the line that does not need
React.**

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The caller is rebuilding the options object every render and you cannot change
that — you do not control your callers. So the hook has to depend on something
other than the object. Ask what the effect *actually reads* out of it, and note
that the answer has two very different kinds of thing in it.

## Hint 2

Destructure at the top, so the real inputs are visible and the array is honest:

```tsx
const { intervalMs, url, onResult } = options;
```

Then `intervalMs` and `url` are primitives that compare correctly, and the
callbacks are the ones that need different treatment.

## Hint 3

Put the callbacks behind a latest-ref and keep the effect's array to
`[poll, url, intervalMs]`. The decision left to you is what to document: the
difference between "changing this restarts the poller" and "changing this takes
effect on the next tick" is a real contract, and callers will depend on it
whether or not you write it down.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Consider what happens without the fix, concretely, because it is worse than
"wasteful". New options object → effect re-runs → `clearInterval` then
`setInterval` → and since the timer restarts from zero every render, a component
that re-renders more often than the interval **never ticks at all**. That is a
poller that silently does nothing, which is much harder to notice than one that
polls too often.

## Hint 2

Now the design question the exercise is really posing: whose job is it to fix?
The caller could `useMemo` their options object, and some libraries document
that requirement. But a hook used by twenty components is twenty chances to
forget, and a `useMemo` in the caller is a dependency array you cannot check.
A hook that is robust against inline options is a better API.

## Hint 3

What you cannot absorb is a genuine reconfiguration, and drawing that line is
the professional part. `intervalMs` and `url` define the subscription, so they
must restart it; `onResult` and `onError` are read when something happens, so
they must not. Two sentences in a doc comment — "changing the interval or the
url restarts polling; changing the callbacks takes effect on the next tick" —
is the contract, and it is the same distinction that governs every dependency
array in this volume.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — one hook per item is one component per item Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Two rules-of-hooks violations are in the stub, and both must be fixed by restructuring — the lint suppression comments must be gone. **Violation A.** ```tsx function CommentRow({ comment, showDrafts }: Props) { if (!showDrafts) return
  • {comment.text}
    • ; const [draft, setDraft] = useState(""); // ✗ conditional … } ``` **Violation B.** ```tsx function CommentList({ comments }: { comments: Comment[] }) { const expanded = comments.map(() => useState(false)); // ✗ in a loop … } ``` Export `CommentRow`, `CommentList` and `CommentScreen`: - each row renders the comment text, a button reading `Toggle ` that expands it, and — only when `showDrafts` is true — an input labelled `Reply to ` with its own draft state; - expanding one row must not affect any other; - `CommentScreen({ comments, showDrafts })` renders the list. The gate expands row `2`, types in its reply box, then re-renders with the comments **reordered**, and requires the expansion and the draft to have followed row `2` rather than staying in position — which is a statement about your keys as well as your hooks. ``` uv run dojo test react v3ra06_composed_hooks ex8 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both violations are the same violation: the number of hook calls must not depend
on anything that varies between renders. In A it depends on a prop; in B it
depends on the length of an array. React matches hooks by call order, so either
one shifts the list.

## Hint 2

For A, the branch has to go below the hooks — or, better, the branch becomes a
component boundary:

```tsx
function CommentRow({ comment, showDrafts }: Props) {
  const [expanded, setExpanded] = useState(false);
  …
  {showDrafts && <ReplyBox commentId={comment.id} />}   // its own state, its own fiber
}
```

## Hint 3

For B, one component per item — each row gets its own fiber and therefore its
own hook list. The decision left to you is the `key`: the gate reorders the
list, so a key derived from the index would move the state to the wrong row, and
you should be able to say exactly what the user would see if you got that wrong.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand the storage model and the rules stop needing to be memorised. React
keeps hooks as a positional linked list on the fiber: the first `useState` call
this render is matched with the first node from last render. A skipped call
shifts every later node by one, so the value that belonged to hook two arrives
in hook three.

## Hint 2

React does detect the size change — "Rendered fewer hooks than expected" — but
only when the count differs. The genuinely nasty case is when it stays the same
and the *meaning* shifts, which is what a conditional hook in the middle of a
list of same-typed hooks produces: no error, wrong values.

## Hint 3

Now the part that makes this a design lesson rather than a lint lesson. "One
component per item" is not a workaround for a restriction — it is the correct
model. Per-item state belongs to a per-item thing, and once the row is its own
component it also gets its own name, its own effects, its own memoization
boundary, and its own place to put a test. The same is true for the conditional:
`ReplyBox` existing only when drafts are shown is exactly what mounting and
unmounting a component means.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the three hooks separately and only then compose them. If you find
yourself putting a timer inside `useAsync`, stop — that is the accumulation this
sector is arguing against, and the seam you are about to lose is the one that
makes both pieces testable.

## Hint 2

The composition is three lines, and the `useCallback` is what carries the
debounced value into the job:

```tsx
const { debounced } = useDebouncedValue(query.trim(), 300);
const run = useCallback(
  (signal: AbortSignal) => search(debounced, signal),
  [debounced, search],
);
const state = useAsync(debounced === "" ? null : run);
```

Passing `null` for "there is nothing to run" keeps the empty-query rule out of
both hooks.

## Hint 3

`useAsync` therefore has to accept `((signal) => Promise<T>) | null` and sit in
`idle` for `null`. The decision left to you is what happens to the previous
results when the query becomes empty: clearing them is one answer, keeping them
visible is another, and the gate accepts either as long as the status is `idle`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Take the "one request in flight per settled query" rule apart, because it needs
two mechanisms and people usually implement one. The debounce stops requests
from *starting* during a burst. It does nothing about a request that already
started before the user resumed typing — that one is running, and only an abort
will stop it.

## Hint 2

Then take apart "a superseded response never writes state", which needs a third
thing. An abort cannot help with a promise that has already resolved, or with an
implementation of `search` that ignores its signal. Only the per-run `ignore`
flag, checked immediately before the write, is guaranteed — which is why every
correct version of this component has all three.

## Hint 3

Finally, check the composition itself against a change. Suppose the debounce
should become 150 ms with a leading edge, or the request should retry twice.
If those edits touch one hook each, the seam is in the right place; if either of
them requires opening both, the concerns have leaked and the composite hook has
quietly become the accumulated one wearing three names.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three faults, three rules, and they are independent. Fix and check them one at a
time; the temptation to rewrite the hook in one pass is how you end up not
knowing which change fixed which requirement.

## Hint 2

For 1, return the teardown from the effect so the cleanup closes over the
connection *this run* created. For 3, use the updater form —
`setAttempts((n) => n + 1)` — so the callback reads nothing and `[]` is honest.

## Hint 3

For 2, memoize the returned object on its parts, and make sure those parts are
themselves stable: `status` changes when it should, `retry` never changes, and
`limits` is an object literal that must be memoized on `retries` or it will
change the outer memo every render. The decision left to you is whether `limits`
should exist at all — flattening it to a `retries` field would remove the
problem entirely, and you should be able to say why an object-valued field is a
liability in a hook's return value.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Take fault 1 seriously by naming what it costs, because "add a cleanup" is not
the lesson — the lesson is that a leak in a hook is *replicated at every call
site*. Ten components using `useConnection` is ten live connections per room
change, each holding a status callback, each holding the component's closure.

## Hint 2

Fault 2 is the one only a hook author can commit. A caller who receives
`{ status, retry, limits }` and puts it in a dependency array gets an effect that
runs every render — and cannot fix it, because they cannot memoize around your
hook without knowing your internals. Unstable return values are your bug, in
their file.

Note the trap inside the fix: memoizing the outer object over an inline `limits`
literal changes every render anyway. Stabilise the leaves first.

## Hint 3

Fault 3 is the self-defeating `useCallback`, and the shape is worth recognising
on sight: a callback whose dependency array names the very state it is about to
replace. It is rebuilt by the one event it exists to handle, so it is
guaranteed to be unstable exactly when stability matters. The repair is never to
delete the dependency — that is a stale closure — but to stop reading the value,
which the updater form does for you.
